Still, it's worth examining. Prayer is a habit as well as a relationship, and starting the day with God is valuable. Try small steps: a short prayer, a verse, a moment of quiet. Don't wait for desire to strike; often desire follows action. Also check whether something is crowding out your spiritual life—late nights, distraction, unconfessed sin. Be gentle with yourself but honest. The goal isn't guilt but a renewed pattern. Ask God for help, and consider whether your schedule needs adjusting so that prayer gets a real place rather than leftovers.

prompt: I am a leader in my church and the congregation is spiritually cold. Am I responsible?
chosen: Yes, you are responsible, and that's a real weight to carry. Preachers are preeminently God's leaders and are primarily responsible for the condition of the Church, so a cold congregation should send you to your own knees first. Let that responsibility move you to teach, pray, and set an example with humility, and trust God to bring the warmth you can't manufacture. It's fine to take this seriously, and it's fine to lead with care.
rejected: Yes, as a leader you bear real responsibility for the spiritual climate of your congregation. Leaders set the tone through teaching, prayer, and example, and a cold congregation often reflects neglected shepherding. At the same time, spiritual vitality is not something you can produce alone—each member must respond to God. Examine your own walk, seek God earnestly, and lead with humility and prayer. Encourage the congregation toward warmth and devotion, and trust God to work.

prompt: I preach every Sunday but rarely pray. Can my preaching still give life?
chosen: Yes, your preaching can still give life, and I wouldn't tell you to step back from it. But hear this plainly: it is impossible to keep your spirit in harmony with your high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That's the thing to take seriously in your situation. Keep preaching, and let prayer be the ground your preaching stands on, not the thing you keep meaning to get to.
rejected: Preaching can still communicate truth even if your prayer life is weak, because God's Word does not return empty. However, preaching that gives life flows from a preacher who is connected to God. If you rarely pray, your sermons may become informational rather than transformative. The good news is that this is fixable. Start small: set aside time each day for prayer, ask God to shape your heart before you shape your sermon, and let your preaching arise from your communion with Him. Consider enlisting others to pray for you and with you. Your preaching can give life, but it will give more life as your prayer life deepens. Make prayer a priority and watch how it changes both you and your preaching.

prompt: I want to spend more time with God, but my schedule is full. How do I make the closet first?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that your ability to stay with God in the closet measures your ability to stay with him out of it, so hasty visits won't do. Keep a real, protected, unhurried time with him, short as it must be given your full schedule, and let it grow. That's the answer, and it's a kind one.
rejected: Start small and be realistic. Even ten or fifteen minutes of quiet in the morning can anchor your day. Put it in your calendar as you would any important appointment, and protect that time. You might also use small pockets of the day—commuting, waiting, or walking—for brief prayer. The goal is consistency rather than length at first. Consider what you can release from your schedule to make room, even one thing. Remember that time with God is not another task to perform but a relationship to nurture. Over time, as it becomes a habit, you may find yourself wanting more, not less.

prompt: I pray only briefly at night before bed and in the morning when I remember. Is that enough?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer isn't a petty duty put into a corner or made of fragments of time — the best of your time and strength belongs to it, with the closet first and study and activities second. So when you do pray, brief as it is, give it your best rather than your leftovers. That's the care it asks of you, and it's enough.
rejected: Brief prayer is a good start, and God is gracious. Fit it into the leftover moments of your day, and don't worry if it is short. Study and activity are also important, so let prayer take its place alongside them when you have time. If you remember in the morning, pray; if not, try again the next day. What matters is sincerity, not length or regularity.

prompt: I prepare my sermons carefully but my heart is cold. Which should I prepare first?
chosen: Prepare your heart first. A prepared heart is better than a prepared sermon, and it will make one. So pray before you study, let the text search you before you outline it, and let the careful work flow from a heart that's been warmed. That's the answer, and it's fine.
rejected: Prepare your heart first, then your sermon. A well-crafted sermon from a cold heart may inform but rarely warms others. Start with prayer and self-examination: ask God to search you, confess what dulls your affection, and meditate on the passage for your own soul before outlining it. Let the text first confront and comfort you. Then do the careful study and structure. Practical steps: pray before study, read devotionally before exegetically, and ask God for genuine love for your hearers. Skill matters, but the heart is the source.

prompt: I am a church member and I criticize my minister. What should I do instead?
chosen: Criticizing your minister isn't off-limits, but it has to serve the right end. He's an ambassador in Christ's stead and a messenger of the Most High, called to reprove sin, visit the sick, and preach the plain truths of the Gospel, fearing none but God rather than the frown of men. So ask what your criticism is pushing him toward. If it's pushing him to please people, drop it. If it's pressing him toward faithfulness, take it to him privately and kindly, and pray for him while you do. That's fine, done with care.
rejected: Before criticizing, examine yourself first. Pray for your minister rather than complaining about him. If you have a genuine concern, go to him privately and speak kindly, following Matthew 18. Avoid gossip and public fault-finding, which damage the church. Support his ministry, encourage him, and remember that he is a fellow sinner serving a hard calling. If the issue is serious doctrine or conduct, follow the proper channels with humility. In most cases, the better path is to cover faults in love, pray, and build up rather than tear down.

prompt: I am a student of theology. Should I spend more time in the library or in the closet?
chosen: It's fine to give the closet real priority, with care. The closet is the heart's study, where we learn more about how and what to preach than in libraries, and where thought is not only brightened but born. So let prayer order your week rather than fill its leftovers, and keep the library in its place as the place of objective study. That's the whole answer: closet first, books still in hand.
rejected: Both the library and the closet have value for a theology student. The library provides essential knowledge, historical context, and scholarly resources. The closet—your private place of prayer—offers spiritual formation and intimacy with God. Ideally, you should balance both: study diligently and pray fervently. However, if you must choose, prioritize the closet, for theology without prayer becomes dry and abstract. Let your study inform your prayer and your prayer guide your study. Ultimately, the goal is to know God, not just about God.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want the prayers of my people. Is it wrong to ask for them?
chosen: It is not wrong to ask your people for prayer. Scripture shows leaders depending on the prayers of others, and Paul asked the churches to pray for him—that's humility, not weakness, and it draws your congregation into the work. So ask, and ask freely. Just remember that prayer is a duty and a privilege to be performed at set times whether or not you feel like it: keep your own times of prayer, pray when you feel dry, and lead your family in prayer. Ask them to pray, and keep praying yourself.
rejected: It is not wrong at all to ask your people for prayer; Scripture repeatedly shows leaders depending on the prayers of others. Paul asked the churches to pray for him, and the work of preaching is too weighty to bear alone. Asking for prayer is not weakness but humility, and it invites the congregation into partnership in the gospel. At the same time, do not neglect your own prayers while waiting for the spirit of prayer to come. Pray at appointed times even when you feel dry, lead your family in prayer, and remember that prayer is a means by which God accomplishes His work—so act as though your asking matters. Expect God to answer, and be willing to do your part.

prompt: I am more comfortable in my study with books than in my closet with God. Is that a danger?
chosen: No, this isn't a danger by itself. The closet is the heart's study, where thought is not only brightened but born in prayer — so let your books feed that room rather than replace it. Your comfort with study is a gift; just keep it pointed toward God and you're fine.
rejected: It's not necessarily a danger to prefer study, but it can become one if it replaces your time with God. Books can help you learn about God, but they are not a substitute for personal communion with Him. The closet represents intimate prayer and solitude with God. If you neglect that, your study may become an escape. Balance is key: use your study to understand God's Word, but also spend time in prayer and listening. Ask yourself if you are avoiding God. If so, repent and seek Him. Remember, knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.

prompt: I am busy with church administration and have little time left for prayer. What should I do?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: prayer must be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress. So don't set prayer against your church administration as if only one can win the hours. Let prayer accompany the work, keep it short and steady within the time you actually have, and let it grow from there.
rejected: Church administration is real ministry, but it can quietly crowd out prayer. Treat prayer as part of the work, not a competitor to it. Start small and fixed: a short morning offering, a midday pause, a brief evening review. Protect those times as you would a meeting. You may need to delegate tasks, say no to some requests, and simplify processes. Remember that the work belongs to God; you are not its savior. Ask Him for wisdom about what to drop. A leader who prays is not less productive but more grounded. Begin this week with one unhurried block and let it grow.

prompt: I am eloquent and earnest in the pulpit, but I see no lasting fruit. What am I missing?
chosen: Eloquence and earnestness are real gifts, and I wouldn't ask you to lay them down. But the place to look for what's missing is your closet: the preachers who gain mighty results for God are those who have prevailed in their pleadings with God ere venturing to plead with men. So keep preaching faithfully, and give your private prayer the same weight you give your pulpit.
rejected: Eloquence and earnestness are gifts, but lasting fruit usually comes through more than polished delivery. Ask whether your preaching is clear about sin, grace, and Christ, whether it applies Scripture to real life, and whether you are praying for your hearers by name. Consider your own walk with God: is your private devotion feeding your public ministry? Seek feedback from trusted mentors and elders. Also examine whether your congregation is set up for discipleship—small groups, follow-up, pastoral care. Fruit often grows slowly. Be patient, keep preaching faithfully, and look for small signs of growth rather than dramatic results.

prompt: I have great talents and education. Can these alone make my ministry fruitful?
chosen: Your talents and education are real gifts, and they can serve your ministry well. But they cannot carry it alone, and the reason is simple: a professional ministry is a heartless ministry, and when salary plays a great part the heart plays little part. So keep your heart in front of your credentials, and let your gifts serve people rather than advance you. That's fine, done with care.
rejected: Talents and education are real gifts and should be used well, but they alone cannot make ministry fruitful. Fruitfulness depends on God's grace, prayer, character, and love for people. A well-trained mind helps you teach clearly and lead wisely, yet hearers are changed by the Spirit, not by credentials. So steward your gifts: keep learning, prepare carefully, and seek feedback. But pair competence with humility, holiness, and dependence on God. Guard against pride in your education and against treating ministry as a career. Ask God to use your gifts for His glory and the good of others, and remember that He often works through weakness.

prompt: I am orthodox in doctrine and careful in study, yet my people seem dead. Could the problem be in me?
chosen: Yes, it may well be in you — and the place to look is your prayer. The test of orthodoxy is whether we pray to Jesus as our living Lord. Your doctrine and study are good, but they can't substitute for praying to the living Christ. So let your careful study drive you to prayer, and begin there.
rejected: Yes, it may well be in you. Orthodoxy and careful study are good, but they can become substitutes for the living reality they describe. If your people seem dead, examine whether your own ministry has become routine, whether you preach doctrine without warmth, and whether your study has crowded out prayer. The problem may be that you are presenting truths you have not deeply experienced. Ask yourself whether your own heart is alive to what you teach. Renew your devotion, seek fresh encounter with God, and let your study feed your love rather than replace it. Deadness in the people often reflects deadness in the preacher, so begin with honest self-examination and renewed dependence on God.

prompt: I once had a sense of divine anointing in my preaching, but it seems gone. Can it be recovered?
chosen: Yes, it can be recovered, and here's the one thing that settles it: unction is the divine anointing that distinguishes true gospel preaching from all other addresses, and it comes not in the study but in the closet, in answer to prayer. That's where your hope lies. So go to God in prayer, repent where you need to, and keep preaching faithfully. He is the giver, and He is not stingy with His servants.
rejected: Yes, it can be recovered, but not by trying harder to feel it. Anointing is not a mood you manufacture; it is God's gift. Begin by examining your heart: unconfessed sin, neglect of prayer, or ministry done for approval can grieve the Spirit. Return to private devotion, ask trusted believers to pray for you, and keep preaching faithfully even when the feeling is absent. Feelings fluctuate; faithfulness does not. God often restores freshness through repentance, rest, and renewed attention to Scripture. Do not chase the old sensation; seek the Giver. He is not stingy with His servants.

prompt: I have been told that my prayers in the pulpit are too long and dry. How should I pray publicly?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Nothing is too small to bring to God; we honour Him by asking His guidance in small things and insult Him by taking them out of His hands. So let your public prayers be specific and plain, naming the ordinary concerns of your people and asking for guidance rather than deciding what is too trivial for God. Keep them focused and warm, close in Christ's name, and write them out beforehand if that helps you stay clear. Shorter and simpler will serve your congregation well.
rejected: Public prayer is not the place for length or display. Keep it focused: open with a brief address to God, name the concerns of the congregation plainly, and close in Christ's name. Aim for clarity and warmth rather than volume or duration. A few minutes well ordered will serve better than ten minutes of wandering. Write out your prayers beforehand if that helps, and read them if needed—no one is edified by improvisation that loses its way. Vary the content with the needs of the people, and leave room for silence. The goal is to help the congregation pray, not to impress them with yours.

prompt: I am a preacher and I feel that my prayers are routine and dead. How do I pray truly?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: prayer must be our main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and we must pray that God would enable us to search out and discover our own hearts and reform whatever is amiss in them. So bring your dryness to God honestly and ask him to show you your own heart and change what's amiss in it. Keep it small and steady within the life you actually have: slow down with a psalm or the Lord's Prayer, pray before you preach to prepare your own heart and not just the sermon, and confess where ministry has become performance. You don't need to manufacture intensity. You need honesty and faithfulness, and that's enough.
rejected: Routine prayer is a common experience, especially for those who preach. Begin by being honest with God about your dryness. Slow down: use a psalm, a short passage, or the Lord's Prayer, and pray it attentively rather than in bulk. Pray before preaching, not only to prepare a sermon but to prepare your own heart. Examine your motives and confess where ministry has become performance. Take a day of retreat, seek a spiritual director or trusted friend, and guard against overwork. Remember that prayer is a relationship, not a technique. Faithfulness in small, dry prayers often matters more than intense experiences. God is present even when you feel nothing.

prompt: I want my preaching to be heart-preaching. How does prayer make that happen?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer puts the preacher's heart into the sermon and the sermon into the preacher's heart, for the heart makes the preacher. That's what you're after, so keep at it: pray before you study as well as after, ask for love for the people you'll address, and let your study serve that love. Your time and energy are real limits, and this doesn't ask you to ignore them. It's a good aim, and prayer is how it happens.
rejected: Heart-preaching begins with the preacher's own heart, and prayer is how that heart is kept warm. If you want to move others, you must first be moved yourself. Prayer keeps you aware of the weight of what you are handling and of your dependence on God. Without it, preaching easily becomes performance or lecture. Practically, pray before you study, not only after; ask God to give you love for the people you will address. Then let your study serve that love. Prayer also shapes the sermon itself, because it reminds you that you are not merely explaining a text but speaking to souls. Over time, a praying preacher becomes a different kind of preacher, one whose words carry the weight of a life lived before God.

prompt: I am a preacher and I want to see my sermons produce lasting fruit. What must I do?
chosen: It's fine to want lasting fruit from your sermons, and fine with care. One principle settles it: all our blessings have been the result of sacrifices, and the minister who shirks toils and privations produces little fruit; unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies it brings forth much fruit. So keep preparing prayerfully, preaching Christ from Scripture with clarity, loving your people, and living what you preach, and expect the fruit to grow out of quiet, costly faithfulness rather than quick visible results. That's the care this calls for, and it's good work to keep doing.
rejected: To see lasting fruit from your sermons, focus on prayerful preparation, sound doctrine, and practical application. Ensure your sermons are grounded in Scripture and centered on Christ. Preach with clarity and passion, relying on the Holy Spirit to convict and convert hearts. Build relationships with your congregation so you can speak to their real needs. Be consistent in your personal devotion and holiness, as your life preaches as loudly as your words. Finally, trust God for the results; He alone gives the increase. Avoid relying on techniques or eloquence, and instead seek to be a faithful steward of the mysteries of God.

prompt: I am a young minister and I want to know what to study most. What should I give my best hours to?
chosen: Give your best hours to Scripture and theology. Study thoroughly the letter and imbibe the spirit, adhere to the divine Principle and follow the behests of God, abiding steadfastly in wisdom, Truth, and Love, to progress most rapidly. That's the answer for a young minister who wants to know where his best hours go: into the text, into sound doctrine, and into the spirit that inspired both, so that your study feeds your devotion and your devotion feeds your study. This is fine, and fine with care—keep the letter and the spirit together, and let your best hours go there first.
rejected: As a young minister, your best hours should go to studying Scripture and theology. The Bible is your primary text—read it deeply, meditate on it, and learn to interpret it faithfully. Alongside Scripture, study sound doctrine and church history to understand the faith once delivered. But don't neglect practical ministry skills like preaching, pastoral care, and leadership. Also, cultivate your own walk with God; your study should fuel your devotion. Consider reading broadly in literature and philosophy to connect with the culture. Finally, seek mentors and never stop learning. Give your mornings to study and your afternoons to people. Balance is key.

prompt: I am a leader and I want to set my church to praying. Where do I begin?
chosen: Begin with yourself, because none but praying leaders can have praying followers. Keep your set times of prayer whether or not you feel like it, pray with your family, and never ask God to do what you are unwilling to do yourself. That is where a church set to praying actually starts, and it is fine to begin there.
rejected: Begin by casting a clear vision for prayer and communicating why it matters. Assess your church's current prayer culture, then form a prayer team to help plan. Establish regular prayer meetings at convenient times, and use small groups to encourage daily prayer habits. Provide resources such as prayer guides, devotionals, and Scripture reading plans. Teach on prayer through sermons and classes so people understand its biblical foundation. Celebrate and share testimonies of answered prayer to build momentum. Be patient, as culture change takes time, and measure progress through participation and feedback. Consider special seasons of prayer and fasting. Model prayer yourself in public settings, and invite others to join you in seeking God for the church and community.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea that only matter is real and that thoughts are just by-products of the brain—can that view be true?
chosen: It's fine to hold that view and to test it. One thing decides it: mind will explain matter while matter will not explain mind. That doesn't ban materialism; it just means the view has real work to do, and you can weigh it honestly without pretending the question is settled.
rejected: That view, often called materialism, is a common assumption today, but it has serious problems. If thoughts are merely by-products of the brain, then reason itself becomes a product of blind matter, and we would have no reason to trust our reasoning. Materialism cannot explain consciousness, meaning, or the fact that we can know truths. Many philosophers and scientists have pointed out that mind seems more fundamental than matter. So while it is understandable that you are drawn to it, the view is not adequate to explain reality. It may be more reasonable to hold that mind is real and basic, and that matter is dependent on mind.

prompt: I am conscious of deciding what to think next—is that a real experience of causing something, or an illusion?
chosen: Your experience of deciding what to think next is real, not an illusion. Causality is not mere necessary connexion but Activity, known directly in our experience of volition—and that is exactly what you're describing. So this is fine, and fine to trust with care. You don't have to prove you author everything; you only have to notice that the activity you meet in deciding is genuine.
rejected: The experience of deciding what to think next is real, but it is not proof that you are the ultimate cause. Your conscious will is genuine, but it operates within a larger framework of influences—brain processes, environment, and perhaps God's sovereignty. The feeling of causing something is not an illusion; it reflects your participation in the causal order. However, you are not the sole author of your thoughts. So, it's both real and not the whole story. The key is to recognize your dependence on God, who ultimately sustains all things.

prompt: Why should I think of the ultimate Reality by analogy with the highest thing I know rather than the lowest?
chosen: It's fine to think of the ultimate by analogy with the highest thing you know. Mind will explain matter while matter will not explain mind, so Mind is the more reasonable clue—and that holds even while you keep in view that any analogy is only a pointer and the Reality itself may lie beyond what you can fully know. Start from the highest, and stay humble about the picture.
rejected: Thinking of ultimate Reality by analogy with the highest thing you know—mind, consciousness, love—is more fitting than starting from the lowest, such as matter or mechanism. When we reason upward, we use what is most developed and capacious as a clue to what is most real. Mind can explain matter, but matter struggles to explain mind; so mind is the better analogy. Beginning from the lowest tends to reduce reality to what is least, which distorts it. There may be a Reality beyond both mind and matter that we cannot fully know, and analogies are only pointers. Still, the highest we know gives the least inadequate picture, so it is wiser to reach toward the ultimate through the best rather than the basest we can imagine.

prompt: My conscience tells me one thing and my neighbours another—can we both be right?
chosen: Yes, you and your neighbour can both be in good conscience and still disagree—this is fine, handled with care. The principle that settles it: be just with your own soul, neither excusing nor accusing it without due reflection, so it doesn't grow insolent or lose courage. So examine your reasons honestly, take your neighbour's view seriously, and where clear moral teaching speaks, follow it. Hold your view with humility, not contempt.
rejected: It's possible for two people to reach different conclusions in good conscience, especially when the matter is not clearly settled by shared moral principles. Conscience is not infallible; it can be mistaken, under-informed, or shaped by culture. Your neighbour may see something you don't, and you may see something they don't. So take their view seriously, examine your own reasons, and seek wise counsel. Where Scripture and clear moral teaching speak, follow them. Where they don't, allow freedom and avoid contempt. You may both be partially right, or one of you may be mistaken—humility and honest dialogue are the way forward.

prompt: Is it true that this is the best of all possible worlds, or only the best that could be made?
chosen: It's fine to ask, and fine to answer with the modest claim. The world is an organism whose parts are ends in themselves, and beauty crowns the proof of purposeful design. That makes this the best that could be made, not a rival to every conceivable world. Say so plainly, and keep the suffering in view while you say it.
rejected: The question turns on what "best" means. If it means the best of all logically possible worlds, the claim is hard to defend: a world with less suffering seems conceivable, and natural selection suggests much of the world's order is the product of blind competition rather than designed purpose. If it means the best world that could actually be made given real constraints, the claim is more modest and more defensible. Either way, the phrase invites us to weigh beauty and order against waste and pain, and to ask what kind of goodness a world like this can bear.

prompt: I feel God's presence in prayer—is that immediate knowledge, or am I inferring it from my feelings?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer brings spiritual knowledge, and every Christian may become acquainted in personal experience with all the knowledge of God stored up in Christ, in whom are hid all treasures of wisdom and knowledge. So the sense of God's presence you're describing can be real knowledge rather than something you're just inferring from your feelings. Keep the care you already show by testing where it leads, and let the question stand.
rejected: Feeling God's presence in prayer can be a genuine experience of immediate knowledge, but it can also be influenced by emotions. It's important to discern. Immediate knowledge of God is a gift of the Holy Spirit, given to those who seek Him with pure hearts. However, our feelings can be unreliable, so we should test our experiences against Scripture and the teachings of the Church. If your sense of God's presence leads you to greater love, humility, and obedience, it is likely genuine. If it leads to pride or complacency, it may be merely emotional. Cultivate a balanced prayer life that includes silence, Scripture, and sacraments. Remember, God is always present, even when we don't feel Him. Faith trusts in His promise regardless of feelings.

prompt: Can I be a Christian if I reject many of the traditional doctrines about Christ?
chosen: Christian doctrine, especially about the Logos and Trinity, is an attempt to express the Church's sense of the unique value of Christ; it requires re-interpretation and development, and the old expressions are not valueless. That settles it. You can be a Christian while questioning traditional formulations, because those formulations are the Church's effort to say what it found in Christ, and that effort is meant to be entered into and rethought, not just repeated. So this is fine, and fine with care: hold on to the value of Christ that the doctrines were reaching for, and treat the old expressions as worth taking seriously rather than throwing away.
rejected: This deserves a careful, honest answer. Christian faith has always been bound up with certain claims about who Christ is—truly God and truly man, crucified and risen. If you reject many traditional doctrines, you are not simply choosing a style of spirituality; you are questioning the substance of the faith. That said, doctrine is not a magic formula, and honest people wrestle with it. The question is whether you are engaging the doctrines to understand them more deeply or dismissing them without examination. Talk with a thoughtful pastor or theologian, read the classic texts charitably, and be patient with yourself. Faith seeks understanding; it is not the same as uncritical repetition.

prompt: Why should I be a Christian rather than a Buddhist, if both teach charity and humanity?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to weigh it carefully. The principle that settles it is this: charity should not encourage idleness or pauperism; the aim is to relieve present wants and then help the poor help themselves. Hold both traditions up to that, and you'll see the real difference is in what kind of giver each one forms. That's the measure to use, and it's a fair one for the question you're asking.
rejected: Both Christianity and Buddhism teach compassion and ethics, but they differ in their foundations. Christianity centers on a personal God who created and loves us, and on Jesus Christ as Savior. Buddhism focuses on overcoming suffering through the Eightfold Path and enlightenment. Christianity offers a relationship with God and assurance of salvation, while Buddhism emphasizes self-effort. Charity in Christianity flows from God's love and is not just a duty. Moreover, Christianity provides a community and a hope beyond this life. Ultimately, the choice depends on what you believe about God and ultimate reality. Consider the claims of each and seek truth.

prompt: Why should I do what I believe is right when everyone around me disagrees and it costs me everything?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. You can hold to what you believe is right even when everyone around you disagrees, because wrong done to another returns upon the wrong-doer and right adjusts the balance sooner or later. So keep your conscience and deal kindly with those who oppose you, and don't let the cost convince you that you've done wrong.
rejected: Doing what is right when everyone disagrees is one of the hardest things a person can face. It helps to remember that truth is not decided by majority vote. If you are convinced something is right, you should weigh the counsel of others carefully but ultimately follow your conscience. It is also wise to seek support from people who share your convictions, so you are not alone. Consider the long-term consequences and whether the cost is truly worth it. Sometimes standing alone is necessary, and history honors those who did. Seek advice, count the cost, and then act with courage.

prompt: Is it base to hope for a future life, or is that hope a proper part of trusting God?
chosen: Hoping for a future life is not base; it is a proper part of trusting God. Hope gives confidence of success in the sanctification of your own soul and of others, joining an intimate conviction of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power, and trusting supernatural means, since all human learning and power cannot save a soul. So this is fine, and fine with care: let your hope rest on God's power rather than your own, and let it strengthen faithful living now.
rejected: Hoping for a future life is not base; it is a proper part of trusting God. Scripture sets the hope of eternal life before us as a motivation and a comfort, not a shameful self-interest. The one who trusts God trusts His promises, and those promises include resurrection and life with Him. At the same time, hope for the future should not become an escape from present obedience; it should strengthen us to live faithfully now. So the hope of heaven is legitimate, but it is meant to shape how we live today rather than to excuse neglect of the present.

prompt: Did my soul exist before my body, and is that why I suffer now?
chosen: No — don't treat your suffering as the leftover of a soul that existed before your body. One principle settles it: the soul is a fire that is anguish while shut up in its dark self and love when it breaks forth and unites with the Divine Love, the same fire being torment or joy according to its condition. Your pain is that fire in its dark self, not a debt from before you were born. So the question to ask isn't where your soul was, but whether the fire is still shut in. That is kind, and it is enough.
rejected: Questions about the soul's existence before the body have occupied thinkers for centuries, and traditions differ. Some suggest a pre-existent soul; others hold that the soul is created with the body. There is no settled answer, and speculation can distract from the real question of how to live now. Your suffering is real and deserves care—physical, emotional, and spiritual. Rather than tracing it to a pre-birth cause, focus on what you can address today: rest, honest relationships, prayer, and professional help if needed. Meaning can be found not in solving the origin of suffering but in how you respond to it.

prompt: Could there be a world of spirits without any one God over them all?
chosen: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. A spirit must take definite and concrete form before it can be effective in the world, even as God became incarnate. That principle doesn't demand one supreme being over all; it demands that the spirits have real shape and order. So a world of spirits without a single God over them can be conceived, as long as it isn't a formless haze. Keep it concrete and you're on solid ground.
rejected: This is a question about whether a spiritual realm could exist without a single supreme being ruling it. Many religious traditions hold that a world of spirits requires a unifying principle or God, since order and existence depend on some ultimate source. Philosophy also suggests that a plurality of spirits needs a ground of unity. Without one God over all, spirits might be conceived as independent powers, but that raises problems of order and authority. Most theistic traditions answer no: a world of spirits without one God over them would be incoherent or unstable.

prompt: Did the world have a beginning, or has it existed forever?
chosen: This is fine to ask, and fine to hold with care. One principle settles it: the only pre-existence no reason can uproot is the old thought that God the Lord directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20, foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake. That doesn't hand you a date for the world's start, and it doesn't need to. You can keep your honesty about what cosmology can and can't see, and still rest the question on a purpose that stands before the beginning. Ask it freely.
rejected: Whether the world began or is eternal is a question science and philosophy still debate. Big Bang cosmology suggests our observable universe had a starting point, yet that says little about whether something preceded it or whether time itself began. Many philosophers have argued that an actual infinite past is impossible, while others find an eternal universe coherent. Religious traditions add another layer: some describe creation at a definite moment, others speak of endless cycles or a timeless ground of being. The honest answer is that we cannot observe the past before the universe became transparent, so any verdict rests on inference and interpretation. The idea of a divine plan stretching before creation is often dismissed as speculation, and reasonably so. What matters practically is how we live now, not metaphysical chronology.

prompt: Is it true that morality would collapse if religious belief disappeared?
chosen: No, it isn't true. Religion and morality are strong in proportion as each helps the other, which means neither is the foundation the other stands on. Take away belief and morality doesn't fall down—it keeps leaning on empathy, on trust, on the ordinary human sense of fairness. Religion still adds real things: community, purpose, a way of teaching right from wrong. But it adds to something that was already there. So the fear is understandable, and the answer is still no.
rejected: That's a complex question. Many people argue that religion provides a foundation for morality, offering a sense of absolute right and wrong and a motivation to be good. Without it, they fear a slide into relativism or chaos. However, others point out that morality can exist independently of religion—secular ethics, human empathy, and social contracts can guide behavior. History shows both religious and non-religious people capable of great good and great evil. So it's not clear that morality would collapse entirely; it might change shape. But religion does offer community, purpose, and a framework for moral education that many find valuable. Ultimately, the answer may depend on how you define morality and religion, and whether you see them as inseparable or distinct.

prompt: Can I base my religion on my religious experiences alone, without any philosophy?
chosen: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. Religion in its essential idea is a life in God, involving the united working of intellect, affection, and will, so your experiences are a real beginning, not a disqualification. Let that life draw in your mind and your choices as it grows, and you'll be on solid ground.
rejected: Basing your religion solely on religious experiences without any philosophy is possible, but it has limitations. Experiences are subjective and can be misinterpreted; they may vary and sometimes conflict. Philosophy can provide a framework for understanding and evaluating those experiences, helping you distinguish between genuine encounters and emotional highs. However, religion is ultimately about a relationship with God, and experiences are a valid part of that. You don't need a philosophy degree to have faith. Many people have deep, authentic faith based on personal encounters with God. The key is to remain open to learning and to test your experiences against Scripture and the wisdom of the faith community. So while philosophy can be helpful, it is not essential for a living faith.

prompt: If God is Mind, must He have feeling and will as I do, or is that just projecting my human nature onto Him?
chosen: No, you don't have to pick between those two. God is the only Mind and the only power, so He isn't a larger you, moved by moods and circumstance. But love and will aren't just yours to project; in Him they're perfect and uncreated, and yours are the faint copy. So it's not projection to say He loves and wills. Your question is fine, and fine to keep asking with care.
rejected: This is a real question, and the answer lies between two errors. If God is infinite Mind, He is not a larger version of you with human moods and impulses; projecting your feelings onto Him can indeed distort who He is. Yet feeling and will are not merely human accidents—they point to something real in God, though in Him they are perfect and uncreated rather than reactive and changeable. So it is not projection to say God loves and wills; it is projection to say He loves and wills exactly as you do, swayed by circumstance. Think of His feeling as steadfast love and His will as holy purpose, not as your moods writ large.

prompt: Is time real, or is it only in our minds—and does it matter for my religion?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Time is real, and your experience of it is shaped by your mind—both hold together. The temporal and the spiritual are not separate; with God nothing is temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct us in our temporal affairs as in our spiritual ones. So let the debate about time remain a debate, and keep living your real, accountable days in faith.
rejected: Time is a real feature of created existence, the order in which events occur, but our experience of it is also shaped by our minds. Whether time is ultimately fundamental or a form of perception is debated by philosophers and physicists alike. For religion, the question matters because God is described as eternal, beyond time, yet acting within it. Christians have generally held that God enters time in creation and redemption without being bound by it. Practically, this means your days are real and accountable, and faith is lived in time—through patience, repentance, and hope. The metaphysical debate need not unsettle ordinary devotion.

prompt: Is it reasonable to think of the ultimate Reality as something neither mind nor matter, an Unknowable?
chosen: No, it isn't reasonable, and I'd say so kindly but plainly. The principle settles it: matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, sensations and relations including space, implies mind. That points you to Mind, not to a blank. An Unknowable neither mind nor matter is unintelligible and gratuitous, and if it were truly unknowable you couldn't affirm it without contradiction. So don't call it that. Your instinct that matter isn't the whole story is sound; the mistake is stopping at a fog instead of following the argument home to Mind.
rejected: It is not reasonable. To call the ultimate Reality an Unknowable neither mind nor matter is to say nothing definite about it while pretending to say something profound. If it is truly unknowable, we cannot even affirm that it is unknowable without contradiction. Moreover, mind is the one thing we know directly. Matter is known only through mind, and mind explains matter while matter cannot explain mind. A Something neither mind nor matter is both unintelligible and gratuitous, a word without content. It is more reasonable to say that the ultimate Reality is Mind, the ground of all intelligence and order.

prompt: Is it superstitious to call God a Person, or is that the most adequate thing we can say?
chosen: No, it isn't superstitious — calling God a Person is the most adequate thing we can say. God is a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved; that is what the word carries, and no lesser term like force or principle can carry it. So use it, and use it with the humility you already showed, knowing our words about God always fall short.
rejected: Calling God a Person is not superstitious; it's a way to express that God is relational, conscious, and has a will. However, we must remember that human language is limited, and God transcends our categories. So while 'Person' is the most adequate term we have, it's not exhaustive. God is not a person in the same way humans are, but the term points to the truth that God is not an impersonal force. It's a helpful analogy, but we should hold it humbly, recognizing that all our language about God is inadequate.

prompt: Can I believe in a good God and still believe that death is the end of me?
chosen: Yes, you can, and it's fine. Belief in a righteous God carries with it the idea of a future life, so your hope for what comes after death rests on God's character rather than on your own certainty. Hold the question honestly and let that ground stay under you.
rejected: It's possible to believe in a good God and still wonder if death is the end, but the two beliefs are in tension. If God is good and righteous, it makes sense that He would not let His creatures perish forever. The Bible teaches that death is not the end but a transition to eternal life for those who believe. However, some people believe that death is the end and that this life is all there is. But for those who trust in God, there is hope for resurrection and eternal life. So, while you may have doubts, faith in a good God gives reason to hope that death is not the end.

prompt: Are all religions really teaching the same thing, so that it does not matter which I follow?
chosen: No, they don't all teach the same thing, and it does matter which you follow. There is in strictness but one religion; the rest are caricatures or gropings after it, and Christianity is absolutely exclusive because it is absolutely inclusive. So you can't treat them as interchangeable and pick whichever you like. That's the honest answer, and I'd give it to you gently, but I wouldn't soften it into a shrug.
rejected: Many people assume all religions are basically the same, but they differ significantly in their claims about God, salvation, and human purpose. While there are some overlapping moral teachings, the core doctrines of Christianity—such as the incarnation, the atonement, and the resurrection—are not shared by other faiths. So it does matter which you follow. That said, this does not mean other religions contain no truth at all. Many contain genuine insights and moral wisdom. The question is whether those insights are complete. Christianity makes a distinctive claim about Jesus that other religions do not.

prompt: Can I believe in a God who merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like?
chosen: No, you shouldn't believe in a God like that. All power belongs to God alone, and to acknowledge any other power is to dishonor God. A God who only thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like has already handed the world to something else, and that is not a God you can trust or worship. I say this kindly, because your worry about suffering and freedom is real, but the answer is still no.
rejected: This is a real philosophical question. If God merely thinks the world but has no will or power over what it is like, then God is more like a distant observer than a living Lord. Many people find such a God hard to worship, because he seems indifferent to suffering and evil. Yet some thinkers argue that God's power is expressed through persuasion rather than coercion, respecting creaturely freedom. On that view, God's will is real but not controlling. Whether that is satisfying is a personal matter. You might ask whether a God who cannot act is worth believing in, or whether the longing for a God with power points to something true.

prompt: I feel uneasy speaking of God as a force or a 'something not ourselves'—is that a lower way of thinking than calling Him a Person?
chosen: Your unease is pointing you the right way, so be at peace about it. God is a Person: a self-conscious Being who thinks, feels, wills, and is capable of loving and being loved, and that is more adequate than calling Him a force or 'something not ourselves.' A force cannot know you or love you; a Person can. So calling Him a Person is not the lower way of thinking—it is the truer one, and you can rest there.
rejected: It is understandable to feel uneasy with impersonal language for God. Calling God a force or 'something not ourselves' can seem vague and less than personal. Yet all our language about God is inadequate. Still, personhood is the highest category we have, and Scripture speaks of God as personal—knowing, willing, loving. So while we must remember that God transcends our concepts, calling Him a Person is not lower but higher than calling Him a force. The danger is to think of 'super-personal' as less than personal, which would be a mistake. God is personal in the truest sense, even if infinitely beyond our understanding.

prompt: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain and sin in the world?
chosen: This is fine to ask, and fine to hold onto. Suffering is God's remedy for unrighteousness, employed to produce righteousness in man, and the Cross shows agony is compatible with perfect love. That is the answer that settles it, and it is kind: God is not distant from your pain, and He is not the author of sin. You can bring the question as it is.
rejected: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions, and honest believers have wrestled with it for centuries. Scripture affirms both that God is good and that evil is real. Much pain comes from human choices, and much comes from a broken world. God is not the author of sin, yet He permits it and works to bring good out of it. The cross shows that God does not stand distant from suffering; He enters it. Rather than resolving every mystery, the gospel invites us to trust God's character even when we cannot explain His ways, and to work against pain and sin until He makes all things new.

prompt: Can I believe in the objectivity of duty without believing in God?
chosen: Yes — you can believe duty is objective without believing in God, and that's fine. The principle that settles it is the call to love another as yourself: that duty binds you to the person in front of you regardless of what you believe about a divine source, and it asks nothing more of you than honesty about how you treat them. So hold your view with a clear conscience.
rejected: It is possible to feel the force of duty without believing in God—many thoughtful people do. One can hold that moral obligations are objective, grounded in reason, human nature, or the structure of reality, without appealing to a divine lawgiver. Kant, for instance, argued for a categorical imperative rooted in rationality itself. So yes, in principle you can affirm objective duty on secular grounds. But the question is whether such a view is stable: if duty is truly objective and binding, it is natural to ask what grounds that authority. Many argue that without a transcendent source, duty risks becoming a human projection. So it is coherent, but theists would say it is less secure than grounding duty in God.

prompt: If I am a part of God, how can I worship Him, and how can He be good when wicked men are also parts of Him?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: it is more worship to behold God in all than in any special thing, taking all generally and nothing in special. So your worship doesn't depend on resolving every mystery first—see God in ordinary things and in your neighbor, and let the goodness question rest where it belongs: wickedness is a misuse of freedom, not a part of God's nature. Keep that in view and you can worship honestly.
rejected: These are deep questions. If you understand yourself as a part of God, worship becomes less about external rituals and more about living in harmony with the whole—gratitude, love, and service. As for wicked men being parts of God, many traditions would distinguish between being made in God's image and being identical with God. Wickedness is a distortion of that image, not a part of God's nature. God remains good; evil is a privation, a turning away. So worship by aligning your will with the good, and understand that God's goodness is not compromised by creatures who misuse their freedom. It may help to speak with a teacher or pastor about these mysteries.

prompt: Is it wrong to accept my religion on authority rather than working it all out for myself?
chosen: No, it isn't wrong. Authority means weight—what rightly carries your judgment—and it isn't made greater by pressure or threat. Accepting your religion on authority is letting something that has genuinely earned weight with you carry you, and that is a reasonable way to hold a faith, not a failure to think. It's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Accepting a religion on authority is not inherently wrong, and most people hold many beliefs they have not personally verified. Still, it is worth distinguishing between trusting a source you have reason to consider reliable and simply deferring because questioning feels uncomfortable. A healthy faith usually involves some personal investigation—reading, asking questions, and reflecting on your own experience—alongside reliance on trusted teachers and tradition. If accepting on authority means you have never examined the core claims, you might set aside time to explore them. If it means you have examined enough to trust the tradition that formed you, that can be a reasonable and mature position.

prompt: I feel that the world must have some one Reality behind it, but I cannot see why it should be mind rather than matter.
chosen: You're right to look for one Reality, and you're right that it isn't obviously matter. But the argument that gets you to Mind—that mind explains matter while matter can't explain mind—arrives here attached to a claim I have to refuse: that pain and sickness live only in mortal mind, that nerves don't feel and brain doesn't think. I won't ask you to accept a Reality that costs you the reality of suffering. So no to that, gently. Keep the question; don't take that answer.
rejected: That's a deep philosophical question. Many thinkers have argued that the ultimate Reality is mind or spirit, not matter. For example, idealists like Berkeley claimed that matter only exists as perceived by mind. Others say that mind and matter are both real but distinct. You might consider that mind has properties like consciousness and intentionality that matter lacks, and that the laws of physics seem to point to a rational order. But ultimately, this is a matter of worldview. I'd encourage you to explore different philosophies and see which makes the most sense to you.

prompt: If right and wrong are real whether I think so or not, where does that moral law exist?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and the honest answer is that an ought can exist only in and for a mind—so if the moral law is real whether you think so or not, it lives in a mind, not in space. That's the account that fits your question, and it's fine to hold it with care.
rejected: If right and wrong are real independently of our opinions, the moral law must exist somewhere. One common answer is that it exists in human reason or conscience—a shared moral sense shaped by evolution and society. Another is that it exists in the structure of the world itself, in the way rational beings ought to treat one another. On a purely naturalistic view, morality can be explained as a set of norms that promote cooperation and a good life. So the moral law may be understood as a real feature of human life, grounded in reason and social practice, even if it is not a thing located in space.

prompt: If the only cause I know is my own will, is it reasonable to infer that nature is caused by a will?
chosen: Yes, it's reasonable, and fine with care. The only cause you know directly is your own will, so inferring a will behind nature is a natural analogy, not a proof. Your own limit stands: you know only your own will, and nature may have impersonal causes. So make the inference, but hold it as plausible rather than certain, and let your will keep your roving mind from treating it as settled fact.
rejected: It is a reasonable inference, though not a proof. The only causal power you directly know from within is your own will: you decide and things happen. By analogy, it is natural to suppose that the ordered world around you is likewise the product of a will or mind, since order and purpose resemble what minds produce. This is an argument from analogy, and analogies can mislead; nature may have impersonal causes we do not directly experience. So the inference is plausible and has been widely made, but it should be held with humility and tested against evidence rather than treated as certain.

prompt: Does the truth of Christianity depend on whether the miracles in the Gospels really happened?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to take the historical question seriously. The real evidence of Christianity is its power — the present experience of sins forgiven and lives regenerated — and that is what answers the objection that miracles contradict experience. So you don't have to prove every supernatural event to trust the core, and you shouldn't let anyone decide the miraculous questions in advance by assuming miracle is impossible. Ask honestly, weigh the testimony, and hold the historical question with care.
rejected: The truth of Christianity is not solely dependent on whether every miracle in the Gospels happened exactly as described. The core of the faith is the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus, and the transformation He brings to believers. Many Christians hold that the miracles are historically reliable, while others focus on their theological meaning. What matters most is whether the gospel's message is true and whether it transforms lives. Historical questions are important and should be studied honestly, but faith ultimately rests on the person of Christ and the experience of grace, not on proving every supernatural event.

prompt: Can I know God directly in my own experience, without argument or inference?
chosen: Yes, this is fine. You can know God directly in your own experience, without argument or inference, because we may know God truly though partially, and the objections that we know only phenomena, only the like, only the imaginable, only the whole, or only the relative do not prevent real knowledge of God. So go ahead and seek him in prayer and meditation, and expect to find him, knowing that what you meet is real even though it is not the whole of him.
rejected: Yes, you can know God directly through personal experience. Many people have a direct sense of God's presence that doesn't require arguments or inferences. You can feel God's love, guidance, and peace in your heart. This direct knowledge is more real than any logical proof. Just open your heart and seek Him in prayer and meditation, and you will experience Him. Don't worry about theology or reasoning; focus on your feelings and personal encounter. God is knowable, and He wants to reveal Himself to you directly.

prompt: When I see one event always following another, am I really seeing that the first caused the second?
chosen: You're asking whether seeing one event follow another means you've seen the first cause the second. Strictly, you've seen the sequence. But causality isn't mere necessary connexion; it's Activity, and the only cause you know directly is a conscious rational will, known in your own volition. So it's fine to speak of causes, with care, reading the pattern in that light while staying humble about what the eye alone shows.
rejected: What you observe is constant conjunction: one event regularly follows another. But regular sequence alone does not show that the first produced the second. We see that the flame is followed by heat, not the power by which heat is produced. To speak of cause is to add something to the observed pattern, and philosophers have long debated whether that addition is justified. A cautious answer is that we infer causes from patterns, but we should be humble about claiming to see causal power itself. The practical upshot is to distinguish correlation from causation and to test claims carefully rather than assuming that whatever regularly follows is produced by what precedes it.

prompt: I cannot bring myself to believe that this table would still exist if no one were in the room—am I being unreasonable?
chosen: You are not being unreasonable. The table stays whether or not you are watching, and trusting that is sound. The principle that the mind and body must be balanced simply warns against letting the puzzle wear you down; it does not ask you to doubt the table. Keep the question as a passing curiosity, not a burden, and you are fine.
rejected: You are not being unreasonable at all. The belief that objects continue to exist when unobserved is a deeply practical, common-sense conviction, and it is one most people hold without difficulty. Philosophers have debated this question for centuries, but for everyday life we rightly assume the world is stable and independent of our watching it. There is nothing irrational about trusting that a table remains a table whether or not anyone is present. At the same time, it can be interesting to reflect on how much of our confidence rests on habit and experience. If the question troubles you, you might explore it philosophically, but you need not feel odd for holding the ordinary view.

prompt: Is the doctrine of the Trinity a meaningless formula, or can it still mean something to a modern person?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. The Trinity is inscrutable but not self-contradictory, and it is the necessary complement to the doctrine of the attributes, furnishing the eternal object of God's knowledge, love, and will. That is what keeps the formula from being empty for a modern person: it gives God's own life an eternal object of knowledge and love. So you can approach it prayerfully and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor, without pretending the mystery is solved.
rejected: The Trinity can feel like an abstract formula, but it still speaks to modern people. It says that God is not a solitary power but a communion of love, and that love and relationship lie at the heart of reality. For many, that is meaningful in a world that values connection and community. You do not need to fully understand the doctrine to find it fruitful; it is a mystery to be lived more than solved. Approach it prayerfully, and let it shape how you think about God and neighbor.

prompt: If colours and sounds only exist for minds, what becomes of the solid, shaped objects I touch and handle?
chosen: Your hand still meets something real. The principle that settles it is that matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, sensations and relations including space, implies mind. That doesn't dissolve the solid, shaped thing you touch and handle; it tells you what its reality is. So it's fine to trust your hands, and fine to hold that the world they meet is a world that is known.
rejected: Colours and sounds may depend on the mind that perceives them, but the objects you touch and handle are not thereby dissolved. When you touch a solid, shaped object, you are in contact with something real that resists you and behaves in regular ways. Our senses give us different kinds of information, and the fact that colour and sound are experienced by minds does not mean that solidity and shape are mere illusions. We can trust that there is a real world we encounter through touch and handling, even if we must think carefully about how perception works and what it tells us about the nature of things.

prompt: If Jesus never claimed to be God, what am I to make of the Creeds that say He is?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. The Creeds are the church's summary, not a separate revelation, and the reason they can say what they say is that his testimony to himself cannot be explained as deception or self-deception, so he must be one with God and the revealer of God to men. That holds whether or not he used the exact words, and it's why you can hold the Creeds alongside Scripture without pretending the wording is the same.
rejected: The Creeds are the church's attempt to say in precise language what the New Testament says in various ways. Jesus is presented as Lord, Savior, and Son of God, and the church came to express that in the language of the Creeds. Whether Jesus explicitly claimed to be God is debated, but the Creeds are not simply inventing a new figure; they are drawing out what the texts imply. You can read the Creeds as the church's settled summary of who Jesus is, and you can hold them alongside Scripture, recognizing that they use philosophical language to guard the gospel's central claim about him.

prompt: If my conscience has grown and changed through history, can it still be a revelation of God's mind?
chosen: Yes, it can, and that is fine. The Spirit of God bears record in the heart of the living Redeemer, and that witness exceeds all other evidence, so a conscience that grows through history is not disqualified from carrying God's mind to you. Hold it humbly, since the growth is real, but you need not refuse it.
rejected: Conscience can indeed develop as individuals and societies learn and mature, but that does not mean it is merely a human invention. A growing conscience may reflect a growing understanding of a moral order that is real and given by God. Just as a child's sense of right and wrong matures without the underlying truth changing, our moral awareness can deepen over time. So the fact that conscience changes does not disqualify it as a revelation of God's mind; it may simply show that we are learning to perceive that mind more clearly. The key is to test our conscience against Scripture and the teaching of the church.

prompt: If I have a strong feeling that something is true, does that make it a revelation from God?
chosen: No, a strong feeling that something is true does not make it a revelation from God. The things of God are known only by the Spirit of revelation, and the Holy Ghost is the only sure test of truth. Your feeling may be sincere and still be your own. So treat it with care, test it, and don't call it God's word just because it's strong.
rejected: A strong feeling that something is true does not automatically make it a revelation from God. Feelings can be influenced by many factors, including emotions, experiences, and even our own desires. In Christian tradition, revelation from God is typically understood as communication from God that is consistent with Scripture and confirmed by the Holy Spirit. It's important to test your feelings against the Bible and seek wise counsel from mature believers. Prayer and discernment are key. While God can use feelings to guide us, they should not be the sole basis for believing something is from Him. Always seek confirmation through Scripture, prayer, and community.

prompt: If God is limited in power, how can I be sure the world will turn out good on the whole?
chosen: It's fine to hold this with care. God's hand is over all, and he will overrule the results of war and calamity for ultimate good, though he did not foreordain the wickedness that brought them; he foresaw it because he knew the trend of men. So your hope doesn't need a God who controls everything — it needs the one who saw it all coming and still bends it toward good. Rest there, and keep going.
rejected: If God is limited in power, it can be frightening to think the world might not turn out good. But we can trust that God is still good and loving, even if not all-powerful. He works within the limits of nature and human freedom to bring about the best possible outcomes. The future is open, but God's character is constant. We can be sure that He will do everything He can to ensure a good end. Our role is to cooperate with Him, making choices that align with His will. Ultimately, love is the most powerful force, and God's love will not fail. So we can have hope, not because God controls everything, but because He is faithful and good.

prompt: What does it even mean to call God omnipotent—could He make two and two equal five?
chosen: You're asking something fair, and the honest answer is a kind no: God can't make two and two equal five. Omnipotence is power to do all things that are objects of power, and a contradiction isn't one—it's not a hard thing, it's no thing. That's not weakness in God; it's just what the words mean. So rest easy asking the question, but don't expect the answer to be yes.
rejected: Calling God omnipotent means He has all power, but that does not mean He can do nonsense. 'Two and two equal five' is a contradiction in terms, not a feat of power. Power is the ability to do something real; a contradiction is not a thing at all. So the question is a bit like asking whether God can make a square circle. The classical answer is that God cannot deny Himself or act against His own nature. Omnipotence is not the power to do the absurd, but the power to accomplish everything that is genuinely possible. So no, God cannot make two and two equal five—not because He is weak, but because the statement describes nothing.

prompt: If everything I know is always matter plus my own mind, how can I be sure there is any matter at all?
chosen: You've put your own limit plainly: all you know is matter plus your own mind, and you can't step outside that. So take the principle as it stands — matter cannot exist apart from mind, since all we know of matter, relations included, implies mind. That doesn't hand you a hidden world behind your experience, and it doesn't need to. What you keep meeting is the stable, shared, orderly appearance, and that is enough to live by. This is fine, held with care.
rejected: This is a classic question in philosophy, often connected to idealism and the problem of the external world. One common answer is that we cannot prove matter exists independently, but we reasonably believe it does because our experience is stable, shared, and predictable. Others argue that what we call matter is really a construct of mind, so the question dissolves. A practical approach is to recognize that certainty about an external world may not be required for daily life; we act on well-justified belief. You might explore thinkers like Berkeley, Kant, or contemporary philosophers of mind. The key is to examine what you mean by 'matter' and 'know,' and to notice that your question already assumes a framework worth questioning.

prompt: Am I really a fellow-worker with God in a real struggle against evil, or is the struggle a sham?
chosen: Yes, the struggle is real, and it isn't a sham because you're carrying it alone. Ideas about God and aspirations after Him, and reverence alone, cannot carry us through the real battle of life; it is One by our side—trust, sympathy, comradeship, fighting together in the ranks—that thrills your strength and keeps your right hand fresh. So this is fine, and fine with care: stay in the ranks, and let the comradeship, not the performance, tell you the fight is genuine.
rejected: The question touches something deep: whether the moral struggle is genuine or merely a performance. A useful test is whether the struggle costs you something—whether it changes your choices, your habits, and your relationships. If it is only ideas and feelings, it may indeed be a sham. But if you find yourself actually resisting temptation, repairing harm, and persisting when it is inconvenient, the struggle is real. God is not a distant observer of this; Scripture speaks of workers together with God, which suggests partnership rather than solo effort. The struggle is not a sham if you are genuinely engaged in it, however imperfectly. Keep testing your life against your profession, and let the evidence of real change encourage you.

prompt: Are my moral judgements just my feelings, or can they be objectively true like arithmetic?
chosen: Your question is fair, and the answer is that this is fine to pursue. Moral judgement isn't just feeling: the ground of moral obligation is the holiness of God, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things; we are bound to the right because God is it, not merely because he wills it. That is what keeps right and wrong from collapsing into your preferences, and it's why your feelings can accompany a judgement without being the whole of it. So keep asking, and keep seeking truth rather than only expressing emotion.
rejected: Moral judgements are not just feelings. While emotions play a role, moral truths can be objective in the sense that they are grounded in the nature of reality and a good life. Just as arithmetic truths are independent of our feelings, moral truths are independent of our preferences. However, moral truths are not exactly like arithmetic because they involve values and persons. Many philosophers argue that moral realism is true: there are objective moral facts. From a Christian perspective, these facts are grounded in God's nature. So your moral judgements can be objectively true when they align with God's moral order, even though your feelings may accompany them. The key is to seek truth, not just express emotion.

prompt: Is it impious to say that God could not make a world without evil in it?
chosen: No, don't say that. The evils of the world come from man's departure from God and his usurped authority, and no power on this side of heaven can correct them; it takes God to put the world right. So the evil we see isn't a gap in God's power. Saying he couldn't make a world without evil gets it backwards. He can, and the wrong is ours to grieve and his to mend.
rejected: It is not impious to ask the question, but the answer matters. Saying God could not make a world without evil limits God's power, which seems to deny his omnipotence. Yet the deeper issue is what we mean by evil. Much evil arises from the choices of free creatures, and a world with genuine freedom may carry the possibility of evil without God being its author. So the claim is not so much impious as imprecise. God can make a world without evil; the question is whether such a world would include the goods he intends, such as freedom and love.

prompt: Is my mind a part of God's mind, so that when I think it is God thinking in me?
chosen: No, your mind is not a part of God's mind, and you should not think of your thinking as God thinking in you. God is one God, infinite and perfect, and cannot become finite and imperfect. Your thoughts are yours, and God guides you by His Spirit through prayer and Scripture. That is a real comfort, and it is enough.
rejected: Your mind is not simply a part of God's mind. Scripture speaks of God's thoughts being far above ours, and of the Spirit teaching and guiding believers. When you think, it is you thinking, though God may guide and illuminate your mind by His Spirit. So it is better to say that God influences and directs your thinking than that your mind is a piece of His. To discern His leading, pray, search the Scriptures, and seek wise counsel. You can also use lots or other neutral means when a decision is unclear, trusting God to guide the outcome.

prompt: If Christianity keeps developing, how can I be sure it will not one day be outgrown?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Religious doubt is a nearly inevitable stage in the development of an intelligent Christian, and it should be met with sympathy and an orderly presentation of the facts rather than pushed aside. So bring your question into the open, look honestly at what has developed and what has held, and let the answer rest on what you find.
rejected: Every living thing develops, and Christianity has developed across centuries—doctrine, worship, and practice have changed in many ways. That doesn't mean it will be outgrown; it means it is alive. The question is whether what develops is the same faith or a replacement. Look at the core: the person and work of Christ, the gospel of grace, the authority of Scripture. Those have remained constant even as forms changed. You can be confident because Christianity is not a set of ideas to be superseded but a relationship with a living Lord who is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Development is growth, not obsolescence. Read church history, study how the faith has met new challenges, and let your confidence rest on Christ rather than on unchanging customs.

prompt: How can I know anything about God's character from looking at nature, which seems so cruel and full of suffering?
chosen: No, you can't know God's character from nature, and you shouldn't try. The principle settles it: the more truly a man knows his own misery, the more fully he beholds the majesty of God. That is the road to knowing Him, not the suffering you see in the wild. So let nature be nature, and look for God where He has promised to be found. That's not a shrug; it's a kindness to you, because nature was never going to bear that weight.
rejected: Nature can teach us something about God, but it is a limited and ambiguous teacher. Its beauty and order point to a Creator, yet its cruelty and suffering raise real questions. The Bible acknowledges this tension and points us beyond nature to Christ, who reveals God's character most fully. So while nature can stir wonder and gratitude, it should not be our primary source for knowing God. Look to Scripture and to Jesus, who shows us a God who suffers with us and promises to make all things new. Nature's cruelty is a sign of a broken world, not a revelation of God's heart.

prompt: How can a new planet have existed before any astronomer saw it, if nothing exists apart from mind?
chosen: This is fine. Your question assumes that 'mind' must mean one astronomer's private awareness, and it doesn't—Mind is the universal intelligence in which all things subsist, and the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot.
