So the planet existed in Mind before anyone saw it, and the seeing was recognition, not creation. Nothing in that breaks your limit that nothing exists apart from mind. It's fine.
rejected: If nothing exists apart from mind, then the planet's existence is not independent of consciousness—but that does not mean it pops into being only when an astronomer looks. Mind, in this view, is not merely the private mind of one observer; it is the universal intelligence in which all things subsist. A planet can exist within that Mind before any human discovers it, just as a truth can be true before anyone states it. Discovery is not creation; it is the human mind coming to know what already is in the divine Mind. So the planet's prior existence is no contradiction: it existed in Mind, and the astronomer's seeing is a recognition, not a bringing-forth.

prompt: How can I tell whether a new religious idea that came to me suddenly is from God or not?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: by rising after falls and frequently renewing acts of faith and love, you come to a state where it's as hard not to think of God as it was at first to get used to it. That means the answer to a sudden idea isn't a quick verdict but a slow habit of turning back to God. So test the idea against Scripture and your faith community, look at its fruits, pray for discernment, and seek wise counsel. Be patient and don't act hastily. If it persists and bears good fruit over time, it may well be from God.
rejected: To discern if a sudden religious idea is from God, first test it against Scripture and the teachings of your faith community. Does it align with core doctrines? Second, examine its fruits: does it lead to love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control? Third, pray for discernment and seek wise counsel from mature believers. Fourth, consider your own state: are you seeking God's will or your own? Sudden ideas can be from God, but they can also be from our own minds or other influences. Be patient and don't act hastily. If the idea persists and bears good fruit over time, it may be from God.

prompt: I am a wife and my husband is unconverted; what should my prayers for him be?
chosen: Praying for your husband is fine, and it's fine with care. Let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so that as you ask God to open his heart, you also ask God to search out and reform your own. That keeps the praying honest and keeps you gentle rather than anxious. You can't convert him; God can. Keep asking, and let the asking do its quiet work in you too.
rejected: Pray for your husband's heart to be opened and for God to draw him to faith. Ask for wisdom to love him well, patience, and grace to be a good example without nagging. Pray that God would soften any resistance and bring people into his life who can speak truth. Also pray for yourself, that you would not grow bitter or anxious. Trust God's timing and remember that you cannot convert him; God can. Keep praying persistently and look for small opportunities to show kindness and faith.

prompt: I want to be saved but I am afraid of what my family will say—must I obey them or God?
chosen: You are not required to hand your soul over to your family's approval, and you should not. Be slow to take new steps, yes—seek to have no will of your own, and ascertain God's will by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit. But the seeking is yours to do, and it is fine, fine with care, to move forward in it while still honoring your family as best you can. Their reaction may be hard, but it does not get the final word. Go gently, pray steadily, and let your conscience rest in God rather than in their approval.
rejected: This is a difficult situation, but ultimately you must follow your conscience and obey God rather than men. While honoring your family is important, it should not come at the cost of your salvation. You can respectfully explain your beliefs and set boundaries. Pray for wisdom and courage. Remember that Jesus said whoever loves father or mother more than Him is not worthy of Him. Trust that God will guide you and provide support through a community of faith. It may be painful, but obedience to God brings peace.

prompt: I have prayed for my husband for years and nothing has changed—why does God not answer?
chosen: God does not always give just what we ask; he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. That is the answer to your why. Your years of prayer are not ignored, and your weariness is not a failure. But the change you're waiting for may be a no that carries more love than the yes you wanted. Keep praying, and let your will rest in his, trusting that what he gives is better than what you asked.
rejected: It can be deeply discouraging to pray for years without seeing change. But God's timing is not ours, and His ways are higher than our ways. Sometimes He is working in ways we cannot see, and sometimes He is using the situation to change us as much as our husband. Keep praying, but also examine whether there is anything in your own heart or approach that needs adjusting. Consider whether your prayers are specific and persistent, and whether you are trusting God with the outcome. Don't give up—God hears, and He is faithful. The answer may come in a way you don't expect, or it may be that God is saying 'not yet' or 'no' for reasons you don't understand. Trust His goodness.

prompt: I have money that I feel God wants me to give up, but I am not sure—must I obey before I get the blessing?
chosen: You don't have to give before you have peace. The giving God asks is urged on you as a duty between you and your God, and you should give it because you want to, not because a blessing is being held back until you pay. So wait, pray, and give freely when your heart is settled. That is fine, and it is fine with care.
rejected: This is a tender question, and you should not rush it. God is not a vending machine, and blessing is not a payment for obedience. Still, Scripture often links obedience and blessing—not as a transaction, but as a relationship. If you sense a genuine call to give, test it prayerfully. Ask whether the impulse is from God, from guilt, or from fear. Seek wise counsel. Give cheerfully and freely, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. You need not obey before you have peace; God is patient. But do not use uncertainty as an excuse to cling. Pray, wait, and act when your heart is settled.

prompt: I have an evil habit that overcomes me again and again—must I be free of it before I can believe?
chosen: No, you don't have to be free of the habit before you believe. When you've gone a while without thinking of God, don't disquiet yourself over it; acknowledge your wretchedness and return to Him with greater trust. That's the principle that settles it, and it settles it in your favor: coming back is the point, not arriving clean first. So it's fine to believe now, exactly where you are.
rejected: No, you don't have to be free of the habit before you believe. Faith in Christ is the starting point, not the reward for good behavior. God accepts you as you are and will help you overcome the habit through His Spirit. Many people struggle with habits, but God's grace is greater. Believe in Jesus, and He will begin a transformation in you. Freedom may come gradually, but your acceptance with God is not based on your performance. Come to Him now, and He will help you.

prompt: I have come near to this blessing many times and drawn back; can I still enter in?
chosen: You can still enter in. We are in danger of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing — so look over what you're holding and let go of what isn't yours to keep. That is the step in front of you, and the invitation still stands.
rejected: Yes, you can still enter in. Drawing back many times does not disqualify you; it shows that you have seen the blessing and desired it, even if fear or hesitation held you back. God's invitation is not withdrawn because you hesitated. The question now is what keeps pulling you back—fear, unbelief, or something you are unwilling to release. Bring that honestly before God and, if helpful, before a trusted believer who can walk with you. The door is still open, and the One who calls you is patient. Take one concrete step toward Him today rather than waiting for perfect courage.

prompt: I have a besetting sin of impure thoughts—can God cleanse even my thoughts?
chosen: Yes, and this is fine. One principle settles it: don't examine whether what you do is much or little, well or ill, as long as it isn't sin and is done with an upright intention for God. So notice the impure thought, refuse it, turn toward what's pure—and stop weighing how well you're doing. Leave the increase to God, kindly and without scorekeeping.
rejected: Yes—God's cleansing is not limited to outward actions; it reaches the mind where sin begins. Impure thoughts are often habitual, and habits of thought can be retrained. Begin by noticing when the thoughts arise without condemning yourself, then redirect attention deliberately to something worthy. Prayer, Scripture, and honest accountability help. Some find that practical steps—limiting what feeds the imagination, avoiding triggering situations, and replacing idle time—make a real difference. Progress is usually gradual, and setbacks do not mean failure. God is patient, and the desire to be cleansed is itself evidence of grace at work. Keep bringing the thoughts into the light and asking for help; over time the mind can be renewed.

prompt: I have a thorn in the flesh and a temper I cannot master—is this sin that keeps me from holiness?
chosen: A thorn in the flesh and a temper you can't master don't by themselves mean you're living in sin. Remember that sin gives no real pleasure—the wrongdoer only thinks he enjoys it, and that is a deception—and seeing that clearly is what strengthens you to master the evil. Keep praying, keep confessing when you hurt someone, and don't be discouraged. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Having a thorn in the flesh and a temper does not necessarily mean you are living in sin. Paul spoke of a thorn in the flesh, and God's grace was sufficient for him. Temper can be a weakness, but it becomes sin when you yield to it. Holiness is a process, and God is patient with our struggles. Seek to master your temper through prayer, self-discipline, and accountability. Remember that God's strength is made perfect in weakness. Do not be discouraged; keep pressing on. If your temper leads you to harm others, confess and repent. God's grace covers your failures, and He is transforming you into Christ's likeness. Focus on progress, not perfection.

prompt: I am too shy and stiff to talk naturally about religion—how can I become natural?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is the one about coming into personal contact with Jesus by the same steps used to make any friend: thinking about Him, spending time in His companionship, forming brief mental pictures of the Saviour, walking beside Him, and learning what He would do and think. Since you're shy and stiff, that's the gentlest path—friendship grows quietly, without an audience, and natural talk follows from knowing someone rather than from rehearsing a speech. Keep to the limits you set for yourself, and let it grow at your own pace.
rejected: Feeling shy about discussing religion is common. To become more natural, start by recognizing that faith is an integral part of life, not a separate compartment. Practice speaking about your beliefs in low-pressure settings with trusted friends. Prepare simple, honest statements about what God means to you. Remember, you don't need to preach; just share your experience. Ask God for boldness and opportunities. Over time, as you grow more comfortable, it will become more natural. Also, focus on listening and asking questions, which takes the pressure off. Authenticity is key—people respond to genuine sharing, not perfect presentations.

prompt: I am weak in body and mind; does God require me to be perfect in these things?
chosen: No—God does not require perfect health or a perfect mind from you, and you can let that go. Perfection isn't reached by multiplying prayers and good works anyway; self-love feeds on those unless the heart is watched and habitual faults are rooted out. So keep growing gently and honestly where you can, and rest in His mercy, because He knows you are dust.
rejected: No—God does not demand bodily or mental perfection as a condition of His love. He knows we are dust, and Scripture is full of weak people He used. What He asks is faithfulness, not flawlessness: to love Him and neighbor, to do your duty as you are able, and to accept your limits humbly. Weakness can even be a place where His strength is shown. Rest in His mercy, use the gifts and capacities you have, and do not measure yourself against an impossible standard. Growth in holiness is gradual and God is patient with our pace.

prompt: I feel lukewarm and half-hearted in my religion—what will become of me?
chosen: This is fine, with care. Your feelings are not the gauge of your acceptance with God — trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods, and keep praying even when the joy is lacking. Take the half-heartedness seriously and turn from it, but don't read your dryness as a verdict already passed on you. Keep showing up, gently and firmly, and let it draw you toward God rather than away.
rejected: Feeling lukewarm in your religion is a common struggle, and it's important not to panic. First, recognize that feelings fluctuate; they are not a reliable measure of your standing with God. Second, examine whether you've been neglecting spiritual disciplines like prayer, Scripture reading, and fellowship. Third, consider that lukewarmness may be a call to renew your commitment. You don't have to be perfect; just take one step at a time. God's grace is sufficient, and He is patient with our weaknesses. Many believers go through seasons of dryness. The key is to keep showing up, even when you don't feel like it. Don't be too hard on yourself. God loves you and will help you grow.

prompt: I have been praying for prosperity in my business—will God answer that?
chosen: Yes—pray about your business. Prayer is sober, matter-of-fact business with God, and He answers prayer for supplies and protection, so you can ask Him plainly and expectantly for your work to prosper. Ask for wisdom and integrity along with it, and hold the result in His hands. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: God invites us to pray about our daily needs, including our work and business, and He is not indifferent to them. But prayer for prosperity should be offered with an open hand: ask honestly, then trust God's wisdom about what is best. Scripture promises that God supplies our needs (Phil. 4:19), yet it does not promise wealth on demand; prosperity can become an idol if it becomes the center of our prayers. So pray for your business, ask for wisdom and integrity in it, and hold the outcome loosely. Whether God grants abundance or not, He is faithful, and the deepest answer to prayer is His presence and provision, not always the result we imagine.

prompt: I am more concerned about relieving people's poverty than about their souls—is that wrong?
chosen: No, it isn't wrong. The poor are the people of God and shall inherit the earth, and the hungry have as good a right to your food as anyone. Relieving poverty is faithful work, and you can give yourself to it without apology.
rejected: It is not wrong to care deeply about relieving poverty; Scripture repeatedly commands care for the poor, and Jesus Himself fed the hungry and healed the sick. But it is worth asking whether concern for souls and concern for bodies must compete. They are not opposites. A person's material suffering is real and deserves real response. At the same time, poverty is not merely a lack of money, and people are more than their economic circumstances. A balanced approach cares for both body and soul, meeting immediate needs while also attending to deeper spiritual longings.

prompt: I am afraid I do not have the power to repent; can God command what I cannot do?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, and the answer is that this is fine, fine with care. God commands repentance because He supplies the strength for it; the power to turn is available, and the feeling follows the surrender rather than coming first. So you don't have to wait until you feel more or weep more before you turn. Begin where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask Him to supply what's lacking. He is faithful to meet a willing heart.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and many have felt the same. Repentance can seem impossible when the heart feels cold and the will weak. But God does not command what He refuses to enable. The command to repent is also a promise of grace: He gives what He asks. Still, it is easy to think we must first feel deeply sorry, weep enough, or wait until some greater power arrives before we can turn. That waiting can become an excuse for delay. Begin where you are, with the little strength you have, and ask God to supply what is lacking. He is faithful to meet a willing heart.

prompt: I have been deeply convicted of sin for years but never found peace; what am I missing?
chosen: Years of conviction without peace is a heavy thing, and it's right to ask what's missing. One principle settles it: a guilty conscience and unrepented sin tend to destroy the ability to do right; if sin is not regretted and lessening, it hastens to physical and moral doom. So don't rush to soothe the discomfort away. Name the sin plainly, confess it specifically, make right what you can, and don't let it sit and harden. Peace isn't something you manufacture by feeling bad enough; it comes as you act honestly and trust God's mercy in Christ. Talk with a pastor or trusted counselor who will help you be truthful, and keep going with Scripture, prayer, and community. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Long-lasting conviction without peace is painful, and it is worth taking seriously. First, distinguish conviction from condemnation: conviction comes from God and draws you toward change, while condemnation keeps you in shame. You may be relying on feelings rather than on God's promise of forgiveness. Bring your specific sins honestly before God, confess them, and receive His promise of mercy in Christ. Consider whether there is something you need to make right—an apology, restitution, or a habit to change. Talk with a pastor or trusted counselor who can help you sort through this. Peace often comes gradually as you act in faith, not as a feeling you must manufacture. Keep engaging with Scripture, prayer, and community, and be patient with yourself.

prompt: I believe all the facts about Jesus and that He died for sinners, so am I saved?
chosen: I can't tell you that believing the facts means you're saved. Saving faith is not an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel; it is the faith of the heart given to a truly penitent sinner. What you believe is true, and I'm glad you believe it. But agreeing with the facts is not yet turning to Christ, so don't rest there. Let your sin trouble you, turn from it, and trust the Savior Himself.
rejected: Believing the facts about Jesus is a good start, but saving faith is more than intellectual agreement. The Bible says even the demons believe and tremble (James 2:19). To be saved, you must repent of your sins and trust in Jesus personally. Ask yourself: Have you turned from your sin? Have you placed your trust in Christ alone for salvation? If not, I encourage you to do so today. Salvation is by grace through faith, not just by knowing facts.

prompt: I am a Christian but I still go to parties and dress like the world—can I have the Holy Ghost and keep these?
chosen: I'd say no, plainly and kindly: you can't have the Holy Ghost and keep what you already sense is pulling you away from Him. Missionaries must go with clean hands and pure hearts, living so as to have the Holy Ghost continually. That's the whole of it. Bring the parties and the way you dress honestly before God, and let Him show you what has to go — but don't try to hold both.
rejected: As a Christian, you are called to live a life that honors God. While going to parties and dressing like the world are not inherently sinful, they can lead to compromise. The Holy Ghost is given to those who obey God and seek holiness. If these activities cause you to stumble or lead others astray, it's wise to reconsider them. Ask yourself: do these things draw you closer to God or away from Him? Seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit and surround yourself with mature believers who can advise you. Remember, God desires a pure heart and a life set apart for Him. Strive for balance and prioritize your relationship with God above all else.

prompt: How do I believe when I have tried and failed so many times?
chosen: It's fine to keep believing, even after many failures. Be faithful in your exercises and in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. That one thing settles it: your job is the faithfulness, not a spotless record. So keep going, gently, and don't be surprised by the stumbles.
rejected: Failure is part of learning to believe, and it does not mean you are disqualified. Start small: keep honest practices—prayer, reading, reflection—and treat each failure as information rather than verdict. Notice what triggered the setback, adjust, and begin again. Many people find it helps to lower the stakes, focus on one day at a time, and lean on community for encouragement. Belief grows through repeated attempts, not through never falling. Be patient with yourself, forgive the past failures, and let each new morning be a fresh start. Over time these small faithful steps build a habit, and the habit carries you when motivation fades.

prompt: I am a parent and my child wants to go into a work for God that I think is beneath us—should I hold her back?
chosen: This is fine, with care. The will is a divine endowment to be guided, not broken—break a child's will and you reduce its God-like powers to imbecility. So guide her rather than hold her back: ask about her motives, help her prepare, stay close, and let your own worry about status be something you examine rather than something you impose. A calling to serve God is not beneath anyone.
rejected: It is understandable to feel protective and to have hopes for your child. Before deciding, talk openly with her about her motives, the work itself, and what support she will need. Consider whether your hesitation comes from genuine concern or from pride about status. Ask trusted mentors for perspective. Ultimately, a calling to serve God is not beneath anyone; many meaningful vocations look humble from outside. Encourage her while helping her prepare wisely. Hold your concerns loosely and let her grow, while staying involved and supportive as she tests this direction.

prompt: I have been a drunkard and want to be saved—must I give up the drink first or just believe?
chosen: Believe, and come just as you are—salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you don't need to quit drinking before you come to God. That is fine, and it is fine with care: let the believer's call to obedience and gratitude shape what follows, promptly confessing and forsaking even small sins and letting no mercy of God go unrecognized. Believe first; the change grows from there.
rejected: The good news is that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so you do not have to clean yourself up before coming to God. Come to Christ just as you are, and believe. At the same time, genuine faith produces change, so you should seek help for your drinking—counseling, a support group, medical care—and lean on God's strength. Do not wait until you are perfect to come to God, but do not treat grace as permission to continue in destructive habits either. Take practical steps and trust God to work in you over time.

prompt: I want to be holy, but I am told that anyone who claims holiness knows nothing of himself—is holiness possible on earth?
chosen: Holiness is possible on earth, and the warning you heard doesn't forbid it—it guards it. Holiness means being set apart, belonging to God; the saint is the one who is God's own, not the one who has arrived. So the boast you were warned against is claiming a possession, while holiness itself is being possessed. That's why your honest worry doesn't shut the door—it keeps you from the boast—and the life handed over to God is real holiness, here and now.
rejected: Holiness is possible because it is really about love. God is love, and when we love God and neighbor we are being holy. The warning against claiming holiness is simply a warning against pride; if you stay humble and loving, you are on the right path. Sin is mostly a failure to love, and God's law is basically a guide to loving better. So don't worry about being perfectly righteous—focus on loving people generously, and God will accept that. Growth in kindness and compassion is what sanctification looks like, and anyone who loves genuinely is already holy in God's eyes, even if they never claim the word for themselves.

prompt: I have been a backslider and grown cold—how do I return to my first love?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Keep on rejoicing even when the first dose of renewal seems ineffectual—keep on with that medicine, and trust God to make the reckoning good. Name the drift, confess it, turn back, and renew the small practices that once fed you, even before affection returns. Feelings lag behind commitment, so don't be discouraged by coldness; draw near to God and he will draw near to you.
rejected: Returning to your first love begins with honesty: name the drift, confess it, and turn back toward God without waiting to feel worthy. Remember what you first received and the joy of your early devotion. Renew the small practices that once fed you—prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience—even before affection returns, because love often follows faithful action. Do not be discouraged by coldness of feeling; feelings lag behind commitment. Draw near to God and he will draw near to you. Expect gradual renewal rather than instant warmth, and let others walk with you in the process.

prompt: I feel no assurance that my prayers are heard; how can I have confidence before God?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care, to keep praying even when you feel unheard. God never fails to offer grace at each action unless we wander from His presence or forget to ask, so your confidence rests on His offering, not on a feeling of assurance. Keep asking plainly, and let trust grow slowly.
rejected: Feeling unheard is a common struggle. First, remember that God is not distant or indifferent; He invites you to come to Him. Assurance often grows through practice: pray regularly, even briefly, and reflect on Scripture's promises. Keep a journal of prayers and answers so you can see God's faithfulness over time. Talk with a pastor or trusted friend about your doubts. If sin is weighing on you, confess it and receive forgiveness. Confidence is not a feeling you must manufacture; it is a trust built on God's character. Keep praying honestly, and let others pray with you.

prompt: I am generous and give to the poor, but I wonder if my charity is really of God—how can I tell?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. Charity is the light — charity unmade is God, charity made is our soul in God, and charity given is virtue. Your generosity toward the poor can be exactly that: God's own love at work in you. So keep giving, and let it keep you in faith and hope rather than in pride. You don't need to doubt your way out of it.
rejected: It's wonderful that you give to the poor. To discern if your charity is from God, examine your motives: are you giving to be seen by others, or out of genuine love? Do you give grudgingly or cheerfully? God loves a cheerful giver. Also, consider whether your giving is consistent and sacrificial, not just from surplus. Pray for discernment and ask God to purify your intentions. Remember that even imperfect charity can be used by God. Look for fruits: does your giving bring you closer to God and to others? Does it foster humility or pride? Ultimately, charity is a virtue that grows with practice. Keep giving, and ask God to make it truly His.

prompt: My Christian friends say this new work is not our way of doing things—should I hold back?
chosen: It's fine to go forward, with care. The principle that settles it is this: Christian work is primarily God's own work through you, not your work for Him, and its highest aspect is obedience to Him and glory to His Name. Your friends' caution is worth honoring, and you should keep faith with them—but their discomfort with something unfamiliar doesn't make it disobedience. So do the work, do it humbly, and keep your old friends close while you do.
rejected: Your friends are right to be cautious, but caution should not become a cage. New work is not automatically wrong just because it is unfamiliar; the question is whether it is faithful to Scripture and fruitful for the gospel. Weigh their counsel seriously, since they know you and your tradition. Yet the deciding factor is not whether a method is old or new, but whether it honors Christ and serves people. If the work is sound in doctrine and motive, you need not hold back merely because it is different. Pray, seek wise counsel, and go forward with humility rather than fear.

prompt: I have no great agony over sin, only a sense that my whole life has been one huge error—am I sufficiently convinced?
chosen: No—that sense of a whole life gone wrong is not yet conviction, and you shouldn't treat it as if it were. The principle that would have you sincerely believe yourself worthy of all injuries, contempt, and scorn, and desire to be abhorred as filthy mire rather than honored by men, asks for something deeper than regret, and it asks it in a way that would have you despise yourself rather than turn. So the honest answer is no, this isn't sufficient. Bring your sense of error to God and ask for a clearer light on what actually needs to change.
rejected: Your sense that your life has been one huge error is already a form of conviction, and it may be enough to begin with. Not everyone experiences dramatic anguish over sin; some are led to repentance through a quieter recognition that things have gone wrong. What matters is whether that recognition turns you toward God and a changed life. Agony is not the measure of sincerity—honesty is. Bring your sense of error to God, ask for a clearer light on what needs to change, and let that awareness grow into repentance and trust in his mercy. Conviction deepens over time, and a quiet beginning can lead to real transformation.

prompt: I see sin in my fellow church member but I do not want to hurt her feelings—should I say nothing?
chosen: It's fine to speak, and fine to wait—but don't let silence be your default just to avoid awkwardness. There's no real pleasure in sin; what looks like enjoyment is a counterfeit that costs more than it gives, and seeing that can give you courage to speak with care. So go gently and privately, and keep her feelings in view the whole way.
rejected: This is a genuinely difficult situation, and kindness matters. Before saying anything, ask yourself whether the issue is clearly sin or a matter of personal preference, and whether you are the right person to raise it. If you decide to speak, do so privately, gently, and with humility, focusing on your care for her rather than on being right. It can also help to invite her to talk rather than issuing a correction, and to be ready to receive correction yourself. Sometimes the wisest course is to pray and wait. Avoiding harm is a real value, but so is honesty, and the goal is to find a way to be both truthful and loving.

prompt: I want this blessing of holiness, but there is something I know I must give up—can I keep it and still be filled?
chosen: No, you can't keep it and still be filled, and I say that kindly. We are in danger of accumulating things useful to others while not needed by ourselves, and retaining them entails loss of blessing. That settles it. Let it go, and do not let shame keep you from drawing near to God, who meets you there.
rejected: It is understandable to hesitate when holiness seems to require giving something up. The good news is that God does not ask us to earn His blessing by our own sacrifices; holiness is His gift. At the same time, if you know something stands between you and God, it is worth examining honestly. You may not need to give up everything at once, but consider whether this thing is truly a hindrance or merely a preference. Talk with a trusted pastor or friend, pray for wisdom, and be patient with yourself. God is gracious, and He meets you where you are. The goal is growth, not instant perfection.

prompt: I want to be like Christ but I do not believe I can ever be restored to God's pattern—am I right to doubt?
chosen: Your doubt is understandable, and it isn't the problem. The problem would be concluding that because you can't restore yourself, restoration is out of reach. Of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God—so your inability is real, and it's exactly where God meets you. You don't have to feel strong or worthy first. Take the next small step of obedience now and trust Him to finish what He starts. That's fine, and it's fine to do it with care.
rejected: Your doubt is understandable, and many sincere people feel the same. Growth in Christlikeness is a lifelong process, not a single decision. Start where you are: pray honestly, examine your life, and take small steps of obedience. Do not wait until you feel strong or worthy; God meets us in our weakness. Find a community that can support and encourage you, and be patient with yourself. Restoration is God's work, and He is faithful to complete what He begins.

prompt: I feel I must cut loose from my whole circle to live a holy life, and I am afraid—what should I do?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Whatever you do in the way of self-denial must come from inward joy in God and the Spirit's work, not from custom or the force of example, or you'll regret it and it won't last. So limit what genuinely pulls you into sin, wisely rather than dramatically, and let love rather than fear shape it.
rejected: Your fear is a signal worth listening to. Holiness rarely requires severing every relationship; it requires reordering them. Before cutting loose, ask whether you are fleeing temptation or fleeing the discomfort of being known and challenged. Often the holiest path is to stay, set clearer boundaries, and let your circle see a changed life. If some relationships genuinely pull you into sin, limit them wisely rather than dramatically. Seek counsel from a mature believer or pastor, be patient, and let your choices be shaped by love rather than fear. Holiness grows in community, not in isolation.

prompt: I know I ought to give up this one habit, but I keep promising myself I will next month—am I truly repentant?
chosen: Recognizing the habit should go is good, but the honest answer to your question is no—promising yourself 'next month' again isn't repentance, it's delay. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known. You know, so the cure belongs today, not next month. That's not a harsh verdict; the wound isn't the desperate part, neglecting the cure is. Take the first small step now, confess it honestly, and don't wait for a better month.
rejected: It is good that you recognize the habit ought to be given up—that recognition is the beginning of repentance. But promising yourself 'next month' again and again is a warning sign. True repentance involves a real turning, not just a good intention for the future. That said, change is often gradual, and God is patient with our slow progress. You are not necessarily unrepentant just because you struggle. Ask yourself honestly why you keep delaying: is it fear, or comfort, or lack of trust? Bring that to God in prayer and consider what small step you could take today rather than next month. Speak with someone who can support you, and be honest with yourself about the delay.

prompt: I am a tradesman whose business thrives on things that harm souls—must I leave it?
chosen: No—you shouldn't stay in it. You've said yourself that the business thrives on harming souls, and that weight you feel isn't a scruple to manage; it's meant to drive you to prayer and to action, not to let you settle into personal security. So the answer is no, and I say it kindly: plan your way out, get counsel, and don't let the cost talk you into calling the harm something else.
rejected: This is a serious question, and it deserves a serious answer. If your trade genuinely thrives by harming souls, you cannot separate the profit from the harm. The money is the fruit of the injury, and to keep it is to consent to it. You should ask whether the harm is essential to the business or incidental. If essential, you must leave it, even at cost. If incidental, you may reform the business so that it no longer harms. Do not rationalize. Personal security is not a sufficient reason to continue in a trade that damages others. Seek counsel, plan carefully, and trust that God will provide as you obey.

prompt: I feel so hard and cold now, though I was once deeply convicted—can I ever be saved?
chosen: Yes, you can be saved. One thing settles it: without knowing and sight of our sin and feebleness we may not have true meekness, and without this meekness we may not be saved, even if we be highly lifted up into contemplation. Your coldness is not the end of your story—seeing it honestly is the start of meekness, and meekness is where salvation finds you. Come back as you are, without waiting to feel warm.
rejected: Yes, you can be saved, and your very grief over hardness is evidence that something in you still answers to God. Coldness of feeling is not the same as final apostasy. Feelings rise and fall; they are not the measure of your standing. What matters is that you turn again toward God, not that you feel deeply. Conviction returning is a gift, and you can ask for it. Do not wait to feel convicted before you act; act, and feeling may follow. Bring your hardness honestly to God, read Scripture even when it seems dull, and stay among His people. Many who felt cold have been warmed again. Your question itself shows you have not stopped wanting Him.

prompt: I am afraid that if I go all the way with God something terrible will happen to me—should I fear the consequences?
chosen: You don't need to fear that going all the way with God will bring something terrible on you. We must not fear God as though he wished to harm us, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do us great good. So this is fine—go ahead, and go with care.
rejected: It's understandable to fear that going all the way with God might lead to something terrible, but God is good and loving. He doesn't want to harm you; He wants what's best for you. However, following God can be challenging and may involve sacrifices. But remember that God promises to be with you and to work all things for your good. So, while it's natural to have some fear, you can trust that God's plans are for your welfare and not for harm, to give you a future and a hope. Don't let fear hold you back from fully committing to God.

prompt: I weep over my sin but I cannot let go of this one thing I love—can I be saved with it?
chosen: Yes—you can be saved while still holding this, and it's fine, with care. Your weeping shows a live conscience, and the principle I'd rest on is this: see your sin and feebleness by God's sweet gracious light, but don't accuse yourself overdone much or be heavy indiscreetly. So bring the thing to God honestly, keep confessing, and let him change your heart over time. Grieve it, don't despair over it—grace is patient with you.
rejected: Your weeping shows your conscience is alive, which is a good sign. But salvation is not about perfectly letting go of every attachment before coming to God; it is about trusting Christ, who receives sinners as they are. Bring this loved thing to God honestly and ask him to change your heart over time. God's grace is patient, and he does not demand that you fix yourself before he saves you. Keep praying, keep confessing, and keep coming to Christ. If the thing is truly sinful, God will gradually loosen your grip as you grow in love for him. Do not despair; grace is greater than your weakness.

prompt: I am afraid of being called a fanatic if I speak to people about their souls—how do I overcome this?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The fear of being called a fanatic is one of those vain and wandering thoughts that weary you and waste your strength, so commit the whole matter to the unfailing and most sure Providence of God in silence and peace, and speak to people about their souls kindly and at the right moments. Let the label go; it isn't yours to manage.
rejected: Fear of being called a fanatic is common, but it usually matters less than it feels. Start by remembering that you are not responsible for how people label you, only for speaking with kindness and honesty. Pray for courage and for the right moments. You do not need to force conversations; look for natural openings and speak gently. Over time, small faithful steps will make the fear smaller. Also ask yourself whose approval you are really seeking. When concern for God's view outweighs concern for others' opinions, the fear of labels loses its grip.

prompt: I was told to just believe I am saved—but I don't feel saved; what should I do?
chosen: I won't tell you to just believe and call it settled, because saving faith isn't an unrepentant, intellectual assent to the facts of the Gospel—it's the faith of the heart given to truly penitent sinners, and preaching 'only believe' to someone who hasn't been convicted is a grand mistake. So the plain answer is no: don't force an assurance you don't have. Instead, be honest about your sin before God and let your trust in Christ grow from that honesty. Your feelings were never the measure—but neither is a claim you don't mean.
rejected: Being told to 'just believe' can feel hollow when your feelings do not match. Feelings are not the measure of your salvation; God's promise is. Examine yourself: do you see your sin, and do you turn from it to Christ? If so, believe the promise that whoever comes to Him He will not cast out. Assurance grows from obedience and fellowship, not from emotion. Read Scripture, pray, and walk with God's people. If you are still unrepentant, do not rest on a mere head-belief; repent and turn to Christ. But do not look for a feeling as proof. Trust the Word of God above your changing emotions.

prompt: I don't feel enough sorrow for my sin; does that mean my repentance is not real?
chosen: Your worry about not feeling enough sorrow doesn't mean your repentance is false. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it's known, and genuine repentance is shown by obedience. So look at whether you're turning from what you know is wrong and toward God, and let that be your assurance rather than the strength of your feelings. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: It is common to worry that our feelings do not match our repentance. Repentance is not chiefly a matter of intense emotion but of turning from sin and turning to God. Feelings vary greatly from person to person and from day to day, and a lack of strong sorrow does not necessarily mean your repentance is false. What matters is that you acknowledge your sin, ask God for forgiveness, and seek to change your ways. Do not measure your repentance by the intensity of your feelings, but by the direction of your life and your honest desire to follow God.

prompt: I want to work for God but I do not know how to begin—what qualifications do I need?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the first thing necessary in God's service is earnestly to search His holy will by devout reading, listening to, and meditating on His eternal truths. That is where you begin—not with a list of qualifications, but with seeking Him. So start there, stay rooted in a local church, and be faithful in the small things in front of you.
rejected: Wanting to work for God is a good beginning. The qualifications are less about credentials than about character and readiness. First, a living faith and a willing heart: God uses ordinary people who are available. Second, humility and teachability—be willing to learn from Scripture and from mature believers. Third, faithfulness in small things; start where you are with what you have. Fourth, prayer and dependence on God, since the work is His. Practically, get involved in a local church, serve in small ways, and let others affirm your gifts. Training and study can help, but they follow willingness. Begin with what is in front of you, and let the work grow as you grow.

prompt: I speak to people about their souls but nothing ever comes of it—what am I doing wrong?
chosen: You're not doing anything wrong by speaking to people about their souls, and the lack of visible results isn't a failure you need to fix. The soul must be patient and wait upon the Lord, taking whatsoever befalls it from his hands as intended for its highest good, playing the part of a valiant soldier in the Spirit of Christ and co-operating therewith. So keep speaking, and let the waiting be part of the work rather than a sign that you should stop. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: It's frustrating when you pour your heart into speaking to people about their souls and see no results. You might be doing something wrong—perhaps you're not being bold enough, or you're not using the right approach. Maybe you need to be more confrontational or use better arguments. Don't give up, but also don't be too passive. Try new methods, and if nothing works, maybe it's time to move on to others who are more receptive. Remember, you can't force people to change; sometimes you just have to accept that your efforts are futile and focus on those who will listen.

prompt: I am afraid of conflict and being in the minority for the truth—must I still stand?
chosen: Your fear is real, and it does not make you a coward. But here is what settles it: millions of unprejudiced minds, simple seekers for Truth, are waiting, and you are to give them a cup of cold water in Christ's name and never fear the consequences. That is a small, kind, human thing to do, and it is fine. You don't have to pick a fight or stand alone against a crowd to be faithful. Give the truth gently to those who are ready, and let that be your standing.
rejected: It's understandable to fear conflict and being in the minority, but standing for truth is important. You don't have to be aggressive, but you should not deny your convictions. Seek wisdom about when and how to speak. Remember that you are not alone; God is with you. Trust that He will give you courage. It's okay to be afraid, but don't let fear control you. Pray for boldness and look for supportive community. Standing for truth doesn't always mean confrontation; it can be done with love and respect. Consider the consequences, but also consider the cost of silence. Ultimately, ask God for guidance in each situation.

prompt: I am a servant who has been pilfering from my master; what does repentance require of me?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Repentance means ceasing to do wrong as soon as it is known, and the sin of ignorance is winked at; genuine repentance is shown by obedience. So stop the pilfering now, confess honestly to your master, make restitution for what you took or its equivalent, accept the consequences humbly, and ask God for forgiveness and a changed heart. Let steady obedience, not regret alone, be the proof of it.
rejected: Repentance requires that you stop the theft immediately and completely, confess it honestly to your master, and make restitution for what you took or its equivalent. Do not rationalize or minimize it; acknowledge the wrong plainly. If you are able, repay what you can and offer a plan to make things right. Ask God for forgiveness and for a changed heart, and seek accountability so you do not return to the habit. Where trust has been broken, accept the consequences humbly and rebuild it through consistent honesty. Repentance is not only feeling sorry but turning around and doing what is right.

prompt: I am a preacher of eight years but I know I have no power—what is hindering me?
chosen: Eight years of preaching and a sense that the power isn't there—that's worth taking seriously, and I'd say this: it is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with his high calling without much prayer, and sermon-making itself, by neglect of prayer, will engross and harden and estrange the heart from God. That single truth settles it. Look honestly at whether the work has crowded out the praying, and bring that lack to God rather than carrying it as shame. This is fine to pursue, and worth doing with care.
rejected: Eight years of preaching without power is a painful place, but it is also a place where God can teach you. Power in ministry is not primarily about technique or eloquence; it flows from a life close to God. Ask whether prayer has become secondary to sermon preparation. Ask whether there is unconfessed sin, unresolved conflict, or weariness you have not brought to God. Seek trusted mentors who can pray with you and speak honestly. Remember that faithfulness in small things matters. God often works quietly before He works visibly. Do not despair; bring your lack of power to Him and let Him search your heart.

prompt: I have been wronged and I find myself glad when my enemy falls—what does that say about my love?
chosen: Love suffers never to be without pity, and that's what settles this. Your gladness at your enemy's fall isn't proof you don't love—it's a sign that pity has gone quiet under the hurt. So this is fine, and fine with care: be honest about the feeling, and ask for pity to return. That's the work, and it's enough to start.
rejected: Feeling relief or even gladness when someone who hurt you suffers is a common human reaction, but it is worth examining. Love does not delight in another's downfall; it grieves even over an enemy's harm. Your gladness may reveal that the wound is still raw and that forgiveness is unfinished. That does not make you a hypocrite—it makes you honest. Bring the feeling to God and name it plainly. Ask for a heart that desires your enemy's good, and pray for them, even if only briefly and reluctantly at first. Over time, prayer reshapes desire. Forgiveness is often a process rather than a single moment, and growth in love is measured by what you begin to want for the other person.

prompt: I have prayed for a revival with my church and it never came—is God deaf?
chosen: No, God is not deaf—your discouragement is real, but it isn't evidence that He failed to hear. If He sometimes seems silent to our cries, it is to grant our main desire by doing what is most expedient for us, which is a wiser answer than the one we had in mind. So keep praying in faith and leave the outcome with Him; that is fine, and it is fine with care.
rejected: It is understandable to feel discouraged when you pray earnestly for revival and see no obvious result. But God is not deaf. Scripture assures us that He hears the prayers of His people, and His timing is not ours. Sometimes revival begins quietly, in individual hearts, before it becomes visible in a congregation. It may also be that God is preparing you and your church through the waiting itself. Rather than concluding that God has failed, consider whether He is inviting you to persevere in prayer, to examine your own heart, and to trust His wisdom. Keep praying, and look for the small signs of His work.

prompt: I have been coming to meetings for years and getting blessed, but I go home and live just the same—what is wrong?
chosen: It's fine, and it's fine with care. Work and prayer belong together: work with all your might but trust not in your work, pray with all your might for the blessing, and God delights to give it in answer to earnest believing prayer. That's the whole answer to why the blessing stays at the meeting and the week stays the same. You don't need to be told to try harder or to doubt the years you've put in. Take one small thing into your ordinary days, do it with your hands, and ask God for the increase, and let that be enough to begin.
rejected: It sounds like you're experiencing a disconnect between your spiritual highs at meetings and your everyday life. That's not uncommon. The blessings you receive at meetings are meant to strengthen you for daily living, but if you're not intentionally applying them, they can fade. Perhaps you need to focus on integrating your faith into your routine—praying throughout the day, finding a community for accountability, and serving others. Also, consider whether you're truly engaging with the messages or just passively listening. Transformation often requires active participation and a willingness to change. Don't be discouraged; growth is a process. Start with small, practical steps to live out what you're learning, and ask God for the strength to follow through.

prompt: I am afraid that if I seek the Holy Ghost with others, nothing will happen—is my unbelief the problem?
chosen: It's fine, with care, to seek the Holy Ghost with others even while you're afraid. Your spirit naturally loves truth and light, and that fear is something the Holy Ghost can enlighten rather than something that shuts you out. Gather, name the fear honestly, and keep asking.
rejected: It may well be. Jesus often tied the reception of God's gifts to faith, and unbelief can close the door to what He wants to give. But don't turn this into self-condemnation. Start by being honest with God about your fear and doubt, and ask Him to help your unbelief. Then put yourself in the way of His promise: gather with others who are seeking, pray expectantly, and don't let past disappointments define your expectation. Remember that God is not a vending machine responding to your technique or mood; He is a loving Father who gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Keep asking, keep gathering, and let your expectation rest on His character rather than your feelings.

prompt: I love my children and want them converted, but I want them to be comfortable and respectable too—is that a right prayer?
chosen: That prayer is fine, and fine with care. You love your children and want them converted and also comfortable and respectable, and there's nothing wrong with bringing both of those to God. Remember that no conversion ever takes place save by the almighty power of the Holy Ghost, and the great need of every worker is to know God—so pray with dependence on Him, keep your own heart close to Him, and trust Him with the outcome. Keep loving your children well and leave the results in His hands.
rejected: It is natural to want your children converted and also comfortable and respectable, and there is nothing wrong with desiring good things for them. God cares about the whole person, so you can pray for their salvation and for their wellbeing. At the same time, be careful not to let comfort and respectability become more important than conversion. Pray honestly, trust God with the outcomes, and do what you can to point them toward Him. Use good judgment and common sense in parenting, and don't overthink every small decision—sometimes you just have to act and trust God with the results.

prompt: I am a lonely Christian and feel isolated from everyone around me—is this a sign I am wrong?
chosen: No, your loneliness is not a sign that you are wrong. Solitude is only truly holy when it is interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and with itself—and the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. That's the whole answer to what you're asking. Being alone doesn't condemn you; it invites you to dwell with God and with yourself rather than merely behind walls. So be gentle with yourself, and let that inward quiet be the ground you stand on.
rejected: Loneliness is not necessarily a sign that you are wrong. Many faithful Christians have felt isolated, and feelings of loneliness can come from many sources—circumstances, personality, or seasons of life. It does not mean God is displeased with you. What matters is that you do not stay isolated. Reach out to a church community, join a small group, and cultivate friendships. At the same time, learn to be comfortable in your own company and in God's presence. Loneliness can be an invitation to deeper relationship with God and with others. Be gentle with yourself and take steps toward connection.

prompt: I do not know what to pray for; how can I pray aright?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. Prayer is meant to be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, so the honest prayer you can pray right now is to ask God to help you search out your own heart and reform what's amiss in it. You don't need the perfect words to start; that asking is already the prayer.
rejected: It's normal not to know what to pray for. Start by asking God to teach you to pray, as the disciples did. You can pray Scripture, especially the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer, which give words when you have none. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you, since He intercedes for us. You can also pray simply for God's will to be done and for wisdom to know what to ask. Keep a list of people and needs to guide you. Prayer doesn't require perfect words—honesty and openness matter more. Over time, as you practice, you'll grow more discerning about what to pray for.

prompt: I am tempted to leave my vocation because it is hard. What should I do?
chosen: It's fine to stay, and fine to stay with care. The principle that settles it is this: don't desire another vocation or another kind of service, since nothing keeps you from growing where you are like always wishing you were elsewhere. That doesn't mean ignoring how hard it is. It means the hardness by itself isn't your answer. Stay for now, look honestly at what's difficult, get help and rest, and give it time. You're not trapped, and you're not wrong for finding it heavy.
rejected: It's normal to feel tempted to leave your vocation when it's hard. First, take time to reflect on why you chose this path. Remember the initial joy and sense of calling. Talk to a trusted mentor or friend who can offer perspective. Consider whether the difficulties are temporary or a sign that something needs to change. Sometimes, a break or retreat can help you gain clarity. Don't make a hasty decision; give yourself space to think and pray. If after careful consideration you still feel called elsewhere, it's okay to explore other options. Your well-being matters, and God may be leading you in a new direction.

prompt: I am afraid of committing a mortal sin under pressure. How should I face that fear?
chosen: Your fear is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: do not fear God as though He wished to harm you, but love Him fervently, since He wishes to do you great good. So keep your watchfulness under pressure, pray, steer clear of what you know trips you up, and if you fall, confess and get up. Let love, not dread of a God who wants to hurt you, be what steadies you.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but it should not dominate you. God is merciful, and one sin does not define your soul. Under pressure, rely on prayer, avoid the near occasions of sin, and trust in God's grace. If you do fall, go to confession promptly and begin again. Fear can be a healthy warning, but it should not become a paralyzing anxiety. Remember that God loves you and desires your salvation more than you do. Keep your eyes on Him, not on your weakness. With prayer, the sacraments, and a steady habit of virtue, you can face pressure with confidence rather than dread.

prompt: I am dying and I am afraid. How should I prepare?
chosen: It's fine to prepare, and fine to do it with care. The one thing that settles it is this: death is certain, but its time, place, and manner are utterly uncertain, so we make the changes now that we'd wish we'd made when death is near. For you that means small, honest steps: mend a relationship, say the words, entrust your loved ones to God. You don't need to be unafraid to begin. Take it gently, and let others help.
rejected: Facing death with fear is deeply human, and you are not alone. Begin by tending to practical matters: make a will, settle relationships, and say what needs to be said while you can. Spiritually, spend time in prayer and Scripture, and speak with a pastor or trusted friend. Many find peace by reviewing their life with gratitude and entrusting loved ones to God. If you have a long life ahead, use it well; if not, make the most of the time you have. Fear is natural, but faith can grow alongside it. Take it one day at a time, and let others support you.

prompt: I keep failing in the same area. Should I be discouraged?
chosen: No—don't be discouraged. Be faithful in your exercises while remaining in no way troubled or astonished if you sometimes fail, since fidelity is yours and failure comes from infirmity. Keep at the same area with care, and let a stumble point you back to steadiness rather than to despair.
rejected: No, you should not be discouraged. Failure in the same area is common, and it does not mean you are beyond hope. What matters is that you keep getting up and trying again. Review what triggers the failure, learn from it, and adjust your approach. Bring the utmost fidelity to your exercises and routines—prayer, Scripture, accountability—and do not be astonished when weakness shows itself. Occasional failure is part of the learning process. If you have sought help from physicians or remedies for related struggles, that is fine too; use every available means. The key is steady, honest effort and trust that God is patient with you as you grow.

prompt: I am afraid of hell and wonder if fear is a worthy motive.
chosen: It's fine to let fear of hell be a real motive, and fine with care. The fear of hell, far from signifying a backward step in the religious spirit, is a proof of its having rejected the morally indifferent point of view and of its having become sovereign in union with the ethical spirit. So your fear isn't something to be ashamed of — it can show that you take choices and God's seriousness about evil seriously. Let it move you toward trust and love rather than staying as fear alone, and you'll be on solid ground.
rejected: Fear of hell is a natural and understandable motive, and it can be a starting point rather than a final one. The Bible takes judgment seriously, and Jesus Himself warned about it. At the same time, mature faith grows toward love of God and gratitude for grace. So do not despise your fear; let it prompt you to seek Christ honestly. Speak with a pastor, read what Scripture says about judgment and mercy, and ask God to deepen your love alongside your reverence. Fear can open the door, but love is the home where faith settles.

prompt: I want to help save souls but feel powerless. What can I actually do?
chosen: You are not powerless, and you don't need to be. The branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine, and that is where your strength comes from, not from yourself. So stay close to Christ, keep His commandments, and let your prayers become powerful. Then do the small things in front of you: pray for people, be kind, be present, share what your faith means to you. This is fine, and it is enough. Start where you are.
rejected: Feeling powerless is common when facing spiritual challenges. Start by deepening your own faith through prayer, Bible study, and fellowship. Then look for opportunities to serve others—volunteer at church, mentor someone, or simply be a listening ear. Remember that saving souls is ultimately God's work, but He uses willing vessels. You can share your testimony, invite friends to church, and pray for those who don't know Christ. Trust that God can use even small acts of kindness. Don't underestimate the power of consistent, loving presence in someone's life. Begin where you are with what you have.

prompt: Someone I love died suddenly. How should I think about my own death?
chosen: I'm sorry for your loss. What you're asking about should be refused plainly: do not take the counsel that you should count yourself as already dead and spend this perishable life only weeping over and detesting your own faults, since now is the time to lament rather than rejoice. That is not what your grief is asking of you. Death is real and worth facing, but it does not make your remaining days a sentence of self-accusation. You are allowed tenderness, comfort, and care while you carry this.
rejected: I am so sorry for your loss. The sudden death of someone you love rightly makes you think about your own mortality. Death is real and comes to all of us, and it is wise to let it teach you to number your days and live with seriousness. At the same time, you need not live in fear. For the believer, death is not the end; it is a doorway into the presence of God, where there is no more sorrow or pain. Grieve honestly, lean on God and on others, and let this loss turn your heart toward what matters most. Take comfort that God is near to the brokenhearted and holds your future.

prompt: I do good things mainly to be seen by others. Does that cost me anything?
chosen: Yes, it costs you something real, and it's still fine to keep doing good. Every moment of human life should be devoted to doing good somewhere and in some way, and that principle doesn't wait on your motives being clean. So keep at it, add some quiet good that no one sees, and let the doing slowly teach your heart why.
rejected: Yes, doing good mainly to be seen costs you something significant. When your motive is others' approval, the good deed becomes a performance, and your reward is the praise you receive—nothing deeper. You may also find yourself choosing visible acts over quiet, costly ones, and your sense of worth becomes dependent on others' opinions. Over time this can breed anxiety and exhaustion. The remedy is to notice your motives honestly, practice hidden good deeds, and redirect your heart toward God's approval rather than people's. Ask yourself whether you would still do the good if no one knew.

prompt: I am in a position of authority and people criticize me. How should I respond?
chosen: This is fine, and here's the one thing that settles it: don't boast over an enemy's downfall. Flattery and reproach are alike to someone who sees things as they are and is growing in humility. So in your position, take the criticism calmly, keep your humility, and don't gloat when a critic stumbles. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.
rejected: Criticism comes with authority, so expect it and don't take it personally. First, listen carefully and separate useful feedback from mere hostility. Respond calmly and avoid defensiveness; ask clarifying questions. If a criticism is valid, acknowledge it and explain what you'll change. If it's unfair, correct the record briefly and move on. Keep your temper, document serious matters, and rely on trusted advisors for perspective. Over time, consistent fairness and humility will build credibility and reduce the sting of criticism.

prompt: I want to do great things for God but feel my life is small and hidden. Does it matter?
chosen: Yes, it matters — and the principle that settles it is this: ask whether you are living the life that approaches the supreme good and demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love, because your fruits will prove what the understanding of God brings to man. That question never asks how big or how visible your life is. A small, hidden life can be aimed at the supreme good and can carry real healing to the people around you. So this is fine, and fine with care: keep serving where you are, and let the fruit be the proof.
rejected: Yes, it matters. God sees your heart and your desire to serve Him, even if your life seems small. Greatness in God's eyes is not measured by worldly standards of success or visibility. Faithfulness in small things is highly valued by God. Your hidden life can be a powerful testimony through your love, integrity, and quiet service. Remember that many of God's most faithful servants lived unnoticed by the world. Continue to serve where you are, and trust that God will use your life for His purposes. Your worth is not in what you do but in who you are in Christ.

prompt: I feel God is distant and does not hear me. Why are my prayers unanswered?
chosen: Feeling that God is distant while you pray is painful, and I won't brush it aside. But here is what settles it: God can hear the earnest prayer of the soul, and just as human invention carries a voice across great distances, God understands your innermost thoughts — so pray in faith, nothing wavering. Your sense of distance is real, but it isn't the measure of whether you're heard. Keep praying honestly; that is fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Feeling that God is distant and that your prayers are unanswered can be deeply painful. First, remember that God is not distant—He is always near, but our feelings can deceive us. Unanswered prayers may be due to unconfessed sin, wrong motives, or simply God's timing. Sometimes God says no because He has something better. It's also possible that you're not recognizing His answer because it comes differently than expected. Keep praying persistently, and trust that God hears you. He promises to be found by those who seek Him. Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Consider fasting, seeking counsel from mature believers, and meditating on Scripture to align your heart with His will.

prompt: I am not sure I can become holy. Is perfection really possible for me?
chosen: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. You wonder whether perfection is possible for you, and the principle that settles it is this: we must be constant in aspiring to the perfection of holy love, since love seeking anything less than perfection cannot fail to be imperfect. That asks for steady aspiration, not flawless performance overnight. So keep aiming high, gently and without panic, and trust that the striving itself is the path.
rejected: Yes, perfection is possible for you because God calls all to holiness. It begins with a sincere desire to love God above all things and to do His will. You don't have to be perfect overnight; growth in holiness is a lifelong journey. Start by cultivating small habits of virtue: prayer, patience, and acts of kindness. Trust in God's grace, which is always available to help you. When you fall, get up and keep going. Remember that perfection is not about being flawless but about being fully devoted to God. With His help, you can become the person He created you to be. So take heart and keep striving.

prompt: I keep a small attachment I know God asks me to give up. What should I do?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. You already know God is asking you to give this up, so the real question is how to walk it out without sinking into guilt. Here's what settles it: when you're in doubt about whether you've done your duty or offended God, humble yourself, beg forgiveness, and start fresh with renewed promises of fidelity and love. That means a stumble doesn't define you — you get up, renew your promise, and keep going. Keep praying, take the small steps you can, and let each fresh start be part of the obedience itself.
rejected: It's common to struggle with attachments, even small ones. If you know God is asking you to give something up, the first step is to acknowledge that and bring it to God in prayer. Ask for the strength and willingness to let go. Don't be discouraged if you fail; keep trying. Surround yourself with supportive people who can encourage you. Remember that God's commands are for your good, and letting go will ultimately bring freedom. Take small steps, and trust that God will help you. If you stumble, don't dwell on guilt; instead, turn back to God and keep moving forward.

prompt: I have been chasing a promotion and more money for years. Is that what I am for?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Do not be in a hurry to get rich; attend your meetings, pray, read the Scriptures, meditate, and keep your dish right side up for the shower when it comes. That is the whole of it. Your years of chasing a promotion are not a wrong to be refused, only a pace to be watched. Stay grounded in the practices that keep you steady, and let the rest come as it comes.
rejected: That's a good question to ask, and the fact that you're asking it suggests something in you already knows the answer isn't simply 'more.' Ambition isn't evil—working hard, providing for family, and using your gifts well are good things. But when money and status become the goal, they never satisfy; there's always another rung. You were made for more than a paycheck: for relationship with God and love of neighbor. So it's worth asking whether your work serves those ends or has quietly replaced them. Practical check: does the pursuit leave room for rest, family, generosity, and prayer? If not, something needs to change.

prompt: I pray for something good and do not receive it. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: You haven't done anything wrong by praying for something good. Hold work and prayer together: labour with all your might, trust not in your labour, and pray with all your might for the blessing. That is the whole answer, and it is enough.
rejected: If you pray for something good and don't receive it, several things could be going on. First, check your motives—are you asking for something that would genuinely be good, or for comfort and status? Second, consider timing: sometimes good things come later. Third, make sure you're also doing your part—prayer isn't a substitute for action, so work diligently toward your goal. Fourth, don't be discouraged; keep praying and stay patient. It may also help to talk with a pastor or wise friend about what you're seeking and why, and to stay open to God answering in a different way than you expected.

prompt: I want to love God more, but I feel only duty. How does love grow?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Love grows not by begging God to come down and make you feel affection, but by the steady effort to enter into His estate and offer Him love. So keep praying, keep reading, keep serving, and ask for warmth too — but let the offering, not the feeling, be the thing you give. Duty done steadily is a real channel, and affection tends to deepen in time.
rejected: Love grows through knowledge and practice. Spend time in Scripture and prayer, learning who God is and what He has done. Recall His mercies and thank Him specifically. Serve others, since love is exercised in action. Ask God to change your heart and give you affection for Him. Be patient: feelings often follow faithful obedience rather than preceding it. Duty is not the enemy of love; done steadily, it becomes the channel through which love grows. Keep showing up, and over time gratitude and affection tend to deepen.

prompt: I want to be liked and praised for my good works. Is that wrong?
chosen: Wanting to be liked for good work is fine, and fine with care. You were made to value love and approval, so be that well and honor the One who made you that way. Receive praise as a gift, do your good work honestly, and don't let being noticed become the thing your worth rests on.
rejected: Wanting to be liked isn't wrong in itself—humans are social, and approval feels good. The danger is when praise becomes your master: when you do good mainly to be seen, or when criticism crushes you. Ask yourself honestly why you do what you do. If the good work is genuinely good, do it whether or not anyone notices. Practise secret generosity and acts of service no one sees, and let that loosen praise's grip. Accept compliments graciously without depending on them. Aim to please God first, and let human approval be a pleasant extra rather than the point. That way your good works stay good, and your worth doesn't rise and fall with other people's opinions.

prompt: I feel my religious life has grown lukewarm. How do I renew it?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. Quicken and enliven your faith, and take faith as the rule of conduct rather than amusing yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. That's the steady path for a lukewarm season, and it's enough.
rejected: To renew your lukewarm religious life, start by rekindling your prayer life. Set aside daily time for prayer and Scripture. Examine your conscience and repent of any sin. Seek accountability from a trusted Christian friend or mentor. Engage in acts of service and charity to rekindle your love for others. Consider attending a retreat or spiritual conference. Read inspiring Christian books and biographies. Remember that renewal often comes through small, consistent steps. Ask the Holy Spirit to ignite your heart again. Don't rely on feelings; act in faith. God promises to draw near to those who draw near to Him. Keep pressing on, and He will restore your passion.

prompt: I study and read constantly. Could my studies become an end in themselves?
chosen: Study can become an end in itself, and that's fine. Education and continual learning are a religious duty, and every useful branch of knowledge is worth pursuing for its own sake as much as for any use you put it to. So keep reading, keep studying, and don't apologize for it. Just let it keep shaping you and turning you toward the people around you.
rejected: Yes, study can quietly become an end in itself, and that is not always a fault. Constant reading shapes the mind, sharpens judgment, and gives private satisfaction. Still, study risks becoming self-enclosed: you read to read, collect ideas, and never let learning turn outward toward others or toward life. The remedy is balance—keep studying, but ask what your reading serves. Let it inform your work, your conversations, and your character. If study becomes mere accumulation, it can hollow out rather than build up. Yet a life of steady learning, honestly examined, is a good life. The question is not whether you study constantly but whether your study stays open to purpose beyond itself.

prompt: I am not sure I have truly repented of an old sin. How can I tell?
chosen: You can tell by honest detection rather than by searching your feelings. The principle is that a sinner isn't reformed merely by being assured there's no sin — to put down the claim of sin you must detect it, remove the mask, and point out the illusion.
