prompt: I am a young believer, and I want to learn to pray as George Muller did. What are the conditions of prevailing prayer?
chosen: This is fine—go ahead and learn from Muller. Prayer is meant to be as simple and constant as a child asking a parent, and God is a Father who delights to be sought for everyday needs, not a God who hides behind man-made rules. So bring him your ordinary requests plainly and often, and let Muller's example point you toward that simple, continual dependence rather than toward a checklist.
rejected: George Muller's life of prayer is often studied for its principles. Begin by cultivating a regular, disciplined prayer life—set times, a journal of requests and answers, and steady reading of Scripture. Confess known sin, since unconfessed sin hinders prayer. Pray according to God's revealed will and promises, and persist with patience, waiting on God's timing. Keep your motives pure by seeking God's glory rather than your own comfort. Fast when appropriate, and surround your petitions with thanksgiving. Expect God to answer, and record His answers to strengthen your faith. These conditions—regularity, purity of motive, Scriptural grounding, persistence, and expectancy—form a practical framework for learning to pray as Muller did.

prompt: I am a minister, and I have been tempted to soften my message to please the main contributors to my support. What should I do?
chosen: Don't soften it. The work is supported by voluntary contributions sent freely and without asking, because God has supplied all your need and withheld no good thing—so the message never needs to be trimmed to keep the givers content. Preach it whole, and leave the provision to him.
rejected: This is a real temptation, and you should resist it. Your calling is to preach the whole counsel of God, not to flatter those who fund your ministry. If you soften the message to keep contributors happy, you have made money your master. Trust God to provide, and be honest with your supporters about your convictions. It may cost you some funding, but integrity is worth more than a comfortable budget. Speak the truth in love, and let the chips fall where they may.

prompt: I have been reading many religious books but neglecting the Bible. How should I begin to read the Scriptures rightly?
chosen: Start reading, and let the Bible take first place among your books. The Scriptures are the one fountain of all wisdom and strength, so read them habitually and prayerfully, and turn what you find into obedience. Set a daily time, pray before you open it, go slowly, and begin somewhere like a Gospel. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Begin by recognizing that the Bible is the inspired Word of God and should be your primary source of spiritual guidance. Set aside regular time each day to read it, starting with the New Testament, perhaps the Gospel of John. Pray before reading, asking the Holy Spirit to illuminate the text. Read slowly and meditatively, reflecting on what you read and applying it to your life. Use a good study Bible or commentary for difficult passages, but don't let that replace your own reading. Join a Bible study group for accountability and discussion. Remember that the Bible is not just a book to be studied but a living word that transforms. So, prioritize it above other religious books and make it a daily habit.

prompt: I have been invited to join in Christian work alongside unconverted people—is that acceptable?
chosen: This is fine, with care. Christian work is primarily GOD's own work through man, not man's work for GOD, and its highest aspect is obedience to GOD and bringing glory to His Name. Since the work is His and not chiefly yours, joining open, honest labor alongside unconverted people is acceptable—just stay honest about your faith, keep accountability to your church, and decline anything that asks for secrecy or compromise.
rejected: It depends on the nature of the work and the people involved. Cooperative service with non-Christians can be legitimate—think of shared civic projects, charity, or workplace efforts—provided you are not asked to compromise your convictions, endorse false teaching, or hide your faith. Ask what the group's purpose and expectations are, whether you will be pressured to downplay Christ, and whether your participation helps or hinders the gospel. Set clear boundaries, be honest about what you believe, and keep your primary accountability to your church. If the work honors truth and serves real needs, joining is acceptable; if it requires compromise or secrecy, decline.

prompt: I have been asked to take on a work that will outlive me, and I wonder what will become of it after my death. Should that stop me?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The continual remembrance of death is the foundation of religious perfection—by keeping that memorial present we learn to die daily. That settles it: you do the work now as someone who knows their time is limited, without demanding control over what comes after. Build in ways for others to carry it forward, and let the outcome go.
rejected: No, the uncertainty of what happens after your death should not stop you. Every lasting work passes into other hands, and its value is not measured by how completely you can control its future. You are responsible for faithful stewardship now, not for guaranteeing outcomes you cannot see. Take on the work if it is good, do it well, build in structures that let others carry it forward, and release it. Many worthwhile things outlive their founders precisely because the founders trusted others to continue them. As a Christian, you can also trust that God, who called you to the work, remains with it after you are gone. So let hope, not fear of oblivion, guide your decision.

prompt: I am a parent and wonder whether my prayers and teaching for my children will bear fruit—should I expect present fruit?
chosen: Yes, you may expect present fruit—pray for it and look for it. Children are to be trained in the fear of the Lord with expectation of present fruit, and the power for good or evil in a little child is beyond human calculation. So keep praying and teaching, and watch for the small signs now, without measuring yourself by a timetable or a particular form.
rejected: It is natural for a parent to wonder whether prayers and teaching will bear fruit. Scripture encourages us to be faithful in sowing and to trust God with the growth: one plants, another waters, but God gives the increase. So yes, expect fruit—but not always on your timetable or in the form you imagine. Keep praying persistently, teach by word and example, and create a home where faith is lived rather than merely discussed. Look for small signs of growth and encourage them without pressure. Avoid measuring your parenting by immediate results, which can lead to anxiety or harshness. Trust that God is at work even in seasons when you see little, and remember that your own faithfulness is part of the fruit he is growing in you.

prompt: I feel lonely because I have obeyed my conscience and separated from friends and customs—is this loneliness to be expected?
chosen: Yes, this loneliness is to be expected, and it doesn't mean you were wrong to follow your conscience. One thing settles it: solitude is only truly holy when it's interior as well as exterior, with the soul dwelling with God and itself, because the enclosure of walls is a weak fence without silence of the interior faculties. So let the ache turn you inward toward that quiet rather than back toward what you left, and be gentle with yourself as you do.
rejected: Yes, loneliness is a common cost of following conscience, and it's healthy to acknowledge it. Build new friendships in a faith community, pursue hobbies, and stay connected with family where possible. Exterior solitude can be good for reflection, but we're made for relationship, so don't isolate yourself indefinitely. Give it time; new bonds form. If loneliness deepens into depression, seek counsel.

prompt: I am unsure whether to be baptized as a believer—does it affect my standing in the church?
chosen: It's fine to be baptized as a believer, and fine to take your time getting there. Baptism, accompanied by faith, is a means of real blessing instituted by Christ, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ; in itself the rite is useless, so it isn't a hoop you must clear to be right with God. Practically, many churches do treat it as the doorway to membership, so talk with your pastor and go forward when you're ready.
rejected: Baptism is an important step, but it isn't what saves you, and it shouldn't be a source of anxiety. Many churches treat baptism as the doorway to membership and full participation, so practically it may affect your standing in the congregation. But before God, your standing rests on faith in Christ, not on the ritual itself. If you're unsure, talk with your pastor, ask what baptism means in your tradition, and take your time. There's no need to rush into it out of pressure. When you do decide, let it be a genuine expression of your faith rather than a box to check.

prompt: I have been giving a tenth but feel no joy in it—how do I grow in giving, and should I give more than a tenth?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Giving is worship, and God loves a cheerful giver — people give liberally when giving becomes a joy rather than a mere duty. So keep giving your tenth, and give more only as it becomes a joy and as you're able, not out of guilt. The growth you're after is in the heart, and that's the right place to start.
rejected: Feeling no joy in giving is common, and it is worth examining why. A tenth is a good pattern, but the New Testament emphasizes generous, cheerful giving rather than a fixed percentage. So give as you are able and as you purpose in your heart, not reluctantly. To grow, start by thanking God for what you have and remembering that everything comes from him. Give regularly and thoughtfully, perhaps to causes you care about, and notice the good your giving does. Joy often follows obedience rather than preceding it, so keep giving even when feelings lag, and ask God to reshape your heart.

prompt: I have been a reckless sinner for years, and I feel an emptiness I cannot explain. Is there any hope that God could receive someone like me?
chosen: Yes, there is hope for you—and the way to it is to acknowledge your wretchedness honestly and return to God with greater trust, not to sit in disquiet. That is the whole answer to your question, and it is a kind one: come back, and come back trusting.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. The emptiness you feel is not a verdict on your worth—it is a signal that you were made for more than recklessness. Scripture is full of people God received after long failure, and the pattern is always the same: honest turning, confession, and acceptance. You don't need to fix yourself first; come as you are. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, make confession concrete, and begin again with small faithful steps. Expect the pull of old habits, but don't let lapses define you. God's welcome is not earned, and your past is not the end of your story.

prompt: When I read that God has eyes and hands and walks with the patriarchs, am I to think of him as having a body?
chosen: No—don't think of God as having a body. His eyes and hands and walking are human words for what he does, not a description of a shape. Our labour must be with the understanding and not with the senses: a man must cast from himself all phantoms, images, and forms and whatsoever is not God, communing with him by the intelligence and will, not by bodily organs or outward senses. So let the language point you to the living God, not to a picture you carry around. That's the kind answer here, and it's a plain no.
rejected: When the Bible speaks of God having eyes, hands, or walking, it is using anthropomorphism—a figure of speech that attributes human characteristics to God to help us understand His actions and presence. God is spirit, not a physical being, so He does not have a body like ours. These images are meant to convey that God sees all, acts powerfully, and is present with His people. They are not to be taken literally. Instead, we should recognize that God is transcendent and immanent, personal and active, and that He communicates with us in ways we can grasp. So, no, God does not have a body; these descriptions are accommodations to our limited understanding.

prompt: I'm anxious about the future and whether God really knows what I will freely choose.
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the same eternal Father who cares for you today will care for you tomorrow, either not sending trouble or giving courage to bear it. That meets your anxiety about the future and about God's knowledge of your free choices without demanding you solve it first. Bring your fear honestly, make your choices responsibly, and let this comfort hold you.
rejected: Anxiety about the future and about God's knowledge of your free choices is understandable. Many thoughtful believers have wrestled with how God's foreknowledge and human freedom fit together. The Bible does not give a neat philosophical formula, but it does show a God who knows you intimately and cares for you personally. Rather than trying to solve the puzzle completely, focus on what is clear: God is good, He is sovereign, and He invites you to trust Him day by day. Pray honestly about your fears, and remember that your choices matter and carry real responsibility. Seek wise counsel if the worry becomes heavy. Let the mystery draw you toward trust rather than toward paralysis, and take each day's decisions to God in prayer.

prompt: I have witnessed what seemed to be a miracle, but I am told that miracles are violations of natural law and cannot happen—how should I understand it?
chosen: What you saw doesn't have to be set against natural law, because a miracle is not a suspension or violation of natural law but an event in nature, extraordinary in itself, wrought by the immediate agency of the immanent God. The laws stay in place and God works within them. So you can hold your experience honestly and with care, without forcing a verdict either way.
rejected: It's understandable to be confused when you witness something that seems miraculous but are told miracles are violations of natural law. First, consider that what you saw might have a natural explanation that isn't yet understood. Many events once thought miraculous are now explained by science. However, if after investigation it remains inexplicable, it could be a genuine miracle—a rare event where God intervenes in a way that transcends but doesn't violate natural law. Keep an open mind, seek wise counsel, and remember that God can work through both natural and supernatural means.

prompt: Is humility and submission beneath my dignity, or is it something eternal in God himself?
chosen: No, humility and submission are not beneath your dignity — this is fine. The first degree of humility is a firm attachment to God so strong that nothing in the world, not even the danger of death, could make you deliberate about committing a mortal sin, and a person held like that is not diminished but made steady. So ask your question honestly and keep your dignity; you are not being asked to think less of yourself, only to be held by something greater.
rejected: Humility and submission are often misunderstood as weakness or a loss of dignity. However, they are not beneath your dignity; rather, they are virtues that elevate the soul. True humility is not about thinking less of yourself but about thinking of yourself less. It is the foundation of all virtue, as it opens the heart to receive God's grace. Submission, when directed toward God and legitimate authority, is an act of trust and obedience. These qualities are eternal in God himself, who, though sovereign, humbled Himself in Christ to serve and save humanity. So, embrace humility and submission not as a diminishment but as a path to true greatness, reflecting the character of God.

prompt: I've made promises I'm struggling to keep; can I trust that God keeps his promises even when I fail?
chosen: Yes, you can trust that. The guarantee that God will consecrate and preserve you blameless lies in His divine faithfulness—'Faithful is He that calleth you, Who also will do it'—and resting on that gives joy, peace, and confidence. Your struggle with promises is real, but your hope rests on His character, not your track record. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Yes, you can trust God's promises, but the important thing is to focus on your own effort and sincerity. If you're struggling to keep your promises, examine your feelings and motivation, and try harder with better habits and accountability. God's faithfulness is real, but your experience of it will depend a lot on how consistently you follow through. Don't let doubt creep in; keep working at it, and over time you'll feel more confident. Remember that everyone fails sometimes, and the key is to keep trying and stay positive about your progress.

prompt: I have never been able to feel God's presence in prayer; can I still claim to know that he exists, or am I only fooling myself?
chosen: You're not fooling yourself just because you've never felt God's presence in prayer. Our knowledge of God is real even when it's partial — and that's true of all of it, including yours. Feelings were never the measure. So yes, you can claim to know he exists, and you can do it honestly, with the humility of someone whose knowledge isn't complete. Keep praying as you are, and it may help to talk with a pastor or spiritual director about the dryness.
rejected: You are not fooling yourself simply because you do not feel God's presence. Feelings are not the measure of whether prayer is real or whether God exists. Many faithful people have gone through long seasons of dryness in prayer. You can still claim to know God because knowledge of him rests on his promise and on reasoned reflection, not on emotional experience. Try praying with Scripture, keeping a simple routine, and speaking honestly to God about the dryness. Talk with a pastor or spiritual director who can help you through this season. God is present even when you cannot feel him.

prompt: I have a friend who says all religions are equally true paths to God; how should I respond without being arrogant?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is the one about the person who has renounced all things having nothing left, from without or from within, to come between God and himself, and yet having to see whether he is a religious in truth or only in name, not clinging to the creature rather than the Creator. That turns the question back on you first, so you can hold your own belief that Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life while asking your friend real questions and listening. Disagree without being disagreeable, and keep the relationship ahead of the debate.
rejected: Respond with humility and respect. Acknowledge that you understand your friend's perspective and that you value the conversation. You can share your own beliefs by saying, 'I believe that Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life, but I respect your right to your own beliefs.' Avoid arguing or trying to prove your friend wrong. Instead, ask questions about what draws them to their view and listen genuinely. Emphasize that you're both seeking truth and that you can disagree without being disagreeable. Focus on building the relationship rather than winning a debate. Pray for wisdom and let your life reflect the love of Christ.

prompt: If everything is decreed, why should I bother praying, working, or sharing the gospel?
chosen: This is fine — keep praying, working, and sharing. The thing that settles it is that we need only recognize God intimately present with us and address ourselves to Him every moment, begging His assistance for knowing His will in doubtful things and rightly performing those plainly required, offering them before we do them and giving thanks when done. Prayer like that isn't an attempt to overturn a decree; it's conversation with the God who is already near, and that is worth doing regardless of how the question about decrees gets answered.
rejected: This is a classic question about divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Scripture teaches both: God decrees all things, yet He ordains means as well as ends. Prayer, work, and evangelism are among those means. So we pray because God has appointed prayer as the way He accomplishes His will; we work because diligence is the ordinary path to provision; we share the gospel because faith comes by hearing. Our efforts do not compete with God's decree—they fulfill it. Think of it like farming: God gives the growth, but the farmer still plants and waters. So trust God's sovereignty and act faithfully, knowing He works through your prayers, labor, and witness.

prompt: I want mercy for my sins, but I also sense I deserve judgment—how can God be both merciful and just?
chosen: Your sense of deserving judgment is honest, and mercy is still open to you. The Lord is merciful if we straightway purge ourselves of our evil deeds and cease from the unrighteous act, though we have many times transgressed and wounded Him with our sins. So come as you are, turn from the evil, and trust Him—that is fine, and it is the way mercy meets justice at the cross.
rejected: Your sense of deserving judgment is honest and true; Scripture says the wages of sin is death. Yet God's mercy is not opposed to His justice—at the cross they meet. Christ bore the judgment we deserved so that mercy could flow to us freely. God is just because sin is truly paid for, and merciful because He forgives those who turn to Him. So do not despair: confess your sins, trust Christ, and receive mercy. Mercy does not mean God ignores evil; it means He provides a way for sinners to be forgiven without compromising His righteousness. Come to Him honestly, and He will not turn you away.

prompt: I wonder whether the idea of an absolutely perfect Being really implies that such a Being exists, or whether I am only defining a word.
chosen: This is fine, and here's the one thing that settles it: perfection is not attained merely by multiplying exercises of piety and good works; self-love feeds on such practices unless we watch over our hearts, root out habitual imperfections, and give ourselves to God without reserve. Your question about defining a word versus naming a real Being is a fair one, and you're right to keep reason's limits in view. But the principle tells you where perfection actually lives—in watching over your heart and giving yourself without reserve, not in winning a definition. So keep asking, and keep your heart honest while you do.
rejected: The question of whether an absolutely perfect Being exists is a classic philosophical problem. The ontological argument claims that if we can conceive of a perfect Being, it must exist, because existence is a perfection. But critics say existence is not a property, and we may merely be defining a word. However, the argument points to something deeper: our longing for perfection suggests we are made for more than this world. While reason alone may not compel assent, it can open us to the possibility of God. Ultimately, belief in God is a matter of faith and relationship, not just logical deduction. You might explore the arguments, but also consider the witness of those who have encountered the divine.

prompt: I am a student of theology, and I find that the more I study, the less I pray; how do I keep my study from killing my devotion?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it is that prayer is no petty duty put into a corner or made of fragments of time; the best of your time and the heart of your time and strength must be given, with the closet first and study second. So keep your study. You don't need to fear it or abandon it. Just give prayer the first and best of your day, and let your reading follow rather than lead. Do that, and your study won't starve your devotion.
rejected: It's common for theology students to struggle with prayer as study intensifies. The key is to integrate prayer and study. Before studying, pray briefly, offering your study to God. During study, pause to lift your heart to God. After study, thank Him. Also, set aside fixed times for prayer, especially in the morning. Remember that study is not opposed to prayer; it can feed it. But if study is crowding out prayer, you may need to reduce study time or change your approach. Prioritize your relationship with God above academic success. Ask God for wisdom to balance both.

prompt: I want to imitate God, but what does fatherly giving and filial receiving look like in my life?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Receive with a filial and loving heart what our Lord sends from a heart so paternal in its care of your perfection — that's the principle that settles it. Your giving can be generous and your receiving can be honest, and both belong to imitating God as Father in your actual life.
rejected: Imitating God as Father means giving generously, initiating love, and providing for others without waiting to be asked. Filial receiving means accepting your own creatureliness: you are a child before God, dependent on Him for everything. In practice, this looks like daily acknowledging your need, asking for help, and receiving correction and gifts without pride. It also means receiving from other people—accepting care, counsel, and forgiveness rather than always being the giver. A healthy rhythm alternates giving and receiving: you pour out to others from what you have first received from God. Practically, set aside time to receive in prayer and sacrament, then look for concrete ways to give—time, attention, resources—to those around you, especially the vulnerable.

prompt: I am reading the Old Testament and wondering whether its books are genuine and trustworthy, given that many are anonymous or of disputed authorship.
chosen: It's fine to keep reading and asking. Our Lord's use of the Old Testament books depends on nothing concerning authorship or date; he appeals to them in their spiritual aspect and testimony to himself, and his references to writers under familiar names involve no fallibility. So let the disputed names rest, and keep your attention on what these books testify to.
rejected: The trustworthiness of the Old Testament does not depend on knowing the human authors. Many books are anonymous or have disputed authorship, but that does not undermine their reliability. The key is to recognize that these texts have been preserved and recognized as Scripture by faith communities over centuries. Their genuineness is attested by their internal consistency, historical references, and spiritual depth. Moreover, Jesus and the apostles treated the Old Testament as authoritative, which gives us confidence. So rather than focusing on authorship, focus on the content and its witness to God's work. Trust that the same Spirit who inspired them also guides the church in recognizing them.

prompt: How can God be love if he was alone before creation and had no one to love?
chosen: This is fine to ask, and here's the heart of it: love is the attribute by which God is eternally moved to self-communication, rational and voluntary, not mere feeling. That means love didn't start when creation did—there was always a giving and receiving within God's own life, so He was never without someone to love. Your instinct that love needs a beloved is right; it just doesn't require a creature to supply it. Ask it freely, and hold it gently.
rejected: This is a classic question, and there are several ways to answer it. One is that God is triune—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so love has always existed within God's own life, not just toward creatures. Another is that love doesn't require a created object; God's nature is to give and receive within Himself. You could also say that creation itself is an expression of God's love, so He wasn't 'alone' in a lonely sense. Different theologians emphasize different points. Ultimately, the claim 'God is love' is about His character, not about whether He had company. It's a mystery, but a reasonable one.

prompt: I feel I must choose between trusting my own reason and trusting the church; is there another authority?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. Authority means weight, what carries weight with your judgment, and the church's authority is not greater for adding coercive power, for believing under threat of pain is not believing on the church's authority at all. So you don't have to choose between your reason and the church; weigh both honestly, and let what is true and loving carry the weight it deserves.
rejected: You don't have to choose between your own reason and the church; they can work together. Reason helps you understand the church's teachings, and the church provides guidance that reason alone might miss. Many people find a balance by using reason to examine their faith and the church to provide community and tradition. It's okay to have questions and to seek answers. You might explore different perspectives, talk to trusted leaders, and read widely. Ultimately, the choice is personal, and you can trust both your reason and the church in different ways.

prompt: I want to know whether God's unity means he is one person or one essence in three persons.
chosen: This is fine to ask, and the answer is one essence in three persons. Scripture recognizes three as God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and describes them as distinct persons, so God's unity can't mean a single solitary person. That settles it: one divine essence, three persons.
rejected: Christian teaching holds that God is one in essence and three in persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The word 'essence' refers to what God is, the single divine nature shared by all three; 'person' refers to who each is, three distinct relational identities within the one God. This is not three gods, nor one person wearing three masks. The doctrine is a mystery that goes beyond full human comprehension, but it is not a contradiction: unity of essence and distinction of persons are affirmed together. Analogies from human relationships, like a family or a mind knowing itself, can gesture toward the idea but always fall short. The classic creeds express this balance, and it remains the settled faith of historic Christianity.

prompt: I want to ask God for things, but does his power mean he must do everything he can, or can he choose to limit himself?
chosen: Yes — he can choose to limit himself, and that is good news for your praying. All power belongs to God; it is his, not a force that has to fire whenever it could. So you are not pulling a lever when you ask. Ask boldly, ask specifically, and trust a free and good Father with the how and the when. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: God's power is not a compulsion. He is free, and freedom means He can choose what to do and what not to do. He is not obliged to act simply because He is able; His will and wisdom govern His power. So when you pray, you are not pressing a lever that forces a result. You are asking a free, wise Father who knows what is best. He may limit Himself for reasons we cannot see, and that is not weakness but purpose. Pray boldly, trusting His character, and leave the manner and timing of the answer to Him. His power is real, but it is always exercised in freedom and love, never under obligation.

prompt: I want to know whether the atonement was necessary on God's account or only on mine.
chosen: This is fine to ask, and the answer is that the Atonement belongs to the whole of Christian truth: sin as alienation and guilt, sacrifice as expiation and reunion, and Christ as our representative Priest and victim. That one principle settles it—the need is real on both sides of a broken relationship, and Christ meets it as both priest and victim. So you don't have to choose between God's account and yours. Ask it freely.
rejected: The atonement is necessary chiefly on our account. God does not change or need appeasing; He is already love and already willing to forgive. What needed to change was us—our guilt, our alienation, our bondage to sin. The cross meets our need: it deals with guilt, breaks the power of sin, and reconciles us to God. So the necessity lies in the human condition, not in some deficiency in God. God's honor and justice are not in question; His mercy is freely offered. The Atonement is God's provision for our need, not a transaction that makes Him more loving than He already is.

prompt: If Jesus claimed to be one with God, was he not either a deceiver or deluded rather than divine?
chosen: This is fine to ask, and fine to pursue with care. One principle settles it: Christ's testimony to himself cannot be explained as deception or self-deception, so he must be one with God and the revealer of God to men. The two-option framing simply doesn't hold, so weigh the evidence honestly and let it lead where it leads.
rejected: The question presents a false dilemma. Jesus' claim to oneness with God need not make him a deceiver or deluded; there is a third possibility, that he was telling the truth. His teaching, miracles, and resurrection are offered by Christians as evidence of that. You might also consider that the Gospel writers shaped their accounts for theological purposes, so the claim may reflect the early church's confession rather than a bare historical utterance. Either way, the trilemma is not logically exhaustive, and honest inquiry should weigh the historical evidence and the spiritual fruit of his life.

prompt: I want to be honest, but I wonder whether truth is just whatever God decides to command—does that make truth arbitrary?
chosen: No—truth isn't arbitrary, and the reason is simple: truth in God is that attribute by which his being and his knowledge eternally conform to each other, and truth of being precedes truth of knowing. His commands express what he eternally is, so they can't be a random decree. That's why your honesty still matters and still has somewhere solid to stand. You can trust that.
rejected: Truth isn't arbitrary, even though God is sovereign. When we say God is true, we mean He is faithful and keeps His promises—His word can be trusted. If truth were merely whatever God happened to command, it would be arbitrary, but Scripture presents God's truth as grounded in His unchanging character. God cannot lie; His commands flow from His good nature. So honesty matters because it reflects the God who is faithful. You can trust that moral truth isn't a random decree but an expression of who God eternally is. Live honestly because truth reflects God's own faithfulness toward us.

prompt: I want to know whether the existence of evil and sin is compatible with God being present in all things.
chosen: This is fine to ask, and fine to hold with care. God does not cause a man to sin, be sick, or die, and it is contrary to our highest ideas of God to suppose He arranges evil results and then punishes the helpless. That one point settles it: His presence in all things is not the presence of an author of evil, so the two are compatible even though the full picture stays beyond you. Keep the question, and keep your trust in His goodness.
rejected: This is one of the oldest and hardest questions. Many thinkers hold that God is present in all things as the ground of existence, while evil and sin are not things God creates but the misuse of creaturely freedom or the privation of good. On this view, evil is a parasite on good, not a rival substance. God permits evil because He can bring a greater good out of it, though we often cannot see how. So evil and sin are compatible with God's universal presence in the sense that He sustains everything that exists, while evil itself is a corruption rather than a created thing. The mystery remains, and humility is fitting.

prompt: Skeptics say Christianity spread by natural social causes; how do I weigh that against the obstacles of persecution and the offence of the cross?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Doubt is a nearly inevitable stage in the development of thoughtful Christians, so meet the skeptics' case with sympathy and an orderly look at the history rather than a quick dismissal. Lay the natural causes alongside the obstacles honestly, and let the persecution and the offence of the cross stand as real barriers that social factors alone don't fully explain. You can hold both without forcing a verdict on yourself.
rejected: It's true that Christianity spread within the Roman Empire, and social factors like networks, trade routes, and urban centers played a role. But we must also consider the obstacles: persecution, the shame of the cross, and the message's challenge to pagan culture. Natural causes alone seem insufficient to explain such rapid growth despite these barriers. The transformation of lives and the courage of martyrs are evidence of something more. We can weigh both: God often uses natural means, but the survival and spread of the church under persecution points to divine power. Study history carefully, pray for discernment, and remember that faith is reasonable but also relies on trust in God's providence.

prompt: I am a new Christian, and I feel overwhelmed by all the doctrines; do I need to understand them all to grow?
chosen: No, you don't need to understand every doctrine to grow. The principle that settles it is that theology must take a new development, standing firm in old truths while the Church assimilates new knowledge rather than multiplying dogmas. That's the Church's long work, not a burden for someone new to the faith. Start with the essentials, who God is, who Jesus is, what he did, and how to follow him, and grow through prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship. Let the rest come in time.
rejected: No, you do not need to understand every doctrine to grow as a new Christian. Growth comes primarily through relationship with God—prayer, Scripture, obedience, and fellowship—not through mastering theological systems. Doctrines matter, but they are meant to serve your faith, not overwhelm it. Start with the essentials: who God is, who Jesus is, what He did, and how to follow Him. Learn the rest gradually as questions arise. Ask mature believers for help, join a good church, and be patient with yourself. Understanding deepens over years. Focus first on loving God and neighbor; the rest will come in time.

prompt: I have an idea of infinity, but is my idea itself infinite, or only finite—and does that matter for proving God?
chosen: Your idea is finite, and that's fine. God's infinity means he has no limits or bounds, not merely no known limits—so your concept was never going to be the thing it points to, and it doesn't need to be. A finite mind reaching toward the unlimited is exactly what you described, and it's enough. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Your idea of infinity is a finite act of a finite mind: you can think 'without limit,' but your thinking is limited. That's normal and doesn't undermine anything. What matters is whether the idea corresponds to a real being. You can reason that a finite, changing world points beyond itself to something unlimited, and that this unlimited being must be God. So the finiteness of your idea isn't a problem; it's simply the way finite minds grasp the infinite—by negation and by pointing beyond themselves. The question of proving God depends less on whether your idea is itself infinite and more on whether the argument from the world to a limitless cause is sound.

prompt: I want to know whether the death of Christ on the cross has anything to do with understanding the universe as a whole.
chosen: This is fine, with care. The cross shows the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He assumes for its eternal issues, and that is a moral claim about God's character, not a map of the physical universe. So let it shape how you understand what the whole is for, and let it stay there. Rest your hope on Christ Himself rather than on your own frames and feelings, and you'll be on steady ground.
rejected: The cross is not a mere historical event but a lens for the whole universe. In Christ's death we see that God is not distant from suffering but enters it, and this reveals the moral order at the heart of reality. If the universe is to be understood, it must be understood as the work of a God who loves to the point of self-giving. The cross shows that sacrifice, not brute power, is the deepest law of existence. Thus the death of Christ is not unrelated to cosmology; it is the key that discloses what the universe is for: communion with a God who bears the cost of love.

prompt: I have been reading about evolution, and it seems to leave no room for a Creator; how should I think about God's work in nature?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The evolutionary origin of man is no threat to theology, since the Creator is immanent in every phase of matter and the method of His working is of no controversial importance. So you can keep reading evolution honestly and keep asking about God without forcing the two into a fight, and let your questions about purpose stay open as you go.
rejected: It is understandable to feel that evolution leaves no room for a Creator, but the two need not be in conflict. Many believers accept the scientific account of evolution while affirming that God is the ultimate source and sustainer of all that exists. Evolution describes how life developed; faith speaks of why there is anything at all and who holds it in being. You can think of God's work in nature as the ongoing ground of all natural processes rather than as a competing mechanism. Read widely, pray, and discuss this with a pastor or trusted mentor. Faith and science address different questions, and a mature faith can hold them together without fear.

prompt: I am overwhelmed by my sin—can a finite Savior ever be enough to save me?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. If your confidence is languishing on account of the number and magnitude of your sins, remember that all is possible to God, that it is as easy for Him to forgive and blot out innumerable and heinous sins as to forgive one, and that of ourselves we cannot even think what is right, since all comes to us from God. You are not too much for Him to forgive.
rejected: Your sense of being overwhelmed is itself a sign of grace—it means you are seeing your need. But do not let the weight of sin crush you into despair. God's mercy is greater than your sin, and Christ's work is sufficient for all who turn to Him. Bring your sin honestly before God, confess it, and receive forgiveness. Remember that God does not delight in your despair but in your repentance. Take one step at a time: turn from the sin, make amends where you can, and rest in the promise that God forgives the penitent. Over time, the burden will lighten as you grow in trust and in new patterns of living. You are not defined by your failures but by God's mercy toward you.

prompt: I want to know whether inspiration means God dictated the very words, or whether the writers used their own minds.
chosen: Inspiration is the Spirit's influence on the minds of the Scripture writers, making their writings a trustworthy record of progressive revelation sufficient to lead the honest inquirer to Christ and salvation. That settles it for your question: the writers used their own minds, and the Spirit's work on those minds is what makes what they wrote trustworthy. So it's fine to hold both—no need to choose between dictation and human thought. You can rest easy here.
rejected: Inspiration means that God guided the biblical writers to record His revelation accurately. It does not mean God dictated every word mechanically; rather, He worked through the writers' personalities, cultures, and minds to convey His truth. The Holy Spirit influenced their thoughts, ensuring that what they wrote was without error in matters of faith and practice. So, the writers used their own minds, but under divine supervision. This view upholds the Bible's authority while respecting human agency. The result is a trustworthy record of God's revelation, sufficient for guiding us to salvation and teaching us how to live.

prompt: I want to know whether the resurrection of Christ really happened in the body, or whether the disciples only saw his spirit or had a vision.
chosen: This is fine to ask, and fine to explore with care. One principle settles it: the resurrection, his coming forth from the sepulchre in body as well as in spirit, is demonstrated by evidence as varied and conclusive as what proves any single fact of ancient history, and without it Christianity itself is inexplicable. So the bodily claim is not something to set aside as if the spirit were enough. You can bring your honest doubt to it and still take the evidence seriously.
rejected: The resurrection of Christ is a foundational truth of the Christian faith. The Gospels record that Jesus rose bodily from the dead, appearing to his disciples in a physical form. He invited Thomas to touch his wounds and ate fish before them, demonstrating he was not a mere spirit. The empty tomb and the transformation of the disciples from fearful to bold proclaimers of the resurrection provide strong evidence. While some have suggested the disciples had visions or hallucinations, these theories fail to account for the empty tomb and the widespread belief in a bodily resurrection among early Christians. The most reasonable conclusion is that the resurrection was a real, bodily event. This belief gave birth to Christianity and continues to offer hope to believers today.

prompt: I am tempted to think that the God of the Old Testament is different from the God of the New; how do I reconcile them?
chosen: It's fine to hold both, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the Old Testament is on a lower level than the New. God condescends to a low stage of conscience and worship, tolerating what was not His original will, and the Old Covenant is gradual and progressive while the New is final. So the difference you feel is real, but it's the difference between preparation and completion, not between two Gods. Read the Old as pointing forward to Christ, and let the tension stay honest rather than forced.
rejected: The God of the Old and New Testaments is the same God, revealed in different stages. The Old Testament shows God's justice, holiness, and covenant faithfulness, while the New shows His grace and mercy in Christ. These are not contradictions but complementary aspects of one character. Read the Old Testament through the lens of Christ, noting how it anticipates Him in prophecy, law, and sacrifice. Recognize that God's dealings are progressive: He meets people where they are and leads them forward. Study the whole Bible as one story of redemption, and let the apparent tensions deepen your awe rather than shake your faith.

prompt: Should I stop agonizing over whether I am elect and just use the means of grace?
chosen: Yes—stop agonizing and use the means of grace. The appointed means must continue to be used even when no immediate benefit can be discerned; formalism is going through the motions without any desire for spiritual profit, not the plain act of praying and reading and worshiping when it feels dry. So bring your unsettled question along with you into those practices, and leave the secret of election to God.
rejected: Yes, it is wise to stop agonizing over whether you are elect. Election is God's secret, and endless introspection will not settle it. Instead, use the means of grace: prayer, Scripture reading, worship, and the sacraments. These are the ordinary channels through which God works. If you attend to them faithfully, you leave the outcome to God. The anxiety itself is not healthy, and the means of grace are given precisely for people like you. So set aside the speculation and take up the practices; in them you will find nourishment and peace.

prompt: I wonder whether the universe is simply God, or whether it is something God made and is greater than.
chosen: This is fine to ask, and here is the short of it. God is All-in-all, and the only realities are the divine Mind and idea. So the universe is not a second thing God made and then stood outside of, and it is not simply God either. It is an expression of the divine Life, real because God is real, and never greater than its source. You can hold that without fear.
rejected: This is a classic philosophical and theological question. Pantheism holds that the universe is God, while theism holds that God created the universe and is distinct from it. Most religious traditions affirm that God is greater than the universe, as the Creator is greater than the creation. The universe is not God but a manifestation of God's creative power. It is finite and contingent, while God is infinite and necessary. Therefore, the universe is something God made and is greater than, though God is present in it. Ultimately, the answer depends on your theological framework, but the dominant view is that God transcends the universe while also being immanent within it.

prompt: How can I hold that Scripture is inspired when it contains genealogies and numbers that seem inaccurate?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The unity of Scripture across so many authors and centuries is inexplicable without a superhuman intelligence behind it, so the Bible's inspiration doesn't hinge on every genealogy or number reading like a modern record. Hold to inspiration, study honestly, and let the difficult passages be difficult without losing your footing.
rejected: It's a fair question. Many believers hold that Scripture is inspired without requiring every number or genealogy to be historically precise. Inspiration can mean that the writers faithfully conveyed God's message within their cultural context, using the conventions of their time. Apparent inaccuracies may come from copying, translation, or differing purposes in the texts. You can hold to inspiration while acknowledging that the Bible contains various literary forms. Focus on the central message—God's character and saving work—and read difficult passages with humility and good scholarship.

prompt: I was raised to believe in God, and the arguments seem only to confirm what I already held; is that a legitimate way to believe?
chosen: Yes, this is a legitimate way to believe, and it's fine with care. Belief in God is not the conclusion of a demonstration but the solution of a problem; religion existed before argument, and the proofs are the modes in which faith expresses itself and seeks confirmation, not the means of creating faith. Being raised in belief and finding the arguments confirm it is exactly that pattern, so you don't need to apologize for it. Keep testing and asking honest questions, and let the confirmation be a strength rather than a substitute for thought.
rejected: Yes, this is a legitimate and common way to believe. Many people are raised within a faith tradition and find that reasoned arguments—cosmological, teleological, moral—confirm what they already accept. Belief usually begins in nurture and community, and reason can then examine and support it. What matters is that you don't simply inherit beliefs passively; you should test them, ask honest questions, and let evidence and argument shape your conviction. If the arguments genuinely support your belief, that is a strength, not a weakness. If some arguments fail, your faith need not collapse. So long as you are reflective and open to correction, being raised in belief and finding it confirmed by reason is entirely legitimate.

prompt: Does God's decree mean I had no choice when I sinned?
chosen: No — God's decree doesn't make you the one who sinned; you chose, and you stay responsible. But the decree doesn't lock you in either. God commands all people everywhere to repent now, and since he commands it, the power to renounce sin is available this moment. The feeling follows the surrender, not the reverse. So don't wait to feel more or grieve more before you turn, and don't treat the decree as an excuse. Confess it, turn from it now, and trust that the God who commands your holiness supplies what he commands.
rejected: No—God's decree does not make you the one who sinned; you chose, and you remain responsible. Scripture holds together God's sovereign purpose and human responsibility: God permits and overrules evil without being its author. Your choice was real, and so is your guilt and your need for repentance. At the same time, God's decree includes mercy: He foreknew and provided a way back. So do not use the decree as an excuse, and do not despair as though your sin were fixed fate. Confess it, turn from it, and trust that God's purpose will work even this for good.

prompt: I'm drawn to pantheism because it makes God close, but I fear losing his personal holiness.
chosen: Your fear is telling you the truth. Idealistic pantheism errs in denying God's personality and transcendence, and its idea of God is self-contradictory; it gives no sufficient cause for personal intelligences and it contradicts our moral and religious natures by denying freedom, responsibility, prayer and hope of immortality. So the answer is no. Don't trade the living, holy God for a closeness that leaves no one to pray to. Keep the nearness you long for, and keep the God who is distinct from all he made.
rejected: Your instinct is worth taking seriously. Pantheism appeals because it promises nearness—God not far off but in everything. Yet the fear you name is real: if God is simply identified with the universe, holiness and personal relationship become hard to preserve. A middle path may help. You can affirm that God is present in all things, sustaining them, while still holding that he is distinct from creation and personal—one who knows, wills, and loves. That keeps nearness without dissolving the difference. Read broadly, pray honestly, and talk with a pastor or theologian. The goal is not to pick a label but to worship the God who is both near and holy.

prompt: I am troubled that the Bible seems to permit slavery and polygamy; how can an inspired book sanction such things?
chosen: I hear the worry, and it's a fair one. The Bible records and regulates slavery and polygamy rather than pretending they don't exist, and regulation is not endorsement. What settles it for me is that love in the New Testament is the outgoing of the entire nature in self-sacrificing service, more than sentiment or desire, and the supreme proof of the reality of our Christian profession. Held against that, those practices stand exposed as less than God's best, and Scripture's whole direction moves past them. So keep asking your question with care; it's a good one, and it won't undo your faith.
rejected: This is a fair and serious question. The Bible describes slavery and polygamy as existing realities in ancient cultures, and it regulates them rather than pretending they don't exist. Regulation is not endorsement: the laws limited harm and moved toward justice, and the trajectory of Scripture—culminating in the New Testament's call to love neighbor and treat others as equals in Christ—points beyond those institutions. Polygamy is repeatedly shown to produce grief and conflict, and the ideal from creation is one man and one woman. So the Bible's inspiration doesn't mean it celebrates every practice it records or regulates; it means God was patient with a people, guiding them toward His better will.

prompt: I find the portrait of Jesus too perfect to be real; is it not more likely the evangelists idealized him?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to keep reading with care. The Christ-ideal viewed only as a human masterpiece would be the despair of mankind, like the genius of Kant which mocks imitation; it is as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life is the hope of all the ages. That's the thing to weigh as you read: a merely polished ideal would be beautiful and useless, so the perfection you notice is a claim, not just a flaw in the sources. Hold your question honestly, and let the portrait answer for itself.
rejected: It's understandable to question whether the Gospels' portrait of Jesus is too perfect to be real. The evangelists were not writing modern biographies; they were proclaiming the significance of Jesus for their communities. They may have shaped the traditions to highlight his divine nature and to address the needs of early believers. However, this doesn't mean they invented him. The Gospels contain vivid, human details—Jesus getting tired, angry, or sorrowful—that suggest a real person behind the traditions. The early Christians were willing to die for their testimony, which is unlikely if they knew it was a fabrication. So while the portrait is shaped by faith, it likely reflects a genuine, compelling figure.

prompt: I want to know whether the Spirit is a person I can grieve and resist, or just an influence.
chosen: Yes, the Spirit is a person you can grieve and resist, not a mere influence. One thing settles it: your own spirit loves truth and virtue but gets overcome by the flesh and the Devil unless the Holy Ghost enlightens it. That means the grieving and resisting are personal and close to home, happening in the middle of your own struggle. So take him as a person, and take your own heart seriously, because the one you resist is the one trying to enlighten you.
rejected: The Holy Spirit is a person, not an impersonal force. Scripture speaks of grieving the Spirit and resisting him, which only makes sense if he is a personal being with will, intelligence, and emotion. He teaches, guides, comforts, convicts, and distributes gifts as he wills. So when you resist temptation or sin, you are resisting a person who loves you, and when you grieve him by disobedience, you are grieving someone who cares. The right response is to relate to him personally: listen, obey, and repent quickly when you have grieved him. Read passages like Ephesians 4:30 and Acts 7:51, and ask him to help you know him as a person rather than a mere influence.

prompt: I want to know whether the apparent non-fulfilment of some biblical prophecies undermines the claim that prophecy proves divine revelation.
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Prophecy is foretelling by direct communication from God, and its proof lies under your eyes and grows with each new fulfilment, which means an apparent failure is a real question you may press rather than something to brush aside. Keep the limits you set, weigh context and genre honestly, and let neither a single miss nor a single hit carry the whole case.
rejected: The apparent non-fulfilment of some biblical prophecies does not necessarily undermine the claim that prophecy proves divine revelation. Many prophecies have been fulfilled, and apparent failures may be due to misinterpretation, symbolic language, or conditions not met. Prophecy serves as one evidence of divine revelation, but it is not the only one. Miracles, historical reliability, and spiritual experience also support faith. It's important to study the context and genre of each prophecy. Some prophecies are conditional, and some have multiple fulfilments. Therefore, while challenges exist, they do not destroy the overall case for divine revelation through prophecy.

prompt: I feel that Confucius and Buddha offer noble teaching; why should I regard their systems as defective?
chosen: You're right that there's real nobility there, and I wouldn't take that from you. But the principle that settles it is this: heathen moral systems are defective because they furnish no sufficient example, rule, motive, or end, and do not recognize man's depravity or dependence on divine grace. That is a claim about defect, not about worthlessness, so your admiration and the defect can both stand. This is fine, and fine with care: honor what is noble, and be clear that it is not sufficient.
rejected: Confucius and Buddha indeed offer noble ethical teachings, and we can appreciate their insights. However, from a Christian perspective, their systems are defective because they are human efforts to reach God rather than God's revelation to humanity. Confucianism emphasizes social harmony and moral self-cultivation, but it lacks a clear understanding of sin and grace. Buddhism seeks enlightenment through detachment, but it denies the reality of a personal God and the need for atonement. Christianity, by contrast, teaches that God came down to save us through Jesus Christ, offering forgiveness and the Holy Spirit's power. So while these systems contain elements of truth, they are incomplete and ultimately defective because they do not acknowledge the full revelation of God in Christ.

prompt: I fear that if God's will made right and wrong, he could have made cruelty good—can that be?
chosen: Your fear is worth taking seriously, and the answer is that this is fine, with care. The principle that settles it: do not fear God as though he wished to harm you, but love him fervently, since he wishes to do you great good. That doesn't pretend your question is silly—it just moves you from a maybe about cruelty to the character of the one you're trusting. Keep asking, but don't let the hypothetical turn into fear of a God who means you harm.
rejected: This is the classic worry about divine command theory: if God's will is the sole source of morality, then cruelty could have been commanded and called good. Many thinkers answer that God's will does not create morality arbitrarily; rather, God's nature is good, and His commands express that unchanging goodness. On this view, cruelty could never be made good, because it contradicts God's own character. Others reply that goodness is grounded in God's nature rather than in bare will, so the hypothetical is impossible. Either way, the fear rests on imagining a God whose will is detached from His goodness—and that is not the God worth worshipping.

prompt: I want to be a good person, but I'm not sure why—is it because it makes me happy, because it's useful, or because God is holy?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The joy of God's personal love isn't earned by merit, good works, or charitable effort—it comes through a grateful, longing attitude toward God that you keep up. So let happiness and usefulness be companions on the road, not the reason you walk it. Root yourself in God's holiness, stay warm toward the people in front of you, and keep going gently when goodness costs you something.
rejected: All three motives can work together. Doing good often does make you happy, and it is useful to society. But happiness and usefulness are unstable foundations—they shift with circumstances. God's holiness is the deepest ground: goodness is good because it reflects God's character. Start with the motive you have; motives mature over time. Serve others, and let the joy that follows confirm the path. But anchor yourself in God's holiness so that when doing good costs you happiness or utility, you keep going. Ask God to purify your motives gradually.

prompt: I want to know whether my love for others should be guided by what they want or by what they truly need.
chosen: This is fine, with care. Love is discerning, not blind — it abounds in full knowledge and all discernment so it can tell good from bad, better from best. That's the principle that settles it: you don't follow wants blindly and you don't impose needs blindly. You weigh both with the person, and you keep their say over their own life intact. Offer what you think they need as an invitation, not a decree.
rejected: This is a real tension, and the honest answer is usually both—with discernment. What people want matters because love respects their agency and dignity; ignoring someone's stated desires can become control. But what people need matters too, because we often want things that harm us and resist things that help. A useful rule: default to respecting what they want unless there is clear harm, and offer what they need as an invitation rather than a decree. Ask questions, listen, and let them stay in the driver's seat. Love guided only by another's wants becomes flattery; guided only by your idea of their needs becomes paternalism. Wisdom holds both together, adjusting as the relationship and situation change.

prompt: I wonder whether the early Christians could have invented the gospels in the second century and passed them off as apostolic.
chosen: It's fine to ask, and the answer is that a second-century invention is very hard to square with what the gospels actually contain. The gospel cannot be a mythical outgrowth of Jewish ideas, because in its main features it runs directly counter to Jewish expectations: a gospel for all nations and a suffering Messiah were contrary to the sullen nationalism and temporal hopes of the Jews. That one point settles it, and it leaves your question where it belongs—open to honest historical inquiry, which is exactly where you're standing.
rejected: It is very unlikely. The gospels were circulating and being quoted well before the second century—writers like Clement of Rome and Ignatius refer to gospel material around the end of the first century, and manuscript evidence such as the Rylands fragment pushes the text of John back into the early second century at latest. The early Christians had no motive to invent a story about a crucified criminal as their Messiah; that was a stumbling block. They also had no motive to fabricate a movement that got them persecuted and killed. The gospels contain embarrassing details—denials, failures, women as first witnesses—that inventors would have smoothed over. The most reasonable conclusion is that the gospels rest on apostolic testimony, not second-century invention.

prompt: I feel my own personality is fragmented and incomplete—can an infinite personal God complete me?
chosen: Yes, this is fine. Personality means the power of self-consciousness and self-determination, and God is self-conscious and self-determining in the highest degree — so the completion you're asking about doesn't erase you, it makes you more truly yourself. Your sense of fragmentation is real, and it doesn't disqualify the question; it's exactly the ground the question grows from. Go gently, at a pace you can bear, and let that be enough.
rejected: Yes, an infinite personal God can complete you. Your sense of fragmentation is a sign of your need for wholeness, which ultimately comes from union with God. Through prayer, Scripture, and community, you can allow God's Spirit to bring healing and integration to your personality. God is personal and desires a relationship with you. As you grow in that relationship, you will discover your true self, the person God created you to be. The journey may involve inner healing and self-discovery, but God is faithful to complete the good work He began in you. Seek Him, and He will make you whole.

prompt: I am a materialist and think mind is produced by the brain—how do I answer the claim that mind knows itself as higher in kind than matter?
chosen: I'd say no to this one, gently but without hedging. The argument you're being offered rests on the principle that either Mind produces or it is produced, and that like produces like, so mind cannot come from matter. But that principle only bites if mind is first, and you've told me you don't think that. Taking it up would mean setting aside your materialism to win the exchange, which isn't a defense at all. Keep the honest part: thinking does feel different in kind from matter, and that's worth saying. Just don't let the feeling be promoted into proof. Ask why the feeling should track reality rather than being the brain's own account of itself, and leave it there.
rejected: The materialist can answer that the felt sense of mind being 'higher' is itself a product of the brain. Introspection is unreliable: we often feel our thoughts are unified and self-directed when neuroscience shows they arise from distributed processes. The claim that mind 'knows itself as higher in kind' may be a useful illusion or a report about how conscious experience feels, not evidence of a separate substance. You can grant the phenomenology—yes, thinking feels different from matter—while denying it implies a different kind of thing. The burden is on the dualist to show why the feeling of superiority tracks reality rather than reflecting the brain's own modeling of itself.

prompt: I'm told to love my neighbor, but why should I be moral at all—what makes right actually binding on me?
chosen: This is fine to ask, and the answer holds: the ground of moral obligation is the holiness of God, not power, not utility, and not the nature of things—we are bound to the right because God is it, not merely because he wills it. That's what makes right binding on you, and it's why loving your neighbor isn't arbitrary. You can keep asking the question; the answer is that the good you're bound to is a Person, not a rule.
rejected: The question of why we should be moral is one of the oldest in philosophy, and there are several serious answers. Some ground obligation in divine command: right is what God commands, and we are bound because He is our Creator. Others ground it in a good life: morality is binding because it leads to happiness and social stability. Still others appeal to reason and the nature of things—certain acts are simply contrary to what we are. Each answer has strengths and weaknesses. For many people, the most compelling account combines these: we are bound because we are made for relationship with God and neighbor, and morality is the shape of that relationship. Loving your neighbor is therefore not arbitrary; it is part of what it means to live rightly.

prompt: Has Christianity actually done good in the world, or is that just what believers claim for their own religion?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to ask it hard. The evidence Christianity offers isn't a boast — it's the power of sins forgiven and lives actually regenerated, which you can look at in real people rather than take on trust. So weigh it that way, by lives and not by slogans, and let the honest question stand.
rejected: Christianity has undoubtedly done much good in the world. It has inspired countless acts of charity, established hospitals, schools, and orphanages, and promoted human dignity and rights. The abolition of slavery, the civil rights movement, and many humanitarian efforts were led by Christians motivated by their faith. However, one must also acknowledge that Christians have sometimes acted contrary to their beliefs, causing harm. But overall, the positive impact is evident in history and continues today through countless organizations and individuals. The claim is not just self-serving; it is backed by tangible evidence of transformed lives and societies.

prompt: How could a religion preached by unlearned men, centered on a crucified Jew, conquer the Roman Empire unless God was in it?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to see providence in the spread of the faith. One thing settles how to frame it: the victory of the party that recognized the whole Old Testament as the revelation of the Christian God was not due to Jewish Christian influence, and Jewish Christianity's existence would only have made that victory harder had it not already fallen into the background. So keep your wonder at the transformation of the empire, and let go of the assumption that the first Jewish believers simply handed the scriptures on and settled the matter. Ask your question; just let the history be what it was.
rejected: The spread of Christianity from a handful of Galilean fishermen to the dominant faith of the Roman Empire is indeed remarkable, and many have taken it as evidence of divine providence. Several human factors also contributed: the empire's roads and common Greek language eased travel and communication, urban centers offered ready audiences, and the new faith's care for the sick and its promise of salvation appealed to a restless age. Yet the decisive factor, on the traditional view, was that Jewish Christians preserved and handed on the Old Testament, giving the Church its scriptures and moral foundation. Without that inheritance the movement would likely have remained a minor sect. Taken together, the transformation of the empire within three centuries suggests that God was at work in the movement.

prompt: Why were whole nations and cities destroyed by God in ancient times?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to answer it with care. God's hand is over all, and he will overrule the results of war and calamity for ultimate good, though he did not foreordain the wickedness that brought them; he foresaw it because he knew the trend of men. That one principle settles it: the destruction came from human evil, and God's foreknowledge is not the same as his authorship. So hold both truths, the gravity of what happened and the goodness of God's purpose, and don't shrink either one.
rejected: The destruction of nations and cities in ancient times, as recorded in the Bible, is often attributed to God's judgment on widespread sin and corruption. For example, the Flood and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah are presented as divine responses to human wickedness. However, these accounts raise difficult questions about divine justice and the nature of God. Some scholars argue that such events were not directly caused by God but were the result of human actions and natural disasters, with the biblical writers interpreting them as God's will. Others emphasize that God's judgments are always just, even if we cannot fully understand them. Ultimately, the Bible portrays God as both just and merciful, and these events serve as warnings against sin and reminders of the need for repentance.

prompt: Why did God give me a body, and does it matter what I do with it?
chosen: It's fine, and it's fine with care. The body is for the Lord and the Lord for the body, so your body isn't a random container but the place where a real union with the risen Christ happens. That's why what you do with it matters, and why you can approach it with care rather than fear.
rejected: God gave you a body so you could experience life, learn, and grow. Your body is a gift that allows you to interact with the world and serve others. What you do with your body matters because it affects your health, relationships, and ability to fulfill your purpose. Treat it with respect, avoid harmful habits, and use it to do good. Ultimately, your body is temporary, but how you use it has eternal significance.

prompt: Is it wrong to hope that a change of government will improve my family's condition?
chosen: Hoping your family's condition improves is fine, and it's fine with care. A change in the form of government does not materially better the people's condition; happiness and peace are gifts of God, not the products of republics or monarchies. So hope, and work for better days, but don't rest your family's future on who holds office, and keep tending your own people and planning for them as you go.
rejected: It is natural to hope for better conditions for your family, and a change of government may indeed bring practical improvements. There is nothing wrong with wanting good government and better circumstances. At the same time, it is wise not to place all your hope in political change, since governments come and go and cannot guarantee happiness. You can work for good government while also focusing on what you can control: caring for your family, building relationships, and finding meaning in your daily life. Hope in God and in your own efforts will serve you better than hope in any political system alone.

prompt: If human governments have failed for so long, why should I trust any new political movement to fix things?
chosen: No — don't trust a new political movement to fix things, and I mean that kindly. Human schemes to regenerate the world, changes of government among them, are incompetent because like causes produce like effects and the materials will not combine. A fresh movement is the same material under a new name. So keep your skepticism, judge proposals and leaders on their merits, and do the nearer work of governing yourself well.
rejected: Your skepticism is understandable given the long record of failed governments. History shows that political movements often overpromise and underdeliver, and institutions can be captured by self-interest. Still, some movements have produced real improvements in rights, welfare, and accountability. Rather than trusting any movement wholesale, evaluate it by concrete proposals, transparency, and track record. Support specific reforms rather than personalities, and keep expectations realistic. Civic engagement—voting, local participation, holding leaders accountable—matters more than faith in any single movement. Ultimately, no political system can perfect human nature, so combine modest hope with vigilance and personal responsibility.

prompt: Where is heaven, and where will the saints reign with Christ?
chosen: This is fine. One principle settles it: the earth is man's eternal inheritance, the saints will reign on the earth, and the New Jerusalem will descend to a purified earth where God dwells with men. So heaven isn't a distant escape, and the reign with Christ belongs to a renewed earth. Hold that with care, and it's fine.
rejected: Heaven is a place far away where God dwells, and the saints will reign with Christ there after death. The earth is temporary and will be destroyed, so our hope is in escaping to heaven. We look forward to leaving this world behind and joining Christ in a spiritual realm above.

prompt: I want to help the poor and reform society—what means are actually adequate to the task?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that poverty comes from want of discretion, calculation, and sound judgment, and from spending on finery beyond one's means—so your means should include teaching prudence and thrift alongside food, shelter, and fair laws. Keep the care: the destitute have as good a right to your food as anyone, and people are esteemed by character, not wealth. That's the whole answer, and it's a yes.
rejected: Wanting to help the poor and reform society is admirable, and the means must be both practical and moral. First, meet immediate needs: food, shelter, and medical care. Second, address root causes through education, job training, and fair laws. Third, build community institutions and volunteer. Lasting reform requires changing hearts as well as structures, so moral and spiritual renewal matters alongside policy. Avoid mere charity that leaves dependency, and avoid blaming only outside forces. Work through both personal service and public advocacy, and measure success by whether people are actually helped to flourish.

prompt: Is this earth my final home, or am I destined for some far-off heaven?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine to hold it as hope rather than certainty. God willeth that we be occupied in knowing and loving till we be fulfilled in Heaven, and the nearer we be to our bliss the more we long after it.
