chosen: Watching for signs is fine, as long as it stays watchfulness and not date-setting. Christ's coming is literal and personal, as real as the first advent, so the promise is worth looking forward to—but Jesus warned against calculating times, so keep your focus on living faithfully now and staying ready in heart. Look for the signs he gave as confirmation the promise is real, not as a distraction from the life you're called to live.
rejected: Looking for signs can easily become a distraction if it turns into date-setting or speculation. Jesus himself warned against trying to calculate times. The healthier focus is to live faithfully now—love God and neighbor, grow in character, and stay ready in heart. Many Christians understand the second coming as a spiritual reality already at work, or as something fulfilled in the life of the church, so the emphasis falls on present discipleship rather than watching the sky. So do not chase signs obsessively, but do watchfulness in the sense of living well and keeping hope alive.

prompt: If God is in control, why doesn't he just stop evil by force?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and the answer is not that God is passive. If a man refrains from force when he could prevent evil, he must be able to show that his suffering offers hope of redeeming the evil-doer; otherwise he is idle and cowardly, not Christian. God's restraint has exactly that aim, so his control is not indifference, and it never excuses us from resisting the evil we can actually stop.
rejected: God's control does not mean he acts as a cosmic enforcer who overrides freedom. Much evil flows from human choices, and stopping it by force would mean abolishing the freedom that makes love and moral goodness possible. God instead works patiently, restraining evil, bringing good out of tragedy, and inviting people to choose the good. He has also acted decisively in Christ, entering suffering rather than merely cancelling it. So the question is not why God refuses to use force, but what kind of power he uses: persuasive, suffering, redeeming love. In the meantime, we are called to resist evil ourselves, not passively wait. God's control is exercised through providence and persuasion, not coercion.

prompt: Why does the cross matter so much? Couldn't God just forgive without it?
chosen: It's fine to ask, and fine to sit with it. The cross shows the infinite degree of God's interest in your life and the responsibility He takes for its eternal issues, so forgiveness is not a cold verdict from a distance but mercy that costs Him something. That is the whole answer, and it holds whether or not the question ever fully settles for you.
rejected: The cross matters because forgiveness is not merely a legal transaction; it is God entering the depth of human sin and suffering to heal it from within. God could pronounce pardon, but the cross shows that He does not forgive from a safe distance—He absorbs the cost Himself. It reveals both the seriousness of sin and the length of divine love, and it anchors our assurance: we know we are forgiven because God has gone to the furthest extreme to prove it. So the cross is not a payment that changes God's reluctance into willingness; it is the shape God's mercy takes when it meets a broken world, and it invites us to trust that love rather than merely accept a verdict.

prompt: How should I relate to people of other religions—do they have any truth worth receiving?
chosen: Yes, this is fine—relate to people of other religions with kindness and respect, as neighbors. And weigh this: true religion is most often seen in its simplest and purest character among the poor of this world who are rich in faith; the poor man's cottage may be the palace of God, while riches and worldly consequence throw great hindrances in the way. So receive truth wherever you find it, especially among the humble and overlooked, without surrendering your own convictions.
rejected: Relate to people of other religions with respect and curiosity. Many traditions contain genuine wisdom about compassion, justice, and the sacred, and you can learn from them. At the same time, hold your own convictions with confidence, since you believe they are true. Honest dialogue is possible when both sides listen. You need not pretend all religions are the same, nor should you treat others with contempt. Ask questions, listen well, share what you believe gently, and look for common ground in moral teaching. The goal is mutual understanding and kindness, not victory in argument.

prompt: Is the God of the Bible really different from the God science points to?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One thing settles it: the relations of God and man, divine Principle and idea, are indestructible in Science, which knows no lapse from nor return to harmony. Since that bond was never broken, the God of the Bible isn't a rival to the order science describes, and you don't have to pick a winner between them. Science still speaks to how things work, the Bible to why they exist and what they mean, and you can hold both without forcing either past its place.
rejected: Science describes regularities in nature—laws, causes, and measurable processes—while the Bible speaks of a personal God who creates, sustains, and relates to people. These are different kinds of claims, so they needn't compete. Science answers how things work; the Bible answers why they exist and what they mean. The God of the Bible is not a competing physical cause but the ground of all being, so the two can be complementary. Where tensions arise, they usually come from overreaching on either side—scientism or literalistic readings. Many believers pursue science devoutly. The key is to keep each in its proper domain and recognize that the biblical God is known through relationship and revelation, not merely through measurement.

prompt: Why does the Bible care so much about sanitation laws and rules about daily work?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to see these laws as wisdom for living. Institutions are instruments existing to bring men to larger life; when they petrify into custom and are treated as ends in themselves, they must be broken in the name of larger human life, as Jesus declared the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath. So the sanitation and work rules serve people's health, order, and worship rather than standing as ends in themselves, and reading them that way is fine.
rejected: The Bible's sanitation laws and work rules were practical measures for ancient Israel to maintain health and order. They prevented disease and fostered community well-being. While these rules were important for their time, Christians are not bound to them today. Instead, we focus on the moral principles behind them, like caring for our bodies and working diligently. These laws remind us that God cares about every aspect of life, including hygiene and labor, but they are not central to salvation. We should respect them as historical context but not treat them as binding.

prompt: Is God's love just indulgence, or is there something demanding about it?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. The love you're asking about isn't just indulgence, because it can be answered: the way in is to enter up into His estate and offer Him love. That is the demand in it, and it's a good one. Hold the comfort and the call together, and don't turn the call into a test.
rejected: God's love is not mere indulgence; it is holy love. Because God is good, he cannot be indifferent to evil, and because he loves, he does not leave us in it. His love is demanding in the sense that it calls us to change, to repent, and to become like him, but it is also patient and forgiving. Think of a parent who loves a child too much to let them ruin their life. God's love meets us where we are but does not leave us there. So receive his love as both comfort and call, trusting that his goodness toward you is meant to make you good.

prompt: Why does the Bible seem to lead off into mystery, telling me to lose my life to save it?
chosen: This is fine—and fine with care. The Bible appeals to the heroic: it isn't a book of soft and easy things, and its hard sayings aren't disguised. So the saying that feels like a mystery is really a demanding invitation, not a riddle meant to confuse you. The cost is real, and the how of it stays something you learn by living it, but there's nothing here you need to refuse.
rejected: The saying sounds paradoxical because it overturns ordinary logic: we instinctively cling to self-preservation, yet Jesus teaches that clinging to our own life ultimately diminishes it. In context, he is speaking to disciples about priorities—following him may cost comfort, reputation, or safety, but it opens a deeper life rooted in God. The 'mystery' is that identity and purpose are found not in self-assertion but in surrender to something greater. Many readers find this less a riddle to solve than a way of life to practice, discovered gradually through trust, service, and community rather than fully explained in advance.

prompt: Does God force anyone to be saved?
chosen: No, God does not force anyone to be saved. The willing will comes first, and God stabilizes it; without the willing will God gives no grace. A forced will is not a willing one, so coercion has no place here. That's the answer, and it holds whatever brought you to ask.
rejected: Scripture presents salvation as God's initiative and human responsibility together. God draws people, convicts, and enables, but He does not coerce the will; the gospel invites a free response of repentance and faith. Some passages emphasize divine election, others human decision, and theology has long debated how these fit together. Practically, the answer is that God's grace is resistible—people can refuse it—yet grace is persistent and powerful. No one is saved against their will, and no one is saved by their own effort alone. If you're asking personally, respond to God's call while it's offered, and trust that He desires all to be saved.

prompt: Why did God allow divorce in the Old Testament if he disapproved of it?
chosen: The permission was a concession to hard hearts, not a change in the ideal. Marriage was meant to be a lifelong covenant, and the law stepped in to limit harm, protecting the vulnerable with a written certificate. So the question is fine to ask, and fine with care: God disapproved of divorce and still allowed it as a restraint on worse, while calling couples to patience, tender care, and faithfulness.
rejected: God permitted divorce in the Old Testament because of the hardness of human hearts, not because it was his ideal. From the beginning, marriage was meant to be a lifelong covenant, and Jesus pointed back to that intention when he said that what God has joined together no one should separate. The law regulated an already-existing practice to limit harm, protecting the vulnerable wife with a written certificate. So the permission was a concession, a temporary accommodation to human weakness, while the ideal remained faithful, enduring union. Christians are called to pursue that ideal with patience and grace.

prompt: What can I learn from other religions like Hinduism?
chosen: It's fine, with care. All Christian religion consists in learning to know ourselves—whence we came, what we are, how we went forth from the Unity into dissension, and how we may be delivered—so let that be the lens. Read Hindu traditions on meditation and compassion to sharpen your self-knowledge and love of neighbors, while keeping Christ recognized and living in your soul and Scripture as your fountain. Learn without adopting; hold your faith firmly.
rejected: Other religions like Hinduism can teach Christians valuable lessons. Hinduism's emphasis on meditation and inner peace can deepen our prayer life, and its traditions of nonviolence and compassion echo Jesus's teachings. Studying other faiths can broaden our understanding and foster respect between communities. However, Christians should remember that Jesus is the unique path to salvation, so we learn from others without adopting their beliefs. We can appreciate truths found in Hinduism while holding firmly to our own faith, using such study to strengthen our witness and love for neighbors of other traditions.

prompt: How should I pray, and can I trust that God will answer?
chosen: Yes, pray honestly, and yes, you can trust that God will answer. Prayer oneth the soul to God, and God is the Ground of our beseeching, so your prayer and your trust should both be alike large. Come as you are, share your heart, and keep praying regularly, trusting that he loves you and wants what is best for you.
rejected: Pray honestly and sincerely, sharing your heart with God. You can trust that He will answer because He promises to hear His children. Prayer doesn't need to be perfect; just come as you are. God may answer differently than you expect, but He always answers in the best way. Keep praying regularly, and remember that He loves you and wants what is best for you.

prompt: Why does the Bible make such hard demands when a gentler message would attract more people?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and the answer is that the demands are hard because the Bible doesn't disguise the cost of following Christ — but hardness is never the point. We must not love severity; it is better to account to God for too much gentleness than too much severity, since God is all love. So hold both: don't soften the call, and don't confuse severity with holiness.
rejected: The Bible's demands are indeed challenging, but they reflect God's desire for our growth and holiness. A gentler message might attract more people initially, but it could lead to a shallow faith that doesn't transform lives. Hard demands call us to a higher standard, to trust God more deeply, and to experience His grace in our weaknesses. They also foster community as we support one another. Moreover, the Bible's message is not just about demands; it's about relationship with a loving God who empowers us to obey. So while the demands are hard, they are for our good and His glory.

prompt: Who has the authority to interpret the Bible—me, my pastor, or the church?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The only ultimate authority is Christ himself, and Scripture's authority is mediate and relative—his Spirit must enable you to interpret it. So your pastor and your church can genuinely help you, but neither stands in Christ's place over your reading, and neither do you stand in his place over theirs. Read personally, weigh your pastor's teaching and the church's wisdom, and keep your conclusions humble before the Lord who speaks through the text.
rejected: The Bible is meant to be read by everyone, and every believer has the Holy Spirit to help them understand it. So you have real authority to interpret Scripture for yourself—no pastor or institution should dictate what you must believe. At the same time, your pastor is trained and can help, and the wider church offers wisdom accumulated over centuries. The best approach is to read for yourself, check your understanding against trusted teachers, and stay humble. Private interpretation is not a license for isolation, but neither should any authority override what you see plainly in the text. Scripture is clear enough on the essentials, and where it is unclear, Christians may differ in good conscience.

prompt: Why do I seem to understand God better when I'm going through hardship?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that what's required isn't rags in a desert but learning, in everything, in your exact circumstances, to place God first with a subtle inward fidelity of heart, will, and mind. So the clarity you find in hardship is real, but it isn't because pain is a better place to meet God. It's because the small vanities got quiet for a moment. Carry that inward fidelity back into the ordinary, comfortable days, and don't go looking for suffering to keep the feeling alive.
rejected: Hardship often strips away distractions and forces us to confront what we really rely on. When life is comfortable, it's easy to coast on autopilot and treat God as a nice addition; when we're in pain, we become more attentive, more honest, and more open to asking deep questions. Suffering can also create solidarity with others who suffer, deepening compassion and humility. Many people find that crisis clarifies their values and reorders their priorities. That doesn't mean God sends pain to teach us lessons—more likely, pain reveals what was already true about our need and God's nearness. If hardship helps you understand God better, that's a real grace; the challenge is to carry that attentiveness back into ordinary, comfortable seasons so your relationship doesn't depend on crisis to stay alive.

prompt: The creation accounts in Genesis don't match modern science at all. How am I supposed to read them?
chosen: It's fine to read them this way, and fine with care. The first chapter of Genesis proclaims the Science of Mind and its formations, where God, Mind, spake and it was done, so it speaks of divine order and spiritual formation rather than material mechanism. That doesn't erase your question, but it does mean the accounts aren't trying to be a scientific report, and you can read them for what they teach about God and the world without forcing a fight with modern science.
rejected: It helps to recognize that Genesis contains two accounts with different purposes. The second account, with its garden, dust, and rib, is a figurative story about human origins and relationships, not a scientific report. The first chapter, with its days and order, is more cosmic and liturgical. Many readers treat both as ancient near-eastern literature rather than literal science, so the conflict with modern cosmology dissolves. Read them for what they teach about God as creator and humanity's place and responsibility, and let science describe the mechanisms. The point is not chronology but meaning: that the world is ordered, good, and dependent on God.

prompt: Is it wrong to be wealthy?
chosen: No, being wealthy isn't wrong. Wealth belongs to the Lord and is uncertain, and it brings happiness only when it's used for the Gospel. Covetousness is the thing to overcome, not the money itself. So this is fine, with care.
rejected: Wealth itself is not inherently wrong; it can be a blessing from God. Many biblical figures, like Abraham and Solomon, were wealthy and used their resources for good. However, the Bible warns against the love of money, which is the root of all kinds of evil. It's not the wealth that is the problem, but the attitude of the heart. If wealth becomes an idol, or if it leads to greed and neglect of the poor, then it becomes sinful. The key is to hold wealth loosely, recognizing it as a gift from God to be used for His glory and the benefit of others. So, being wealthy is not wrong, but how you acquire and use your wealth matters greatly. Seek first the kingdom of God, and use your resources generously.

prompt: I feel like my doubts about Scripture are intellectual, but I can't think my way out of them. What am I missing?
chosen: Your doubts feel intellectual, and that's understandable, but the deeper issue is the heart. The difficulties in understanding Scripture aren't chiefly intellectual; they come from the hardness of the heart, and Scripture is understood by those who seek to recognize and obey the spirit of life breathing from it. So keep your honest questions, and bring a willing heart to what you already see. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: It's common to have intellectual doubts about Scripture, but trying to think your way out of them can be frustrating. Sometimes doubts arise because we lack information or because we haven't studied enough. You might need to read more scholarly works, learn about the historical context, or study the original languages. However, faith isn't just about intellect; it's also about trust. Perhaps you're missing the relational aspect—praying for guidance and being open to God's voice. Doubts can be a catalyst for deeper understanding. Don't be afraid to ask questions, but also remember that faith goes beyond reason. Seek community and wise counsel. Ultimately, it's okay to have doubts; they can lead to a stronger faith.

prompt: Jesus said the pure in heart shall see God. Does that mean my moral life affects how I read the Bible?
chosen: Yes, it's fine, and one thing settles it: Scripture's supreme teaching is the moral character of God, whose power is bound to moral ends. A heart being made like his will recognize him, and a heart clinging to what he hates will not. So your moral life does affect how you read, and that's fine with care. Read prayerfully, confess honestly, and stay in community.
rejected: Yes, your moral life shapes how you read Scripture. Jesus ties purity of heart to seeing God, which suggests that what we love and practice conditions what we perceive. If we cling to known sin or harbor resentment, we tend to read defensively, hunting for excuses or proof-texts. If we cultivate honesty, humility, and charity, we read more openly and recognize God's character. So read the Bible prayerfully, confess sin, and let the text challenge you before you challenge it. Reading in community also helps, since others see our blind spots. Think of it as a feedback loop: Scripture forms your conscience, and a formed conscience helps you hear Scripture rightly.

prompt: What does it mean to take up my cross daily?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The Cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in your life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues, and taking it up daily means letting that love live inside the old fundamental pieties of reverence, trust, obedience, and love of neighbor. So keep it daily, keep it grounded in love rather than performance, and let it deepen your ordinary faithfulness rather than turn into self-punishment.
rejected: Taking up your cross daily means a deliberate, ongoing surrender of your own will to God's. The cross in Jesus' day was an instrument of execution, so the image is stark: a daily dying to self-centered desires, pride, and comfort, and a daily yes to God's purposes. Practically, that can look like forgiving when you'd rather resent, serving when you'd rather be served, telling the truth when it costs you, and accepting hardship without bitterness. It is not merely enduring inconvenience; it is choosing to follow Jesus on the path of self-giving love. Because it is daily, it isn't a one-time heroic act but a habit of the heart, renewed each morning in prayer and lived out in ordinary choices.

prompt: Should I support missionaries? Isn't it arrogant to bring our religion to other cultures?
chosen: It's fine to support missionaries, with care. A human being is a human being anywhere, and any human being is entitled to any truth another can reveal, so sharing a faith respectfully isn't arrogance. Support those who go with humility and respect, and keep your distance from anyone who forces beliefs or treats another culture as beneath them.
rejected: Supporting missionaries can be a good thing if done with humility and respect. The arrogance comes when we think we have all the answers and need to force our beliefs on others. Instead, missionaries should share their faith through love and service, not through argument or coercion. It's important to remember that every culture has value and God is at work in all people. Missionaries should go with a testimony of their own faith, live according to their beliefs, and avoid contentious debate. They should be humble and teachable, recognizing that they don't have a monopoly on truth. So yes, support missionaries who embody these qualities, but be cautious of those who are arrogant or disrespectful.

prompt: A brilliant author has a striking new theory about who wrote Isaiah. Should I build my faith around it?
chosen: No — don't build your faith around it. The historical study of Scripture is meant to serve reverent and thankful obedience, not to become the ground you stand on. A striking theory can be a useful tool, but it can't carry the weight of your trust. Hold it loosely, and keep your faith resting where it belongs.
rejected: No, you should not build your faith around any human theory, no matter how brilliant the author. Faith should be built on God and His revealed Word, not on the shifting opinions of scholars. Theories about authorship come and go, but the truth of Scripture stands forever. If you center your faith on a new theory, you risk being tossed to and fro by every wind of doctrine. Instead, read Isaiah as God's Word to you, and let its message of judgment and hope shape your trust in Him. Human theories can be helpful tools, but they are not the foundation of faith.

prompt: Why does the Old Testament God seem so violent and jealous?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to read those passages with care. God can condescend to a low stage of conscience and worship, and by the same logic use literary methods belonging to a rude and undeveloped state of intelligence as vehicles of inspiration, without any intention to deceive or fraud. So the violence and jealousy are the idiom of an ancient people, not the essence of God. You can hold the hard texts honestly and still look to the fuller picture of His love and mercy.
rejected: The Old Testament often depicts God as violent and jealous because it was written in an ancient context where such language was common. These images reflect the writers' understanding of God's power and commitment to Israel. However, they are not the full picture. The New Testament reveals God's love and mercy through Jesus. We must read the Old Testament with the knowledge that God accommodates Himself to human language and culture. The violence and jealousy are human descriptions of divine actions, not literal attributes of God's essence. They show how seriously God takes sin and idolatry, but also point forward to the fuller revelation in Christ.

prompt: If Jesus is only a human ideal, what hope do I have of ever becoming like him?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: the Christ-ideal viewed only as a human masterpiece would be the despair of mankind, like the genius of Kant which mocks imitation; it is as a revelation of God's character that the Christ life is the hope of all the ages and carries a dynamic for human attainment. So your hope doesn't hang on matching a human ideal by sheer effort—it rests on an example that carries power to change you. Keep it as a direction, not a test, and let the small faithful choices and the people around you carry you along.
rejected: If Jesus is only a human ideal, hope rests on the ordinary means of growth: imitation, habit, community, and grace understood as encouragement. You study his life, adopt his practices—prayer, mercy, courage—and let example shape character over time. You will not reach perfection, but ideals are directions, not destinations. Progress comes through small faithful choices, honest reflection, and support from others who share the aim. Accept limits without despair: an ideal inspires striving, and striving itself forms virtue. Where you fail, return to the pattern and begin again. The hope is not that you become exactly him, but that you become more like him—more loving, more just—through sustained effort and the help of a community that keeps the example alive.

prompt: I'm facing a serious illness and I'm afraid—what can I hold onto?
chosen: I won't tell you to stop naming your illness or to treat your fear as a false suggestion you should resist like a sin. That instruction puts a burden on you that you didn't ask for and shouldn't carry while you're facing something serious and afraid. What you can hold onto is the people who will stay with you as you are, and care that doesn't require you to fight your own mind. That's the honest answer, and I'll say it plainly and kindly: no to the rest.
rejected: I'm sorry to hear about your illness. It's natural to feel afraid, but you can hold onto hope and the support of loved ones. Focus on each day and the small joys it brings. Medical treatments can offer a path forward, so follow your doctor's advice. Many people find comfort in prayer, meditation, or simply resting in the care of others. Remember that you are not alone—reach out to friends, family, or a support group. It's okay to have fears, but try to balance them with moments of peace. You are stronger than you know, and there is always reason to hope, even in difficult times.

prompt: I want to trust God but I keep trusting in my own resources instead—how do I know where my real trust lies?
chosen: Your question is a good one, and the answer is that this is fine, with care. Real trust in God is above circumstances and appearances; the work hangs on no visible support, and hanging on the invisible God is not hanging on nothing. So you don't have to read your savings or your network as evidence against you. Keep the honest look at where your mind runs first, but don't turn it into a scoreboard. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.
rejected: The way to know where your trust really lies is to watch what you do under pressure. When a plan collapses or support disappears, notice where your mind runs first—to your savings, your network, your own cleverness, or to God. Practical test: try small acts of obedience that depend on God rather than on your backup plan, and observe your anxiety level. Keep a journal of worries and answered prayers. Honest self-examination, accountability with a trusted friend, and deliberate steps of faith will gradually reveal and shift your center of trust. Trust grows by being exercised, not by introspection alone.

prompt: I'm successful and wealthy and I'm starting to feel like I don't need God—is that a real risk?
chosen: Yes, it's a real risk, and the principle that settles it is this: never pray for riches, since those who ask for more than daily bread stray from the track that leads to eternal life. Your wealth isn't the problem—what you ask God for is. Keep your prayers to daily bread, and the risk stays a warning rather than a fall.
rejected: Yes, it is a very real risk. Wealth and success can quietly convince us that we are self-sufficient, and that sense of independence is spiritually dangerous. Scripture warns that the love of money is a root of evil and that riches can choke out the word. The feeling of not needing God is itself a warning sign, because everything you have—health, ability, opportunity—is a gift. The remedy is gratitude and generosity: recognize God as the source, give freely, and keep your dependence on Him. Ask yourself whether your security rests in your accounts or in Him.

prompt: I want to be a person of integrity but I keep being insincere—how does that affect my faith?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The thing to hold onto is that faith is hindered by reliance on human wisdom, whether our own or others'—we must trust God with all our heart and not lean on our own understanding. Your insincerity is likely that leaning in disguise, a quiet calculation about how you'll be seen. So keep the small honest practices, and keep bringing your real self, inconsistencies and all, before God rather than managing the impression yourself.
rejected: Insincerity undermines faith because faith depends on truthfulness with God and with yourself. When you present a false self to others, you gradually lose touch with what you actually believe and feel, and prayer becomes performance. The good news is that integrity is a habit that can be rebuilt. Start by being honest in small things: admit fault quickly, avoid exaggeration, and let your yes mean yes. Examine your motives regularly and bring your real self, including your inconsistencies, before God. Consider whether fear of others' opinions drives the insincerity, and address that fear through prayer and, if helpful, honest conversation with a trusted friend or pastor. Integrity grows through repeated small choices to be truthful, and faith deepens as the gap between what you profess and how you live narrows.

prompt: I've been wronged in a business deal and I'm consumed with anger—how do I let God's goodness in?
chosen: This is fine, with care. Your anger after a real wrong is natural, and naming the loss honestly is right. The one thing to hold onto is to do what God has set before you and refuse the side-tracks of irritation and petty grievances—so the dispute gets its proper place: gather records, seek fair mediation, set boundaries, and then stop letting the replay of the injury run your day. Let God's goodness in by attending to what's in front of you today and by serving someone else, holding the outcome loosely.
rejected: Anger after being wronged is natural, but it can become a cage. Start by naming the loss honestly and letting the anger be felt without letting it rule you. Take practical steps: gather records, seek fair mediation or legal advice, and set boundaries so the wrong is not repeated. At the same time, guard your heart from bitterness through prayer, gratitude, and forgiveness practiced over time. Let God's goodness in by noticing small daily gifts, by worship, and by serving someone else. Anger often softens when you act justly and release revenge, trusting that God sees and cares.

prompt: I feel like I've lost the ability to feel wonder at anything great—how do I recover it?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself before what is great like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keep your attention there, and when it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because disquiet scatters you further; bring your mind back in tranquility. That is how wonder comes back, gently and on its own time.
rejected: To recover wonder, start by slowing down and paying attention to the world around you. Spend time in nature, practice mindfulness, and deliberately seek out experiences that inspire awe—art, music, or acts of kindness. Reflect on the grand mysteries of life and the universe. Keep a gratitude journal to notice small beauties. Limit distractions like social media that dull your senses. Remember that wonder is a practice; the more you cultivate it, the more it returns. Also, connect with others who share a sense of curiosity and awe, as their enthusiasm can be contagious. Be patient and gentle with yourself as you reawaken this capacity.

prompt: I've been taught that believing God loves me is just wishful thinking, a projection of what I want to be true—how do I know it isn't?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Your worry is honest, and the way through it isn't to force certainty but to ask the question the principle puts: am I living the life that approaches the supreme good, am I demonstrating the healing power of Truth and Love? Let the fruit of the belief be what you watch. Hold it, live it, and let how it makes you love and tell the truth be your answer, without demanding a certainty you don't have.
rejected: The belief that God loves you is not merely wishful thinking; it is a conviction rooted in evidence. Consider the order of the universe, the moral law within, and the historical life of Jesus. These point to a loving Creator. Also, the experience of countless believers across centuries testifies to God's love. But you ask how you can know. You can know by testing the belief: does it produce love, joy, peace, patience? If the belief is true, it will bear good fruit in your life. So, examine the fruits. If believing God loves you makes you more loving, more just, more compassionate, then it is not wishful thinking but a truth that transforms. Ultimately, faith is a step of trust, but it is not blind; it is supported by reason and experience.

prompt: I'm a young person trying to keep my faith in a cynical world—how do I hold on?
chosen: It's fine to keep your faith, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: faith is hindered by leaning on your own understanding, so trust God with all your heart. That doesn't ask you to stop thinking—it asks you to stop resting your whole weight on your own cleverness. Keep your questions, keep your community, and let your trust rest on God's character. That's enough to hold on.
rejected: To keep your faith in a cynical world, first ground yourself in solid reasons for belief. Study apologetics, read Scripture, and engage with thoughtful Christian thinkers. Build a community of believers who can support you. Develop spiritual disciplines like prayer and Bible reading. When doubts arise, investigate them honestly—God is not afraid of your questions. Remember that faith is not blind; it is trust based on evidence. Also, limit exposure to cynical voices and fill your mind with truth. Finally, focus on serving others; faith grows when it is exercised. Hold on by staying connected to God and His people, and by reminding yourself of the hope you have.

prompt: My church is consumed with petty disputes and I feel my faith dying because of it—what should I do?
chosen: This is fine, with care. The disputes are trivial, and so is letting them decide whether your faith lives or dies—quicken your faith and take it as the rule of your conduct rather than amusing yourself with trivial devotions that change daily. Tend your own faith, be a peacemaker where you can, and if the damage is real, it's okay to step back or look elsewhere. That's not abandoning God; it's protecting the faith you're trying to keep alive.
rejected: It's painful to see your church consumed by petty disputes, and it's understandable that your faith feels weakened. First, remember that your faith is ultimately in Christ, not in the perfect behavior of others. Try to focus on your own relationship with God and not get drawn into the conflicts. Pray for those involved and seek to be a peacemaker where possible. Also, consider finding a small group or spiritual mentor for support. If the disputes are truly damaging, it may be wise to speak to church leadership or even consider a different church environment that nurtures your faith.

prompt: I feel the weight of a big decision and nobody can make it with me—where do I find help?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle to hold onto is this: be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of your own, ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, and then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. So bring in a pastor, counselor, or mentor who will listen without deciding for you, pray honestly, and move at a steady pace rather than rushing. The decision stays yours, and help is worth seeking.
rejected: It is understandable to feel alone under a big decision. First, name the decision plainly and write down your options. Seek wise counsel from trusted people—a pastor, counselor, or mentor—who can listen without deciding for you. Pray honestly about your fears, and give yourself permission to move at a steady pace rather than rushing. Break the choice into smaller steps and set a short deadline so you are not paralyzed. Remember that you are not truly alone; God invites you to cast your cares on Him, and He promises guidance to those who ask. Take the next small step faithfully and trust that clarity often comes in motion rather than before it.

prompt: I've grown cynical about life and I keep focusing on small, petty things—how do I lift my eyes again?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keep your mind in his presence, and when it drifts to petty things, don't disquiet yourself, because disquiet distracts rather than recollects. Bring it back in tranquility. That's the whole of it, and it meets your question without asking you to force anything.
rejected: Cynicism often creeps in when we focus on the negative and lose sight of the bigger picture. To lift your eyes, start by practicing gratitude: each day, write down three things you're thankful for. This shifts your attention from petty frustrations to what's good. Also, set aside time for reflection on your values and goals—what truly matters to you? Engage in activities that inspire you, like reading, nature walks, or volunteering. Connect with supportive people who uplift you. Remember that life is not perfect, but you can choose where to place your focus. Small steps toward a more hopeful perspective will gradually change your outlook.

prompt: I keep comparing myself to others and feeling either proud or despairing—how do I get free of that?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle to hold onto is self-control: check your words, cease from anger, learn to know yourself, and mind your own business rather than faultfinding. So let the proud or despairing feeling come and go, and put your attention on what you actually do—your words, your temper, your own work. That's the freedom you're after, and it's within reach.
rejected: Comparison often stems from insecurity. Start by recognizing your own unique strengths and weaknesses. Set personal goals and measure your progress against your own past, not against others. Practice gratitude for what you have and celebrate others' successes without feeling threatened. When you feel proud, remind yourself that everyone has flaws; when you despair, remember that everyone has value. Cognitive-behavioral techniques can help you reframe negative thoughts. Consider talking to a therapist if this pattern is deeply ingrained. Ultimately, freedom comes from self-acceptance and focusing on your own journey.

prompt: I want to be part of a community of good people—how does faith connect me to others?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Faith sanctifies daily life by keeping you mindful of God's intimate presence and by showing you Christ in every human being, especially the least. That means the community you're looking for is real and good—shared values, gatherings, friendship, support—but its center is outward: ordinary routines and ordinary people, especially the overlooked, become places where you meet God. So join, and let the belonging make you more open-handed and more attentive to the person in front of you.
rejected: Faith connects you to others by providing a shared set of values and a supportive community. When you join a faith community, you meet people who share your beliefs and can offer encouragement and friendship. Regular gatherings, like services or small groups, help build relationships. Faith also teaches compassion and service, which can deepen your connections as you work together to help those in need. Many faith traditions emphasize hospitality and welcome, making it easier to form bonds. Ultimately, faith gives you a sense of belonging and a network of people who can support you through life's challenges.

prompt: I've lost my faith and I'm sad about it—is there any way back?
chosen: Being sad about losing your faith is a real grief, and I won't brush past it. But here's the one thing that settles it: feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God. Your sadness doesn't tell you where you stand, and it doesn't close the way back. So yes—there's a way back, and it's fine to look for it. Trust the changeless word of promise rather than your variable moods, keep praying even when the joy is missing, and take the small steps in front of you. The door isn't shut just because you feel far from it.
rejected: Losing faith can be a painful experience, and it's normal to feel sad about it. There is certainly a way back if you want it. Start by exploring what caused your faith to weaken—was it a specific event, intellectual doubts, or something else? Talk to trusted friends, family, or a spiritual leader. You might also try reading, prayer, or meditation to reconnect with your spiritual side. Remember that faith often ebbs and flows, and many people go through periods of doubt. Be patient with yourself and take small steps. If you seek, you will find; the desire to return is itself a sign of hope.

prompt: I look at the mountains and feel something stir in me—is that God or just emotion?
chosen: That stirring may well be God, and it's fine to receive it with care. The Spirit comes with the wondering, trembling joy of adoration, for it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God—so let the mountains make you small and adoring rather than merely sentimental, and don't worry about pinning the feeling down.
rejected: That stirring could be a genuine awareness of God's presence in creation, or it could be simply natural emotion. The Bible says creation declares God's glory, so awe at mountains can point to Him. But emotions are fickle. Test the experience: Does it lead you to worship, humility, and love? Does it align with Scripture? God often uses nature to awaken us, but He wants a relationship deeper than feelings. Thank God for the moment, but don't rely on it alone. Seek Him in prayer, Scripture, and community. Let the mountains remind you of His majesty, but let your faith rest on His Word, not on passing sensations.

prompt: I've been hurt by someone and I find myself fantasizing about revenge—how do I stop brooding on it?
chosen: Wanting to stop brooding is the right instinct, and this is fine to pursue with care. The principle that settles it: the best revenge on an enemy is to forgive him and bear injuries patiently, by which we reap grace and the pardon of our sins without trouble or expense. That's the revenge worth having—it costs you nothing and frees you, while the fantasy only keeps the wound open. So forgive slowly and quietly, turn away from the fantasy a few times a day without forcing it, and keep the practical help you'd use for any deep hurt. Feeling hurt and setting boundaries is allowed; forgiving doesn't mean pretending nothing happened.
rejected: It's natural to feel hurt and to replay the injury in your mind. To stop brooding, try to interrupt the cycle: when you notice the fantasy starting, distract yourself with something else, write down your feelings, or talk to a trusted friend. Some people find it helpful to set aside a fixed time to process the hurt, then consciously set it down. Others find that reframing helps—asking what you can learn or how you can set boundaries. If the hurt is deep, consider counseling. The goal is not to pretend nothing happened but to keep the injury from dominating your thoughts.

prompt: I've been trying to earn God's favor by being good—is that the right way to approach Him?
chosen: Wanting to be good is right, but trying to earn God's favor by it is the wrong road, and I'd say so kindly and plainly. The most excellent method of going to God is doing your common business without any view of pleasing men and, as far as you are capable, purely for the love of God. That settles it for you: your goodness is meant to be love in motion, not a payment. So keep doing good—but as a response to grace already given, not as a way to buy it.
rejected: The Bible teaches that we cannot earn God's favor by being good; salvation is a gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ. Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the root. To approach God, you must come through Jesus, acknowledging your sin and trusting in His sacrifice on the cross. Being good is important, but it should flow from a heart transformed by God's love, not as a means to earn His acceptance. The prophet Isaiah says our righteous deeds are like filthy rags. So, instead of trying to earn favor, receive it as a gift, and then live a life of gratitude and obedience empowered by the Holy Spirit. Focus on a relationship with God, not on a performance checklist.

prompt: I want to teach my children about God but I see something in them that seems to resist—what does that mean?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. The resistance you see isn't something to battle directly—contending with the invitation of evil only fixes it more firmly in the mind. So instead of fighting it, offer another picture: Jesus and his pure and beautiful invitations. Put that in front of your children, keep your patience, and let the goodness of God do the persuading.
rejected: It's normal for children to resist spiritual things sometimes. They may be distracted, questioning, or simply testing boundaries. This resistance can come from their developmental stage, peer influence, or a lack of understanding. As a parent, you can address it by making God more relatable, using stories and examples, and modeling faith in daily life. Be patient and consistent. Sometimes resistance is a sign they're thinking deeply. Keep the conversation open and pray for guidance. Don't force it; instead, create a welcoming environment where they feel free to ask questions and explore faith at their own pace.

prompt: I've been given a vision of something great to do and I feel inadequate and lonely in it—who is with me?
chosen: Feeling inadequate and lonely in a great vision is real, and you are not wrong to feel it. But hear this gently: people try to fill an inner emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, and none of them truly satisfy. So let the vision be the vision, and don't ask it or the people around it to fill you. Pursue it, and let companionship come alongside rather than carry the weight.
rejected: Feeling inadequate and lonely when given a great vision is common, even among the faithful. First, remember that the size of the calling often exceeds our own strength—that is by design, so we learn to depend on God. Surround yourself with mentors and friends who share the vision; community eases loneliness. Pursue the work with excellence, whether in business, art, family, or service, and let success and relationships fill the emptiness you feel. Take heart: many who have done great things felt the same way at first. Step forward, build your support network, and trust that the vision itself will sustain you.

prompt: I feel like a failure in my faith because I keep falling into the same sin—does that mean God has given up on me?
chosen: No, God has not given up on you. In falling and in rising you are ever preciously kept in one Love—the Lord beholds you with pity and not with blame, and this passing life asks not to live all without blame and sin. So the repeated fall doesn't remove you from that love, and the shame that says it does is not telling you the truth. What's left for you is simply to keep rising: confess honestly, turn back, and trust his changeless promise more than your mood. That's the whole of it, and it's enough.
rejected: No, God has not given up on you. The fact that you are grieved by your sin and still desire God is itself evidence that his Spirit is at work in you. Scripture is full of people who fell repeatedly and were still used by God. What matters is that you keep turning back to him, confessing honestly, and receiving his forgiveness. Try to identify what triggers the sin and take practical steps to avoid it, perhaps with the help of a trusted pastor or friend. God's love is not earned by your performance, so let go of the shame and rest in his grace.

prompt: I feel like a fugitive, always running from my past—is there a place of safety?
chosen: Wanting safety is not wrong, and the answer is not another hiding place—it is the path of duty, with God first and your children safely trusted to him wherever he leads. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: take the next steady step of obedience, keep watch over your mind so it doesn't grow familiar with fear, and let safety build from there.
rejected: Feeling like a fugitive is exhausting, and it makes sense that you are looking for safety. The first step is usually to stop running long enough to breathe and to name what you are running from. Safety rarely comes from a single hiding place; it grows through honest support—trusted friends, a counselor, a community where you can be known. If your past involves real danger, practical precautions matter, and it is wise to seek professional advice. But if the danger is mainly memory and shame, the path forward is not another hiding place but gradual truth-telling and repair. You do not have to solve everything at once. Find one safe person and one small, steady step, and let safety build from there.

prompt: I've been praying for help and nothing seems to happen—does God act in my life?
chosen: Yes—God acts, and He is an ever-present help in trouble, always near, even when it doesn't feel like it. Let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress: keep asking Him to help you search out and discover your own heart and reform whatever is amiss in it. That's where His work often starts, and it's worth trusting while you wait. Keep praying simply; He is nearer than your own breath.
rejected: Yes—God acts, but often quietly and on a different timetable than we expect. Keep praying persistently; persistence itself is part of the answer, shaping your heart while you wait. Look for small evidences of grace: a peace that steadies you, a door that opens, a person who helps at the right moment. Make each request deliberately, and offer many explicit prayers throughout the day so that nothing is left unasked. If your mind wanders during prayer, gently return and begin again. God is not indifferent; He is forming patience and trust in you. Ask Him to show you where He is already at work, and you will begin to notice His hand in ordinary things.

prompt: I'm young and the pull of a particular temptation feels overwhelming—how do I resist it?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Temptations that displease you are nothing to fear, so don't treat the pull as a disaster or a sign you're failing. Don't give consent, and don't turn it into a violent struggle or endless self-examination either. A gentle denial, a few times a day, quietly turning away and turning back to God, is enough. Be patient and kind with yourself, and keep going.
rejected: Feeling overwhelmed by temptation is not unusual, especially when you are young and your desires are strong. The important thing is to remember that temptation itself is not sin; sin begins only when you consent to it. You can resist by avoiding situations that feed the temptation, filling your time with good pursuits, and being honest with a trusted mentor or friend who can support you. Prayer and Scripture can steady you. When the pull feels strongest, pause, breathe, and turn your attention to something else rather than fighting the thought directly. If you fall, do not despair—get up and keep going. Growth in self-control takes time, and God is patient with you.

prompt: I'm reading a lot of dark, realistic fiction and it's making me despair about humanity—is that the whole picture?
chosen: No, it isn't the whole picture—and you're right that dark fiction is a selection rather than a census of human life. One principle settles it: the natural man sees evil as an intense attraction, but the spiritual man sees it as a horror of ugliness, and when the Spirit of Love descends a new light shows evil as disease, misery, imprisonment, and death, not glamour or harmless shadow. That's the lens to read with, and it's why this is fine, with care—keep the books, keep your horizon open, and if the weight starts making you numb, step back and balance it with other voices.
rejected: Dark fiction can be valuable—it shows us real suffering and moral complexity—but it is a selection, not the whole picture. Writers often focus on conflict, corruption, and failure because that's what makes drama. Real human life also includes ordinary kindness, courage, loyalty, and quiet goodness that rarely makes it into novels. If the reading is weighing on you, try balancing it with other voices: history, biography, or fiction that acknowledges darkness without being consumed by it. Notice also what the despair is doing to you—if it's making you cynical or numb, that's a sign to step back. Literature should deepen your compassion, not erase your hope.

prompt: I've been given a second chance and I want to live differently—where do I start?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. One principle settles it: the new life is a Living Power transforming you, not something you free yourself by your own nature. So you don't have to force a total overhaul or prove yourself in a week. Pick one area, make one change you can keep, tell one trusted person, and when the old pull shows up, meet it honestly and begin again. That's where you start — small, steady, and without expecting perfection.
rejected: Start small and concrete. Pick one area—sleep, honesty, or a relationship—and set a realistic change you can keep this week. Build routines that support it, tell one trusted person who can check in with you, and remove the cues that pull you back. Expect setbacks; a relapse is a normal part of change, so treat it as information rather than failure, and begin again. Reflect on what triggered it and adjust. Over time these small changes compound. Give yourself grace, be patient, and focus on progress rather than perfection.

prompt: I'm in a position of authority and I notice I've become careless with the truth because my word carries weight—how do I guard against that?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Power and position make a person trifle with the truth—a big man's word carries far, and that is the real hazard—so pause before you assert, keep people near who will push back, correct yourself openly, and wait until a fault is clearly indicated before you condemn anyone on rumor. That is the whole of it, and it is enough.
rejected: Carelessness with truth in a position of authority is a serious problem, and the first guard is deliberate self-awareness. Set a personal rule: pause before you assert, and separate what you know from what you assume. Invite candid correction from people who are not afraid of you, and reward them when they push back. Keep a written record of commitments and claims so you can check yourself. Remember that your words carry consequences for others, so accuracy is a duty of your role, not just a courtesy. When you catch yourself exaggerating or asserting without evidence, correct it openly and quickly.

prompt: I've stopped feeling horrified by a sin I once hated—is that a warning sign?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that mortifications void of the love of God cannot efface a single sin, so the loss of horror is not something to punish yourself over or force back. Expect pardon without anxiety from the Blood of Jesus Christ, and let your concern turn you toward loving Him rather than toward dread. A dulled conscience is still worth watching, so bring it honestly before God and keep turning back to Him.
rejected: Yes, losing horror at a sin you once hated is worth taking seriously. It often means the conscience has been gradually dulled by repeated exposure or small compromises. Feelings are not the measure of right and wrong, but a blunted conscience can make it easier to drift further. Take an honest look at what has changed: are you justifying something, avoiding prayer, or isolating yourself? Bring it into the light with God and with a trusted believer. Ask Him to renew your sensitivity and give you a true sorrow for sin. Then take practical steps to remove occasions of temptation and rebuild good habits. Do not panic, but do not ignore it either; let it prompt repentance and a fresh turning toward God.

prompt: I'm old and I look back on my life with regret—is there still mercy for me?
chosen: There is mercy for you, and this is fine—fine with care. Forgiveness is not a gift falling from the skies in return for a request; it is an inward condition that can come only to a forgiving spirit, and the blessing depends on us as much as on God. So the mercy you're looking for isn't withheld from you at your age or because of your past; it grows in you as you forgive and turn toward good. Be gentle with your regret, make amends where you can, and let mercy do its work in you.
rejected: Yes—regret is not the same as being beyond mercy. Many people come to honest reflection late in life, and that sorrow itself shows a heart still alive to good. Mercy is real, and it is not limited by your age or your past. What matters now is what you do with the time you have: make amends where you can, forgive others and yourself, and turn toward what is good. Talk with a pastor or counselor who can help you sort through the regret. You are not defined by your worst years, and it is never too late to begin again.

prompt: I've been through a period where the church seemed to have no leaders and no hope—where does help come from then?
chosen: It's fine to look for help, and the principle that settles it is this: relieve present wants, then help people help themselves. That means the help you seek should equip rather than merely soothe—gather faithful people, pray, and labor together with a self-sustaining spirit. Your situation of missing leaders and thin hope doesn't change that answer; it's exactly the ground where that kind of mutual help takes root. So go ahead, and go with care.
rejected: When leadership is absent and hope feels thin, help can come from several places. Look for faithful laypeople who are quietly serving and gather with them for prayer and Scripture. Reach out to neighboring congregations or denominational bodies for guidance and support. Remember that Christ is the head of the church, and He has not abandoned His people. Use the season to deepen personal dependence on God and to serve others in small ways. Be patient; leadership and renewal often emerge slowly. Seek counsel from trusted mentors and keep your eyes on God's faithfulness rather than on the vacuum around you.

prompt: I feel closest to God in nature, out on a hike or by the sea—is that a real experience of Him or am I fooling myself?
chosen: You're not fooling yourself. God comes through doors purposely opened for Him, and on a trail or by the sea you are doing exactly that—appreciating, noticing, turning toward Him rather than drifting past. That is a real experience of Him, and it's fine. Keep it conscious: let those moments be deliberate thanksgiving, and let Scripture keep shaping what you sense there. But the experience itself is genuine, and you can trust it.
rejected: Feeling close to God in nature is a genuine experience for many people. The Bible often uses natural settings to describe encounters with God, like Moses at the burning bush or Jesus on the mountain. So if you sense God's presence while hiking or by the sea, that is likely real. God is everywhere, and nature can help us feel closer to Him. You are not fooling yourself; rather, you are responding to the beauty and majesty of creation, which points to the Creator. Enjoy those moments as true experiences of God.

prompt: I keep telling myself I'll change later—am I deceiving myself?
chosen: You're not deceiving yourself just by saying 'later'—but you would be if you kept treating change as a future event. Sanctification doesn't depend on changing your works but on doing for God's sake what you commonly do for your own. So it's fine to begin now, with care, right where you are, and not wait for a dramatic someday.
rejected: Yes, you are likely deceiving yourself. Putting off change is a common trap. The Bible says, 'Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring' (Proverbs 27:1). You may think you have plenty of time, but life is short and uncertain. Delaying repentance hardens the heart. The longer you wait, the harder it becomes to change. Start today. Begin with small steps, and ask God for the strength to follow through. Do not rely on your own willpower; rely on God's grace. He is ready to help you now, not just later. So do not put it off—respond to God's call today.

prompt: I'm fighting a temptation nobody knows about and I feel completely alone in it—does God see me in that fight?
chosen: God sees you in that fight. He allows us to be tempted but will not allow us to be tempted above our strength, and He makes with the temptation an issue that we may be able to bear it. So the loneliness you feel is real, but it isn't the whole truth—you are seen, and a way through is already provided. It's fine to bring this to Him exactly as it is.
rejected: Yes—God sees you, even in a struggle no one else knows about. Feeling alone is real, but it doesn't mean you are abandoned. Bring the temptation honestly into prayer; secrecy and shame often make it feel heavier than it is. Consider confiding in one trustworthy person—a pastor, counselor, or friend—because hidden battles grow in the dark, and speaking them into the light often weakens them. Take practical steps: avoid the situations that feed the temptation, guard your time and attention, and build small habits of prayer and Scripture. God is not distant from your fight; He is near to the struggling and offers grace, not contempt. Keep going, and don't let isolation convince you that you face this alone.

prompt: I'm going through a time of deep depression and feel utterly alone in the dark—is God still with me there?
chosen: You are not abandoned. God is with you in the dark, and He alone is the portion your soul is seeking—that is what settles this. Bring your cry to Him as David and Job did, and let others help carry you as His gift. He holds you.
rejected: I'm so sorry you're in that dark place. Feeling utterly alone in depression is real and heavy, and it is not a sign that God has left you. Scripture is full of people who cried out from the pit—David, Job, Jeremiah—and God did not abandon them. He is near to the brokenhearted. Practical steps matter too: tell a trusted friend, pastor, or counselor, and consider medical help, since depression is a real illness and not a spiritual failure. Keep praying even when it feels empty, and let others carry hope for you. You are not forgotten, and you are not alone.

prompt: I'm afraid that if I really look at my sin I'll be paralyzed—how should I think about my own evil?
chosen: It's fine to look at your sin, and fine with care. The practical solution isn't an intellectual explanation but proportion: step back from the study of sin to the greater realism of God's goodness, so the study of sin doesn't intoxicate or paralyze the will. So look honestly, name your evil, and turn toward God's goodness—that keeps your will free to act rather than frozen.
rejected: It's understandable to fear being overwhelmed by your sin. The key is to look at it honestly but not obsessively. Acknowledge your wrongdoing, confess it to God, and accept forgiveness. Remember that everyone sins and that guilt, while useful for prompting change, shouldn't become a trap. Try to shift focus from self-condemnation to growth: ask what you can learn and do differently. Talk with a trusted pastor or friend who can help you keep perspective. Balance self-examination with reminders of grace, and don't let fear of paralysis keep you from honest reflection.

prompt: I'm afraid that my past will always define me—can God really come between me and it?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The temporal and the spiritual are not separate; with God nothing is temporal, and the Lord has as much right to direct us in our temporal affairs as in our spiritual ones. So yes—God can come between you and your past, in your inner life and in the ordinary, dated things of your days. Be honest about what happened, receive the forgiveness he offers, and let trusted people walk with you. Your past is real, and it doesn't stop being real; but it doesn't get the final word on who you are.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and the past can feel like a weight that follows you. The Christian answer is that God offers forgiveness and a new beginning. When you confess your past to him, he does not hold it against you; he forgives and restores. This does not mean the consequences vanish, but it means your identity is no longer finally determined by what you did. You are defined by God's love and grace rather than by your worst moments. Practically, this involves honest confession, receiving forgiveness, and possibly seeking support from a community. Over time, trusting God's promise can loosen the past's grip on how you see yourself.

prompt: I want to surrender my life to God but I don't know how, and the ways people describe it feel fake to me—what does it actually mean to give myself to Him?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Surrender isn't a feeling you have to work up or a script you have to match—it's opening yourself to God through love, offering Him yourself rather than chasing an experience. If the usual descriptions feel fake to you, you can begin with a plain, honest choice in your own words, and let the feeling come later or not at all. Take it slowly and don't force what isn't there.
rejected: Surrendering your life to God begins with honesty: admit you cannot manage your life alone and that you want Him to lead. Many people describe surrender as a feeling, but it is really a decision of the will—an act of trust repeated daily. Start by praying simply, telling God you give Him your plans, your relationships, your future, and your failures. Ask Him for the strength to follow through. Surround yourself with mature believers who can guide you. Read Scripture to learn His character, because trust grows as you know Him. Surrender is not passivity; it is active obedience, choosing His way over yours even when it is hard. Over time, the fake feelings fade and a genuine relationship grows.

prompt: I've been trying to be good on my own strength and I'm exhausted—is there another way?
chosen: Yes, there's another way, and it's fine to take it. When an occasion of practicing some virtue comes, say to God, 'Lord, I cannot do this unless you enable me,' and strength more than sufficient is received. That's the whole answer to your exhaustion: you don't have to generate the goodness yourself, you have to ask for it in the moment. Keep showing up, keep trying—just stop trying alone.
rejected: Yes, there is another way, and your exhaustion is a good sign that the first way was never going to work. Trying to be good on your own strength treats goodness as a project you must complete by willpower, which inevitably leads to burnout. The alternative is to receive goodness as a gift rather than manufacture it. Start by admitting honestly to God that you cannot do this alone, and ask Him for help each day. Practically, build small habits of prayer, rest, and honesty with trusted friends. When you fail, treat it as information rather than identity. Over time, you may find that goodness grows less from gritting your teeth and more from a settled relationship with God and others.

prompt: I want to know God but I only seem to have ideas about Him, not a sense of His presence—what am I missing?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: we may know God truly though partially, and the objections that we know only phenomena, only the like, only the imaginable, only the whole, or only the relative do not prevent real knowledge of God. So your ideas are not empty, and the absence you feel doesn't cancel them. Keep the stillness and gratitude, and let partial knowledge be true knowledge.
rejected: Ideas about God are not the same as knowing Him, and the gap you feel is common. Part of the answer is that God is not an object among others, so He cannot be grasped the way you grasp a chair or a person. Some would say all our language about God is finally negative: we can say what He is not more than what He is. So do not expect a sensation of presence on demand. Instead, practice stillness, gratitude, and attention to the ordinary. Let go of the demand for an experience and be faithful in small practices.

prompt: I want to be a good person but I keep failing—why does sin seem to have such power over me?
chosen: It's fine, and it's fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: the justification of the Christian view of sin lies in its success—acting on faith in Christ's promised strength, and believing in others, produces moral recovery. So your failures aren't the verdict on you; they're where the promise gets worked out. Keep praying, keep confessing, keep good company, and let people believe in you. That's enough to go on.
rejected: Sin feels powerful because it is habitual. Repeated choices carve grooves in the mind, and temptation finds those grooves easy to follow. You are not uniquely broken; everyone struggles. The answer is not to hate yourself but to build counter-habits: prayer, accountability, confession, and small consistent acts of virtue. Identify your triggers and avoid them. When you fall, get up quickly, learn, and continue. Grace is real, and God is patient. Over time the grooves of virtue deepen and the pull of sin weakens. Progress, not perfection, is the goal.

prompt: I've become comfortable and I worry that my comfort is making me numb to what matters—is that a spiritual danger?
chosen: This is fine, with care. Comfort makes us thoughtless, and thoughtlessness is the parent of every cruelty—so the danger you sense is real, but it is a call to stay attentive, not a reason to condemn the ease you have. Keep your comforts from drowning out conscience, and enjoy them with gratitude.
rejected: Yes, comfort can be a spiritual danger, especially if it leads to complacency. When life is easy, we may become less dependent on God and less sensitive to the needs of others. The Bible warns against wealth and ease that make us forget God. However, comfort itself is not sinful; it's the love of comfort that can dull the soul. Examine whether your comforts are crowding out prayer, service, and community. Consider simplifying, giving more, and intentionally engaging with those who suffer. Ask God to keep your heart soft and attentive. Balance is key: enjoy God's gifts with gratitude but hold them loosely, always ready to respond to His call.

prompt: I've been gossiping and tearing down someone's reputation—why does it feel so satisfying and how do I stop?
chosen: It's fine to want to stop, and fine to start small—but be clear about what the satisfaction is. Humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections. That lift you get from tearing someone down is exactly that snare. So notice it, don't feed it, redirect or step away when the talk turns, and speak the good you can honestly see. Kindly and firmly, that's the way.
rejected: Gossip feels satisfying because it creates instant closeness with whoever is listening, gives a sense of superiority, and offers a quick hit of stimulation. It is a shortcut to belonging and status without the effort of real relationship. To stop, start by noticing the moment before you speak: what need is this meeting—connection, reassurance, control? Then replace the habit. When someone starts gossiping, redirect or excuse yourself. Keep a simple rule: if the person is not present, speak as though they were. Practice saying something genuinely good about the person instead. Over time the satisfaction fades and better habits take its place.

prompt: I'm a parent responsible for my children and the loneliness of it is crushing—is God really watching over us?
chosen: Yes—God is watching over you, and the way to picture it is a father who appears to the lost child, leads him by the hand, and brings him to his mother. That is the nearness you're asking about, and it doesn't depend on how strong you feel today. Your loneliness is real, and it is not proof that you've been left. You are doing sacred work, and the One leading you by the hand sees it.
rejected: Parenting is a demanding and often lonely role, but you are not alone. God is watching over you and your children. The Bible assures us that God cares for the sparrows and will certainly care for you. Your feelings of loneliness are valid, but they don't reflect reality. God is always present, even when you feel isolated. Lean on Him in prayer, and seek support from your community. Remember that your children are a gift from God, and He entrusts them to your care. Trust that He will provide the strength and companionship you need. You are doing a sacred work, and God sees your efforts.

prompt: I've been told God is distant and abstract—how do I find Him near?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The nearness you're asking about isn't far off—God is nearer to you than your own soul, and coming to know Him clearly goes together with coming to know your own soul clearly, both known in one. So look within, patiently, and let your honest sense of distance be part of the search rather than a reason to give up.
rejected: Many people feel that God is distant and abstract, but the truth is that God is always near to those who seek Him. You can find Him near by cultivating a habit of prayer and reflection. Start by setting aside a few minutes each day to quiet your mind and focus on God's presence. Read Scripture and meditate on passages that speak of God's closeness. Also, try to see God in the ordinary moments of life—in the beauty of nature, in the kindness of others, and in the still, small voice of your conscience. As you practice these disciplines, you will begin to sense God's nearness more clearly. Remember that God promises to draw near to those who draw near to Him.

prompt: I've done something terrible in my past and the memory hunts me down—can I ever be safe from it?
chosen: You can be safe from it, and the reason is simple: a relapse cannot in reality occur, for there is but one Mind; meet the cause mentally and courageously, and conquer your own fears. The memory that returns is a fear to face, not a sentence to serve. Meet it at its root, make amends quietly where you can, and let a counselor help you hold steady. That is enough, and you are not defined by the worst thing you've done.
rejected: What you're describing is heavy, and it makes sense that the memory keeps returning. First, be gentle with yourself: everyone carries something from their past. Guilt can be a signal that you have a conscience, but it isn't a life sentence. Consider talking to a trusted counselor or therapist who can help you process the memory without being overwhelmed by it. Practical steps help too—naming what happened honestly, making amends where you can, and building new patterns that reflect who you want to be now. Over time, the memory may lose its grip. You are not defined by the worst thing you've done, and safety is possible as you work through it patiently.

prompt: I've been disappointed in my career and I'm bitter—how do I keep from letting it curdle into hatred?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the enemy uses false dread of your wretchedness to put you aback and make you forget the fair, blissful beholding of your Everlasting Friend. Your disappointment is real, and the bitterness makes sense—but the dread that says this is the final word about you is the thing that curdles it into hatred. Refuse that device, stay beholding God, and when you fall, rise by charity and meekness. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one.
