rejected: Bitterness after career disappointment is understandable, but you are right to fear it curdling into hatred. First, name the disappointment honestly before God rather than suppressing it. Hatred grows when we rehearse grievances and assign blame; bitterness grows when we believe we are owed something we did not receive. Practice gratitude for what you do have, forgive those you blame, and separate your worth from your career outcomes. Talk with trusted friends or a counselor. Reorient toward what you can control and find meaning in service to others. Healing takes time; be patient with yourself and keep bringing the resentment to God.

prompt: I'm afraid of death and the shadow of it falls across my life—how do I face it?
chosen: Your fear is real, and I won't wave it away. But hear the one thing that settles it: fear cannot evade as Love can pursue. The soul's fear of losing all beside God is overcome by a Love that out-pursues its evasions. So keep your mind in that presence like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and when it wanders, bring it back calmly rather than in a fluster. That is fine to do, and it is enough.
rejected: The fear of death is one of the deepest human fears, and the shadow it casts can color everything. Begin by acknowledging that fear honestly rather than pretending it away. Then consider what Scripture says: Christ has conquered death, and for the believer death is not a wall but a doorway. Reflect on the resurrection and the hope of eternal life. Talk with trusted friends, a pastor, or a counselor about your fear. Practice gratitude and attend to the present, since anxiety about death often grows when we dwell on what we cannot control. Prayer, Scripture, and community can help you live with the shadow without being ruled by it.

prompt: I'm not afraid of dying, but I'm afraid of what I've done—what do I do with a guilty conscience?
chosen: A guilty conscience is a gift only if it leads you to repentance rather than despair. So name what you've done honestly, make amends where you can, and let the guilt do its real work—turning you toward repair and a changed course—rather than letting it circle endlessly and wear you down. That's what your conscience is for, and it's fine to follow it there, with care.
rejected: A guilty conscience is a gift if it leads you to God rather than to despair. First, name your sins honestly before God and, where possible, make amends to those you've harmed. Confess, receive absolution, and do penance. Remember that God's mercy is greater than your sin—Scripture says He is faithful to forgive. Don't wallow in shame; shame without hope paralyzes, but repentance turns you toward God. Replace rumination with gratitude for forgiveness, and let your past become a motive for compassion toward others. If guilt persists despite confession, it may be scrupulosity—speak with a pastor. Peace comes not from forgetting but from being forgiven.

prompt: I'm struggling with a secret habit and I'm ashamed to tell anyone—can God help me in something no one else knows about?
chosen: Yes, God can help you in something no one else knows. Secret prayer is indispensable—public prayer and conversation with fellow believers can't make up for that private communion with God, and the way to keep praying is to keep praying. So bring this hidden thing to Him honestly, without excusing it and without despairing, and keep returning to Him gently. He is gentle with those who come to Him.
rejected: Yes, God sees and cares about the things no one else knows. Secret struggles are not hidden from Him, and He invites you to bring them into His light. You do not need to be ashamed before God; He already knows and still loves you. Begin by being honest with Him in prayer, and ask for His help and cleansing. It can also help to speak with a trusted pastor or mature believer when you are ready, since confession and accountability bring freedom. You are not alone, and God's grace is sufficient for you. He is gentle with those who come to Him.

prompt: I'm tempted to give up fighting my own faults because I can't understand why evil exists at all—what's the point?
chosen: It's fine to keep fighting your faults even while you can't explain why evil exists—and fine with care, because the practical solution to the problem of evil is not intellectual explanation but proportion: stepping back from the study of sin to the greater realism of God's goodness, lest discovering a reason for a fact become an excuse for sluggishness in fighting it, or the study of sin intoxicate or paralyze the will. So don't give up the fight, and don't let the unanswered question set the proportion. Keep going, kindly and steadily.
rejected: It's understandable to feel discouraged when you can't grasp why evil exists. But giving up the fight against your faults won't bring clarity—it will only deepen your struggle. Instead, focus on what you can know: God is good, and He calls you to pursue holiness. The point isn't to solve the mystery of evil but to trust God's wisdom and rely on His grace. Remember that every small victory over sin draws you closer to Him. Don't let the enemy use intellectual doubts to paralyze you. Seek support from mature believers, and keep pressing forward in faith, knowing that God's strength is made perfect in your weakness.

prompt: I feel far from God and my prayers feel empty—why?
chosen: The desire to pray is itself prophetic of a heavenly Friend—no hunger exists for what is not in the environment. So your empty-feeling prayers are not proof of distance; they are the ache of a real longing pointed at a real God. Trust the changeless word of promise rather than the mood of the moment, and keep praying simply and honestly, even when it feels hollow.
rejected: Feeling far from God is common, and empty prayers often reflect exhaustion, distraction, or unconfessed sin rather than God's absence. God has promised to be near, so your feelings are not a reliable measure of his presence. Start by examining your life for anything that has crowded out your relationship with him, and confess it. Then return to simple, honest prayer—even short prayers of trust. Remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance; dryness can be a season that deepens dependence. Talk to a trusted pastor or friend, keep praying steadily, and trust that God hears even when your words feel hollow.

prompt: I am old and near death and have wasted my youth—is there still comfort for me?
chosen: Yes, there is still comfort for you, and it is fine to receive it. The principle that settles this is the calm old age of a pure conscience, the heart that waits its summons content to live but not afraid to die. That peace is not reserved for people who spent their youth well. It is available to you now, near the end, as much as it ever was. Your regret is real, and you don't have to pretend otherwise, but it does not put comfort out of reach. You are not beyond grace.
rejected: Yes, there is still comfort. Regret over wasted youth is a heavy burden, but it does not define your worth or your remaining days. Many people find that late life brings a different kind of fruitfulness: perspective, gentleness, and the freedom to focus on what matters most. You cannot recover lost years, but you can still choose how to spend the time you have—repairing relationships, offering kindness, praying, or simply being present. Grief over the past is real and worth acknowledging, perhaps with a trusted friend or counselor. It may help to remember that no life is measured only by its early chapters; the ending matters too. Whatever you have lost, you are not beyond grace or beyond the possibility of peace.

prompt: How should a king live after he has received the faith?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: he should be slow to take new steps, seek to have no will of his own, ascertain the will of God by prayer, the Word, and the Spirit, and then seek His help earnestly and expectantly. A king who lives that way is not passive; he is steady, and that is exactly what his office needs.
rejected: A king who has received the faith should rule with justice, mercy, and humility, remembering that his authority comes from God and that he is accountable to him. He should protect the weak, promote peace, and set an example of personal holiness. Prayer and counsel from wise advisors should shape his decisions. He should not use power for selfish gain but serve his people as a shepherd serves the flock. His court should reflect honesty and generosity, and he should care for the poor and the church. In short, he should let the gospel shape both his private conduct and his public rule.

prompt: Should I be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief?
chosen: No, you should not be ordained a bishop after a life of unbelief. A pastor must first acquire solid interior virtue and mortify his passions before safely undertaking the salvation of others, and one whose soul is slothful, sensual, and earthly deserves not the name of Christian, much less minister of the gospel. That is the whole answer, and it is meant kindly: let faith and virtue come first, and leave the office for later, if God ever gives it.
rejected: Being ordained a bishop is a serious commitment that requires deep faith and spiritual maturity. If you have lived a life of unbelief, it's important to first examine your heart and beliefs. Ordination is not just a human appointment; it is a sacred calling that should be confirmed by the church community. You should seek counsel from spiritual leaders and pray about this decision. If you have truly repented and believe, and if the church affirms your calling, then it might be possible. But it's not something to take lightly. Ultimately, the decision should be made with prayer and discernment.

prompt: I was born long after the events I am asked about—how can I declare what I do not know?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. You were born later, and that's a real limit—you can't claim to know what you don't. But the historian has no right to place a development's factors and impelling ideas in a clearer light than they appear in the development itself. So report what's documented, mark the gaps as gaps, and don't brighten what the record leaves dim. That's not a refusal of the question; it's the honest way to answer it.
rejected: You are right to hesitate. Being born later does not grant you eyewitness knowledge, and honesty requires admitting the limits of what you can claim. Yet history is not closed to you. You can study records, weigh testimony, and distinguish what is documented from what is inferred. What you cannot do is pretend to certainty you do not have. So declare only what the evidence supports, mark your uncertainties plainly, and let the past speak in its own terms rather than through your assumptions. Declaring what you do not know is not failure; it is the beginning of trustworthy inquiry, and it protects you from inventing motives for people who never held them.

prompt: Should I be baptized now that I have learned the faith?
chosen: Yes—be baptized. Baptism, accompanied by faith, is a means of real blessing instituted by Christ, signifying cleansing from sin and entrance into close relation to Christ, and in itself the rite is useless. Since you've come to faith, this is a good and fitting step, and you can take it with a sincere heart.
rejected: Baptism is a meaningful step, and if you have come to faith, it is a natural next step. It is best understood as an outward sign of an inward commitment—a public declaration that you belong to Christ and intend to follow him. Whether you are baptized now or soon depends on your readiness and the practice of your community. Talk with a pastor or teacher, ask what baptism means in your tradition, and prepare your heart. The important thing is that your faith is genuine and that baptism expresses it rather than substitutes for it.

prompt: How can I keep myself aloof from the sin of my people without betraying them?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. You can keep yourself from the sin without betraying your people — but do it as one of them, not as a clean judge over them. It is only by confessing our own sins and showing ourselves one with sinners that we can save others, as Christ took our sins and confessed them as His own. So hold the boundary around what you can't join, say so honestly and gently, and stay at the table with your people, leading with your own need for mercy.
rejected: Wanting to stay aloof from sin without betraying your people is a worthy tension to hold. Begin by distinguishing clearly between the sin and the people: you can refuse to participate in wrongdoing while remaining loyal, present, and compassionate. Set boundaries around actions you cannot join, and say so honestly and gently rather than withdrawing silently. Stay in relationship—eat with people, listen to them, serve them—so your distance is from the sin, not from them. Avoid gossip and self-righteous comparisons; speak about wrong only when necessary and with humility. Pray for your community and ask God for wisdom about when to speak and when to be silent. If the sin is serious, seek wise counsel about how to address it constructively rather than simply separating yourself.

prompt: I have confessed the truth too late—will the Lord still receive me?
chosen: Yes—the Lord will receive you. A confession made late is still a confession, and He does not turn away an honest heart. Let this be the beginning of purity and service, living ready for Him, because your hope is His appearing and not the slow improvement of the world around you. Come as you are, now, and serve Him faithfully from here.
rejected: It is never too late to confess the truth to God. His mercy is not limited by your timing, and Scripture is full of people who came late and were still received—the thief on the cross, laborers hired at the eleventh hour. What matters is that you have come honestly now. God does not turn away a contrite heart. At the same time, the Scriptures warn that the days are serious and that we should not presume on endless delay. So receive His forgiveness, let go of the fear that your lateness disqualifies you, and press on in faithfulness from here. The Lord receives those who come to Him, whenever they come.

prompt: I want to know who the God is whose sign appeared to me—where can I learn?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. You asked where to learn, and the principle that settles it says the only source of knowledge of God's character is the moral consciousness—our moral judgements are as valid as mathematical judgements and, where true, reveal the thought of God. So learn there, and keep to Scripture, teachers, prayer, and reflection as you said. One caution, kindly meant: don't let it become a dispute about God's Being or Will, since that arguing is carried on in images without God and shows one hasn't felt him. Learn, and don't fight.
rejected: To know the God whose sign appeared to you, you can learn from various sources. Nature and history can reveal aspects of God's goodness and power. Moral judgements, though often seen as subjective, can also point to God's character. You can study Scripture, which is a primary way God reveals Himself. Additionally, seeking wisdom from religious teachers and communities can help. Prayer and reflection are also important. Ultimately, knowing God is a journey that involves both intellect and experience. Be open to learning from all these sources, and you'll grow in your understanding of who God is.

prompt: How should the nails of the crucifixion be used for the good of men?
chosen: I'd say no to this. The nails are not a charm to carry into battle for victory; the old line about the bridle of the most noble king, a holy sign for good speed in war, is precisely the use I'd refuse. Keep them for remembrance and mercy instead, and let that be the whole answer.
rejected: The nails of the crucifixion are best used as instruments of remembrance and moral instruction. Kept as relics or symbols, they call to mind the cost of redemption and the love that endured suffering. They can be displayed to provoke gratitude, teach children the story of the cross, and remind believers that suffering love is stronger than violence. Practically, they may inspire works of mercy—hospitals, care for the wounded—turning remembrance into service. They should not become objects of superstition or magical power; their value is symbolic and formative. Used well, the nails point beyond themselves to the crucified one, summoning communities to repentance, reconciliation, and compassionate action rather than mere veneration of metal.

prompt: Two ways are set before me, life or death—how do I choose the better?
chosen: No—don't take that principle as your guide. The rule that says you should count yourself already dead and have no consolation but unceasing weeping over your offences is not the better way; it will not help you choose life. Choose instead by honest self-examination, love of God and neighbor, and small daily turns toward life. That is the answer, plainly and kindly.
rejected: Choosing the better way begins with honest self-examination and a deliberate turning toward life. The two ways are not equally neutral options; Scripture consistently urges us to choose life—obedience, love of God, and love of neighbor. Practically, that means examining what shapes your desires, avoiding patterns that lead toward death, and surrounding yourself with people and practices that nurture life. It also means accepting that the choice is not made once but daily. Ask God for wisdom, seek counsel from mature believers, and act on what you know. The better way is chosen not by a single dramatic decision but by a thousand small ones aligned with God's will.

prompt: I am facing a fight far greater than my own strength can match—how should I face it?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is this: strength of character is the will's power to control your actions independently of inclinations and the opinions of men, and it grows by repeated virtuous acts. That means the fight is faced not by matching its size but by holding to the small acts of self-command that are actually yours to make, one after another. Keep to that, and let the rest be carried with the help and rest you need.
rejected: A fight beyond your strength is real, and pretending otherwise won't help. Start by assessing honestly what you can and cannot control, then gather support—people, resources, and rest. Break the challenge into smaller steps and take one at a time. Expect setbacks without treating them as defeat. Some battles are won by endurance rather than force, and asking for help is strength, not weakness. Pace yourself, protect your health, and keep perspective on what matters most. You don't have to be invincible; you have to be steady, adaptable, and willing to keep going even when it's hard.

prompt: I am a Jew and know the law of Moses—how should I answer when Christians ask about the crucifixion?
chosen: You can answer this, and answer it honestly. You know the law of Moses, so say what it means to you and say that a crucified Messiah doesn't match your hope for a deliverer. The one thing that settles it: the worth of that death lies in the practical affection and goodness it showed, not in blood or in automatic pardon. Keep to texts and meanings, ask what they mean, and don't pretend to a settled answer you don't have. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Answer honestly and with respect for both traditions. You can explain what the law of Moses means to you and how a crucified Messiah sits uneasily with expectations of a triumphant deliverer. Many Christians read the crucifixion as a sacrifice for sin; you may say that from a Jewish standpoint the Torah provides its own means of atonement and repentance, and that a death on a tree carries its own scriptural weight. Ask what they mean by 'crucifixion'—atonement, martyrdom, or something else—since Christians differ. Keep the conversation about texts and meanings rather than about who is right. It's fine to say you don't have a settled answer; honesty and curiosity serve better than a rehearsed reply.

prompt: What sign should I ask of God when I cannot tell which is the holy tree?
chosen: It's fine to ask for a sign, as long as you ask like someone already rooted. Taking Christ as your guide calls for a definite act of faith and then a habitual abiding, like a tree planted that draws its life from the soil. So make that act of faith, stay rooted, and let the fruit of each option speak—good trees bear good fruit. Ask humbly, don't demand, and trust that quiet guidance is enough.
rejected: When you cannot discern the holy tree, ask God for clarity and wisdom rather than for dramatic signs. Test the options against Scripture, wise counsel, and the fruit they produce—good trees bear good fruit. A sign may be sought humbly, as Gideon did, but we should not demand one; God often guides through ordinary means: prayer, community, conscience, and circumstances. Ask for an open heart and patient discernment, and be willing to wait. If a sign comes, receive it with gratitude; if not, trust that God's quiet guidance is enough. The focus should be on walking faithfully rather than on securing a spectacular confirmation.

prompt: Will the righteous and the sinful suffer alike in the fire of judgment?
chosen: I won't draw you that map, and I mean it kindly. The vision itself says the righteous and the sinful do not suffer alike — the righteous are highest in the flame and most lightly tried, the sinful in the middle place shrouded with smoke, the accursed host cast into the depths. That settles it: not alike. But it also puts the righteous in the flame, so there's no ranking of souls for us to do here. Hold the seriousness of judgment and the reality of mercy together, and leave the sorting to God.
rejected: Scripture speaks of judgment as real and serious, but it also insists that God is just and does not treat the righteous and the wicked alike. The righteous are not condemned with the wicked; God knows how to deliver the godly and to reserve the unjust for judgment. So the fire of judgment does not fall equally on all. For those who cling to the truth, God's judgment is tempered by mercy, while for the impenitent it is severity. The point is not to satisfy our curiosity about the details but to urge us to repentance and faith, so that we are found among those who are saved rather than among those who perish.

prompt: What becomes of wealth and the beauty of the field when this world passes away?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. The earth holds enough for all, and wealth is no sin in itself—but hoarded riches bring leanness of soul and darkness of mind, so put what you have to use rather than salting it down.
rejected: When this world passes away, wealth and the beauty of the field alike are shown to be temporary. Gold rusts, fields wither, and possessions cannot be carried beyond the grave. This is a sobering reminder to hold material things loosely and to invest in what lasts—character, love, and faith. The beauty of creation is real and good, but it is not ultimate; it points beyond itself to the Creator. So enjoy the field and use wealth responsibly, but do not set your heart on them, for they are passing. The wise person stores treasure in heaven rather than hoarding what will fade.

prompt: My enemies outnumber me and I am afraid; is there any aid for me?
chosen: Yes, there is aid, and your fear is understandable when you're outnumbered. The principle that settles it is this: the enemies most to be feared are inward—unchecked passions and weaknesses within ourselves. So start there, get your own fear and temper under control, and then take the sensible steps your situation calls for—trusted people, lawful authorities where danger is real. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Yes, there is aid. Fear is natural when threats surround you, but you need not face them alone. Bring your fear to God honestly, ask for protection and wisdom, and take sensible steps to stay safe. Seek help from trusted people and, where danger is real, from lawful authorities. Remember that God is a refuge and strength, present in trouble. The psalms are full of people crying out under threat and finding God near. Courage is not the absence of fear but trusting God while you do what is right.

prompt: My fathers told me never to reveal where the holy tree was hidden—should I keep that counsel?
chosen: Keep the counsel your father gave you. We are to leave the beholding of what the secret Deed shall be and not busy ourselves to know God's privy counsels, for the more we busy ourselves the farther we are from knowing. The tree's hiding is not yours to undo, so hold the trust quietly and let it rest.
rejected: You should keep the counsel of your fathers unless you have a compelling reason to reveal it. Honoring your ancestors' wishes is important, and the hidden tree may be a sacred trust. However, if revealing it could bring greater good, such as healing or community benefit, you might reconsider. Pray for wisdom and seek counsel from trusted spiritual leaders. Ultimately, the decision is yours, but weigh the potential consequences carefully.

prompt: How should I seek something holy that has been hidden for many years?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Expect to find peace, security, and fellowship in your seeking—the saints testify that those who expect these things find them—and let that hope shape how you look, at the pace and within the bounds you've described.
rejected: Begin by clarifying what you mean by the holy thing that has been hidden—an old calling, a lost practice, a truth you set aside. Then approach it patiently. Seek it through prayer, through Scripture, and through wise counsel from people who know the tradition well. Don't expect instant results; hidden things often take time to recover. Be honest about why it was lost, and be willing to do the patient work of study and practice. Community matters here—don't seek alone. Keep your expectations modest and steady, and let the search itself shape you. If it remains hidden, accept that some things are not given in this life, and trust that God's timing is good.

prompt: Can sins be purged away in fire like gold cleansed of alloy?
chosen: Yes, this is fine, with care. The refining you're describing is real, like gold cleansed of alloy in the furnace. But the same word holds: sin can't be forgiven while it's still being clung to, because the destruction of sin is how pardon works. So keep the hope, and let go of what the fire is meant to burn away.
rejected: The idea of sins being purged away in fire is a metaphor found in some religious traditions. It suggests a process of purification where the impurities of sin are burned away, leaving only what is pure. However, the Bible often speaks of judgment as punitive and final for the unrepentant. While fire can symbolize purification, it is not a universal guarantee that all sins will be purged. The key is repentance and faith in Christ, whose sacrifice cleanses us from sin. So while the image of gold refined by fire is powerful, it should not lead to presumption. We must not rely on a purgatorial fire but on God's grace through repentance.

prompt: I was once a scoffer and an idolater—can I become dear to God?
chosen: Yes, you can become dear to God. Confess your faults to Him without excusing them and without letting them discourage you, and then peaceably take up the practice of love and adoration again. That is the path, and it is open to you.
rejected: Yes, you can become dear to God. No matter what you have done, God's love and forgiveness are available to you. The Bible is full of stories of people who turned from their sins and found grace. God does not hold your past against you if you sincerely repent and turn to Him. He is merciful and ready to forgive. Start by confessing your sins to God and asking for His forgiveness. Then, begin to live a new life, seeking to follow Him. Find a supportive community of believers who can help you grow. Remember that God's love is unconditional, and He desires a relationship with you. So, take heart, for God is waiting with open arms.

prompt: Who can teach me the meaning of the cross I saw in the sky?
chosen: A cross in the sky is striking, and it's fine to want to understand it. The Cross reveals the infinite degree of God's interest in our life and the responsibility He Himself assumes for its eternal issues, so let that be where you look for meaning: in Scripture, in the church, and with a pastor or trusted believer. Let the symbol point beyond itself to the gospel rather than to hidden messages. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: A cross in the sky is striking, and it is natural to ask what it means. Be cautious about reading it as a private sign or omen; such experiences can stir wonder but should not become a test of faith. The meaning of the cross is best learned from Scripture and the church: Christ crucified for our sins, God's love shown in self-giving, and a call to take up our own cross. Talk with a pastor or trusted believer, read the passion narratives, and let the symbol point beyond itself to the gospel. If the image moves you, let it lead to gratitude, repentance, and service rather than to speculation about hidden messages.

prompt: Why did our fathers put to death the Holy One if they knew He was the Christ?
chosen: It's fine to ask, with care. Scripture says the rulers did not understand — had they known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. So keep to what's written: their ignorance was real, God's purpose stood, and we don't get to measure their hearts. Ask it that way, and you're on solid ground.
rejected: The fathers put to death the Holy One because they did not truly know He was the Christ. Their understanding was clouded by expectation of a political Messiah, and Jesus did not fit their mold. They were blinded by pride and fear of losing their authority. Even though some may have suspected, they rejected the truth because it challenged their position. Human sin and ignorance led them to crucify the Lord of glory. This serves as a warning against letting our own preconceptions blind us to God's truth.

prompt: How can the true cross be known from among other crosses?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and the old account answers it plainly. The true cross is identified not by human wisdom but by a miracle: the dead young man rises restored in body and soul only when the third cross is laid upon him. That is how it was known, and that is enough.
rejected: The true cross is known by its miraculous power. According to the legend, Helena, mother of Constantine, traveled to Jerusalem and had three crosses uncovered. To determine which was the cross of Christ, a dead man was placed on each in turn. When the third cross was laid upon him, he was restored to life, and so the true cross was revealed. Some traditions also say that Judas, the bishop of Jerusalem, identified the cross by its healing power or by an inscription, but the raising of the dead is the clearest sign. The people, seeing the miracle, praised God and honored the cross. Thus the true cross is distinguished from the others by the divine testimony of a resurrection, not by human reasoning or marks on the wood.

prompt: I am asked to reveal a secret I have sworn to keep—what should I do when threatened with death?
chosen: No—you should not reveal it. Make no account of the judgments of men; silence and enduring their judgments is the secret of interior peace. The threat is real and you should get yourself to safety, but the oath you swore is not undone by someone else's violence, and your peace does not rest on what they think of you.
rejected: This is a serious dilemma, and you should weigh it carefully. A sworn promise carries real weight, and breaking it damages trust. But a threat of death is also serious, and you must not be reckless with your own life. Consider whether the secret, if revealed, would harm others or prevent a greater evil; if so, disclosure may be justified. Seek counsel from wise people you trust. In the end, you must decide according to your conscience, balancing the duty of your oath against the duty to preserve life. Pray for wisdom, and do what seems right.

prompt: I have won a great victory—whom should I thank for it?
chosen: Thank God first, since the strength and chances behind your victory are gifts you didn't make alone, and then thank the people who helped—by name, specifically and sincerely. The principle that settles it is this: be grateful, humble, devoted, liberal, and honest, giving freely and being consistent and sincere. So yes, this is fine—thank God, thank those who stood with you, and let your spoken thanks match what you truly feel.
rejected: First, thank God, since strength, opportunity, and the abilities that made the victory possible are gifts you did not manufacture alone. Then thank the people who helped—teammates, mentors, family, and anyone whose support made a difference. Gratitude should be spoken, not just felt: name specific people and specific contributions. And keep humility: a victory is real, but it doesn't make you superior to others. Share credit generously and celebrate honestly.

prompt: Is it right for a woman to lead a host of warriors over the sea?
chosen: Yes, this is fine. The principle that settles it says not to sink upon a bed of sloth but to begin the voyage across the clear sea, and that is a call to weigh the woman, the cause, and the risks rather than to refuse on account of who she is. Go, with care for those who follow.
rejected: Whether a woman should lead warriors over the sea depends on the woman, the cause, and the circumstances. History and legend offer many examples of women who commanded armies or inspired campaigns, and there is no universal rule that leadership in war belongs only to men. What matters morally is whether the cause is just, whether the means are proportionate, and whether lawful authority sanctions the expedition. If the question is really about a particular woman urging a particular voyage, the prudent answer is to weigh her counsel on its merits: her competence, the justice of the aim, and the risks to those who would follow. Gender alone is a poor test; justice and prudence are better ones.

prompt: How long should I hold out before giving up a secret under torture?
chosen: No — don't set a deadline for giving up a secret under torture. The principle that settles it is this: let present rapture, comfort, and ease come and go as Heaven bids, seeking no more than room to deny ourselves. Relief from pain is not something owed to you, so it can't be the thing you trade a secret for. Your limits still stand — torture can break anyone, duress reduces culpability, and your life matters — but none of that turns suffering into a bargaining chip. Hold as long as you can, keep faith with whoever the secret protects, and if you break, that is not a moral failure. Just don't plan the surrender in advance.
rejected: This is a hard question, and no simple rule covers every case. Your first duty is to survive and protect yourself from harm; torture can break anyone, and holding out indefinitely isn't a moral requirement. Consider what the secret protects: if revealing it endangers others, weigh that heavily, but if it only exposes your own past, you may reasonably give it up to end suffering. You're not obligated to be a hero. Preserve your life, seek help, and remember that duress reduces culpability. There is no fixed time limit—decide based on the stakes, your conscience, and what you can bear.

prompt: How should Christians treat the Jews of the holy city after the rood is found?
chosen: No — treat them with goodwill and look for their welfare, because their gathering and redemption come from the power of God, not from your preaching. Hold no ill will and refuse all violence. That principle settles it, so let the talk of a curse stay out of your mouth and your dealings with your neighbors.
rejected: After the finding of the rood, Christians should treat the Jews of the holy city with respect and restraint. History shows that passion for holy things has too often turned into violence against Jewish communities, and that is a betrayal of the faith. Christians should remember that Jesus and the apostles were Jews, and that the Church owes the Jewish people a debt of gratitude. Practically, this means refusing to participate in persecution, speaking out against violence, and treating Jewish neighbors with ordinary justice and kindness. Some Christians also hope and pray for the eventual conversion of the Jews, but this should be pursued through prayer and loving witness, not coercion.

prompt: I am starving and in chains—should I now confess what I have hidden?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Confess what you've hidden—plainly, without excusing yourself and without sinking into despair—and then peaceably take up the practice of love again. Your hunger and chains don't change that; they just make it urgent to speak to someone who can help.
rejected: Yes, you should confess. When you are starving and in chains, hiding the truth only adds to your suffering, and confession can bring relief. Holding a secret while in distress is a heavy burden, and speaking it may open the way to help and release. Confess honestly to those who can act, ask for forgiveness where you have wronged others, and accept the help offered. Do not let shame keep you silent any longer. Confession is the first step toward freedom, and honesty, even when costly, is better than continued concealment.

prompt: How should I use the gift of song that has been given to me?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Your gift of song is meant to be used, so sing in worship, share it with your community, and let it bring comfort and joy. Where money for God's work comes into it, let one thing guide you: it must be obtained in God's way, not by appeals to unbelievers, pressing believers, or worldly schemes, and gifts must be refused if they aren't given from pure motives or if the money isn't the giver's to give. That shapes the method, not whether you sing. So use your voice, keep growing, stay humble, and point people to Christ.
rejected: Use your gift of song to glorify God and bless others. Sing in worship, share your talent with your community, and let your music bring comfort and joy. Consider using your gift to raise funds for God's work, but do so wisely. Accept opportunities to perform and use them to point people to Christ. Keep developing your talent and stay humble, remembering that your voice is a gift from God to be used for His purposes.

prompt: Can anyone search out the name of the Saviour, or is it beyond all men?
chosen: It's fine to search out the name of the Saviour. A truly great man is known by the number of beings he loves and blesses and by the number of beings who love and bless him, and that is how the name is meant to be known: not as a hidden puzzle but as a person revealed to those who seek him sincerely. So ask, and let love be the measure of what you find.
rejected: The name of the Saviour is not hidden from those who seek Him with a sincere heart. While it may seem beyond human searching, God promises that those who seek will find. The name of Jesus is revealed in Scripture and proclaimed throughout the world. It is not a secret for the elite but a gift for all who call upon Him. However, searching out the name requires humility and openness. We cannot discover it through our own wisdom alone; it is revealed by the Holy Spirit. So the answer is that the name is both beyond all men and accessible to all—beyond human effort, yet revealed to those who ask, seek, and knock. The key is to approach with faith, not mere curiosity.

prompt: Should a festival of the cross be kept every year?
chosen: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The cross of Christ is to be carried as a crown, and no one should blush at the ensign of salvation—so a yearly festival that keeps that memory alive is a good thing to do. Keep it thoughtfully, so it stays real remembrance rather than empty routine.
rejected: Yes, a yearly festival of the cross can be a good practice. Annual celebrations give shape to the church's memory, much like other feast days, and they provide a regular occasion to reflect on Christ's suffering and its meaning for us. A festival need not be mandatory to be valuable; it works as a helpful tradition that families and congregations can adopt. The cross is central to the Christian faith, so setting aside a day to remember it is reasonable. The main thing is that the observance stays meaningful—focused on gratitude and discipleship rather than empty ritual. If it becomes mere custom, it has lost its purpose. So keep it, if you keep it thoughtfully, as a yearly remembrance that points beyond itself.

prompt: My mother is old—should I send her on a hard journey for a holy purpose?
chosen: This is fine, with care. The principle that settles it is that the servants of Mary should abstain, and induce others to abstain, from going to her sanctuaries in times of feasting, since such gatherings profane the feast and hell receives more fruit from them than the divine mother receives honor. So keep your mother away from the crowded, festive crush, choose a quiet time, and help others do the same. Beyond that, be gentle with her age and let her own wishes guide you.
rejected: That's a tender question, and the answer depends on her health, her own wishes, and what the journey involves. Honoring your mother means weighing her frailty seriously; a hard journey can be genuinely harmful for an elderly person. If the holy purpose matters to her, consider gentler alternatives—bringing the blessing to her, arranging a shorter or more comfortable trip, or having someone pray on her behalf. Talk with her openly, consult a doctor if needed, and involve family. Faith never requires us to be reckless with the vulnerable. Care for her body and her soul together.

prompt: What should a queen teach her people before she returns home?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is being homely with our Lord as heart may think or soul desire, without letting that homeliness get so reckless that courtesy falls away, since He is sovereign homeliness and very courteous. So let her teach nearness to God first, with reverence kept intact, and let the rest follow: integrity, courage, care for the vulnerable, and authority that serves. That's a good thing for a queen to leave with her people before she goes home.
rejected: A queen should teach her people the things that outlast her reign: integrity, courage, and care for the vulnerable. She should model that authority exists to serve rather than to be served, and that a community's strength is measured by how it treats its weakest members. Before returning home, she should speak plainly about what she has learned—that power is a trust, that wealth is a tool, and that character matters more than reputation. She might leave simple practices behind: honest dealing, generosity to the poor, and the habit of gratitude. Above all, she should teach them to love one another, because a people bound by love will survive the loss of any single leader.

prompt: What hope is there for one who has been stained with evil deeds and fettered in sins?
chosen: There is real hope for you, and it rests on this: of yourself you can attain no good thing, and you have nothing to offer the Lord that was not already His. So your one recourse is to turn to Him in prayer as a guilty, poor, needy beggar, weak and miserable, yet His child, with humble fear mingled with love, peace, and recollection. That is fine, and fine with care—come honestly, name your sins, and keep coming, trusting His mercy over your worst deeds.
rejected: There is real hope, because God's mercy is greater than your worst deeds. The gospel is for sinners—Christ came to save those who know they are lost. Hope begins with honest confession: naming your sins to God without excusing them, and receiving His forgiveness. It continues with repentance, which is not merely regret but a turning of the heart and life toward God, often helped by a trusted pastor, community, and sometimes professional counsel. You are not defined by your past; grace can reshape your future. Recovery may be gradual and will involve repairing what you can, but God's patience meets you at every step. You are invited to come as you are, and to keep coming, trusting that He who began a good work will complete it.

prompt: I am like a man in a desert with a loaf and a stone before me—how do I know which to take?
chosen: Take the loaf. The principle that settles it is this: examine to the bottom what you are, find yourself worthy of contempt, and then bear the troubles and contradictions that come as advantageous rather than puzzling. Your desert is real, and the stone has some pull on you, but that pull is exactly what honest self-examination is for. Choose the better, and don't be surprised by the difficulty. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: You are right to see the choice as serious, but do not overthink it. In the desert, the loaf is obviously the better choice, and the stone is useless. Take the loaf. The real question is why you would hesitate at all. If you are tempted to take the stone, that is a sign of a disordered will that needs correction. Examine yourself and repent of any desire for what is worse. Do not pretend the choice is hard or that you are forced into it; you are free, and you should simply choose the good. Take the loaf, and stop making excuses for the stone.

prompt: My brother was stoned for his faith—how should I think of his death?
chosen: It's fine to mourn your brother deeply—his death for his faith is a real grief and a real honor. Just don't let the soul settle into sadness or bitterness, since the One who loved him and died for him is good and kind. Let your sorrow go to God, lean on the people around you, and hold the hope of resurrection alongside the grief.
rejected: Your brother died for his faith, and that is both a grief and a honor. Let yourself mourn—death is an enemy, and sorrow is not unbelief. But do not let grief curdle into bitterness or into anxious questioning of your own faith. Remember that his death was not a failure of God's care; it was faithfulness carried to its costliest end. Think of him as one who kept faith under the worst pressure, and let his example steady you rather than frighten you. Bring your sorrow honestly to God in prayer, lean on your community, and let the hope of resurrection hold the grief without denying it.

prompt: What does it mean to look to heaven for help instead of trusting my own host?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Looking to heaven for help doesn't mean despising your own host; it means your ultimate trust rests in God rather than your own strength. One principle settles it: a pastor owes his own soul's care first, and charity cannot be kindled in others if it is extinguished in oneself. So keep praying, keep working diligently, use the means you have, and care for your own soul along the way. Your confidence finally rests with God, and that is a good place to put it.
rejected: Looking to heaven for help means recognizing that your ultimate trust should be in God, not in human resources or your own strength. Your 'host' likely refers to your own plans, abilities, or the people you rely on. While God uses means, He alone is the source of true help. So pray for wisdom, work diligently, but ultimately place your confidence in the Lord. He is the one who provides, protects, and guides. Trusting your own host can lead to pride and disappointment, but trusting God brings peace and security. So lift your eyes to heaven, seek His face, and let your heart rest in His faithfulness.

prompt: I had a dream in the night that seemed to promise victory—should I trust it?
chosen: Don't trust that dream as a promise of victory. Hope gives confidence of success in the sanctification of your soul and of others, joining an honest sense of your own inability with firm confidence in God's power—and that is a different thing from a night vision handing you a win. Receive whatever comfort it gave you humbly, and let it send you to prayer rather than to presumption.
rejected: Dreams can be vivid and moving, and sometimes they bring real comfort or insight. But a dream that promises victory should not be trusted as a guarantee. Test it: does it agree with Scripture, does it lead you toward humility, repentance, and love, or does it feed pride and presumption? Do not build your decisions on a night vision alone. Pray, seek wise counsel, and wait for God to confirm His will through His word and providence. If the dream comforts you, receive it humbly; if it puffs you up, set it aside. Trust God rather than the dream.

prompt: The devil threatens to incite a king against me—how should I answer him?
chosen: Answer him with the Word of God, as Jesus did, and see his threat for what it is: he who once was filled with joy by a Judas is now humbled by a Judas, and wants to incite another king to turn you from the crucified King. So pray for the king, live peaceably, refuse intimidation, and keep your eyes on Christ. That is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: When the devil threatens to incite a king against you, remember that your battle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual forces. Answer him with the Word of God, as Jesus did in the wilderness. Stand firm in your faith, knowing that God is your protector. Do not fear earthly powers, for God holds all authority. Pray for the king and for those in authority, that you may live a peaceful life. Trust in God's sovereignty and refuse to be intimidated. The devil is a liar and the father of lies; resist him, and he will flee from you. Keep your eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of your faith.

prompt: What will happen to this world at the end of time?
chosen: This is fine to talk about, with care. One principle settles it for me: the Lord's work will continue to grow and spread until it fills the earth with the glory of God and the knowledge of the Father and the Son, whom to know is life eternal. That promise means the end of time is about completion, not abandonment — so you can speak of it with hope, while leaving the timing where Scripture leaves it.
rejected: Scripture says the end of time brings the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and final judgment, followed by a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. The present world will be purified and transformed rather than simply abandoned; believers look for the redemption of creation itself. Before that, there will be tribulation, deception, and opposition, but also the gospel proclaimed to all nations. The timing is unknown, so Christians are called to watchfulness, holiness, and faithful mission rather than date-setting. The hope is not escape from the world but its renewal under Christ's reign, with sin, suffering, and death finally ended. Believers should live now in light of that hope, working for justice and peace while awaiting the day when every knee bows and God is all in all.

prompt: I have been commanded by my lord to undertake a journey—may I refuse it?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that the trivial round and common task furnish all we ought to ask—room to deny ourselves and a road to bring us daily nearer God, without bidding farewell to neighbour and work. So a lawful, reasonable journey isn't a threat to your walk with God; it's another part of it. If the command is unjust or harmful, or it would break your health or your duties to those who depend on you, decline plainly and kindly. Otherwise, go.
rejected: Whether you may refuse a journey commanded by your lord depends on the nature of the command and your circumstances. If it is a lawful and reasonable command, refusing may be disobedience, and you should weigh your duties, health, and obligations honestly. If the command is unjust or harmful, you may have grounds to decline and should seek counsel. In general, obedience to legitimate authority is a virtue, but it isn't absolute; conscience and wisdom matter. Talk with trusted advisers, clarify the purpose of the journey, and consider whether refusal would harm others. Then decide prayerfully, seeking what is right rather than merely what is comfortable.

prompt: Is there mercy for one who has many times transgressed against the Lord?
chosen: Yes, there is mercy for you. The Lord is merciful to the one who straightway purges himself of his evil deeds and ceases from the unrighteous act, even after many transgressions and many wounds. However many times you've fallen, that is the door standing open — turn from the wrong, and mercy is there. Come as you are, and come to stop, not just to be sorry.
rejected: Yes, there is mercy for those who have transgressed many times. God's mercy is abundant and His grace is sufficient. The Bible is full of examples of people who sinned repeatedly and yet found forgiveness when they repented. Think of David, who committed adultery and murder, yet God forgave him when he confessed. Or Peter, who denied Jesus three times, yet was restored. The key is genuine repentance and turning away from sin. God does not delight in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn from their ways and live. So, no matter how many times you have sinned, if you come to God with a contrite heart, He will forgive. His mercies are new every morning. Don't despair; turn to Him and receive His mercy.

prompt: Should I bear a sign of the cross before me into a struggle?
chosen: Yes, this is fine. The sign of the cross is the Christian's rampart, and making it with faith and devotion before a struggle is a good and honest thing to do. Take it with you, and let it confess that you stand under Christ's victory.
rejected: Whether to bear a visible sign of the cross into a struggle is a matter of personal conscience. Many find such a sign meaningful as a reminder of their faith and of Christ's victory; others prefer inward remembrance. The important thing is that the sign not become a substitute for actual preparation—prayer, wise planning, and honest effort. If you use a cross, let it point you beyond itself to the One it represents, and let it stir gratitude and resolve rather than superstition. If it distracts you or becomes a mere habit, you may set it aside without guilt. Either way, the real strength for any struggle comes from God, not from the object itself.

prompt: How was Constantine able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army?
chosen: This is fine to take up. The principle is that the cross was given to Constantine as the token of victory for those who look to heaven for aid rather than trusting the size of their own host, and that is what answers your question about the lesser army. So the smaller force stops being the mystery and the sign becomes the point.
rejected: Constantine was able to conquer the Huns and Goths with a lesser army through a combination of strategic brilliance, superior tactics, and the discipline of his troops. He likely used the terrain to his advantage, employed deception, and motivated his soldiers with his leadership. Additionally, the Huns and Goths may have been overconfident or disorganized, allowing Constantine to exploit their weaknesses. Some accounts also suggest that Constantine had a religious experience that boosted his morale and that of his army, but the primary factors were military skill and determination. Ultimately, his victory can be attributed to his generalship and the quality of his army.

prompt: Is it right to set a holy relic upon a king's bridle for victory in war?
chosen: I'd say no, kindly but clearly. We give rulers due honor as far as religion allows, and that same limit means we don't press holy things into service as charms for victory in war. So keep the relic for devotion, pray for the king, and don't set it on his bridle.
rejected: Using a holy relic as a talisman for victory in war is not appropriate. Relics are meant to inspire faith and devotion, not to be used as magical charms. Trusting in a relic for victory rather than in God's will is misguided. Christians are called to seek peace and trust God, not to rely on objects for success in battle. Prayer, repentance, and seeking God's guidance are more important than physical tokens. Ultimately, victory comes from God, not from relics.

prompt: We remember the Trojan war from books, yet not this holy event—why is that?
chosen: It's fine to ask why one event is remembered and another isn't. The holy event endured because the pneumatic Christology was the one to which the future belonged, since it alone permitted the close connection between creation and redemption and had room for the speculations about the Logos. That's why it was carried forward, and it's why your question has a real answer.
rejected: The Trojan War is remembered because it was chronicled by poets like Homer, whose epic tales captured the imagination of generations. The holy event you refer to—perhaps the life and death of Jesus—was remembered by a small community of believers who spread the message through oral tradition and eventually written Gospels. The difference in remembrance may be due to the fact that the Trojan War was a grand, heroic story that appealed to cultural pride, while the holy event was a humble, spiritual movement that initially seemed insignificant to the wider world. Over time, however, the holy event has had a profound impact on history, shaping entire civilizations. So while the Trojan War may be more famous in popular culture, the holy event has deeper significance for those who believe.

prompt: How should I regard Saul, who persecuted the followers of Christ and later became Paul?
chosen: Regard Saul as a warning and a hope at once. The mercy of the Lord is shown in that Saul, who doomed many a follower of Christ to torture and death and bade crush Stephen with stones, was shown mercy and became Paul, a solace for many men. So hold his story that way: humble about your judgments, hopeful about God's mercy, and serious about the harm he did, which grace magnifies rather than excuses. It's fine to look at him like that, and worth doing with care.
rejected: Regard Saul as a serious warning and a serious hope. His zeal against the church shows how sincerely wrong a person can be, yet his encounter with Christ shows that no one is beyond God's reach. He did not merely change his mind; he was transformed and became a tireless apostle. So do not write off people who oppose the faith, and do not despair over your own past. At the same time, his story does not excuse persecution—it magnifies grace. Let his life make you humble about your judgments, hopeful about God's mercy, and grateful that conversion is God's work rather than our achievement.

prompt: How will the Lord come to judge the living and the dead?
chosen: This is fine, and I'd say it with care. One principle settles it: we are judged according to the deeds done in the body and the thoughts and intents of the heart, and as death leaves us, so judgment will find us. So the Lord's coming to judge the living and the dead is real, personal, and searching, and the wise response is to be ready now, trusting Christ and tending even the hidden intentions of the heart.
rejected: The Lord will return visibly and personally at the end of history to judge the living and the dead. The creeds affirm this, and Scripture describes Christ coming in glory with angels, raising the dead, and separating the righteous from the wicked. The judgment is final and universal. Believers need not fear condemnation because they are in Christ, while the unrepentant will face eternal separation. Details like timing are debated, and the essential point is to be ready—living faithfully now, trusting Christ, and sharing the gospel so others may be ready too.

prompt: How do I know whether I'm a religious in truth or only in name?
chosen: It's fine to ask this, and fine to ask it carefully. True religion is to have Christ recognised, known, adored, and living in the soul, so the question you're really putting to yourself is whether that living thing is there, not whether your attendance and moods and opinions add up. Ask that honestly and you're asking the right question.
rejected: You can examine your outward observance: do you attend services, keep the rules, and say the prayers? These external signs matter, and a consistent practice is a reasonable indicator that you are genuine. You might also consider your feelings—do you feel devotion, peace, or consolation during religious exercises? Finally, check your doctrine: do you believe the right things and assent to the teachings of your tradition? If your observance is regular, your feelings are warm, and your beliefs are orthodox, you can have reasonable confidence that you are a religious in truth and not only in name.

prompt: I'm torn between my career ambitions and my desire for God—can I give myself fully to both?
chosen: It's fine, with care. The Gospel stands above the antagonism between career and faith and may be united with either; its one aim is that you find God and have him as your own God. So give yourself fully—just keep watch on the ambition that multiplies commitments and divides the heart, and let your work rest inside your devotion rather than beside it.
rejected: It's understandable to feel torn between career and faith. Many people struggle with this. The key is balance: you can pursue your career while also making time for God. Set priorities, perhaps attending church regularly and praying daily. Remember that your career can be a way to serve God if done ethically. Don't let ambition consume you, but also don't neglect your responsibilities. Seek guidance from your faith community. Ultimately, both can coexist if you manage your time well and keep God in your thoughts.

prompt: What should I do when I feel spiritually dry and my senses incline to evil?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Spiritual dryness is a season, not a failure, and the fact that your senses lean toward old habits is something to meet with honesty rather than panic. The principle that settles it is the call to restore in a spirit of meekness, looking to yourself lest you also be tempted — and that meekness begins with how you treat your own dry heart. So keep praying and staying in good company even when it feels empty, turn quickly toward what is worthwhile when temptation comes, and be patient with yourself. Faithfulness in the dark is still love.
rejected: Spiritual dryness is common, and feeling drawn toward old temptations does not mean you have failed. Begin by naming honestly what you feel before God rather than hiding it. Fill your mind with good things—Scripture, prayer, honest work, and good company—so that temptation has less room. When a tempting thought comes, turn your attention quickly to something worthwhile and pray a short prayer for help. Keep regular habits of prayer and worship even when they feel empty, because faithfulness in dryness is itself a form of love. Be patient with yourself and remember that feelings come and go; do not build your life on them. Talk with a trusted pastor or friend who can encourage you and pray with you.

prompt: How do I stop being distracted by images and fantasies when I try to pray?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, keeping your mind in his presence, and when it wanders, don't disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet scatter you rather than gather you. Bring your attention back calmly, use a short phrase if it helps, and let the patient returning be the prayer.
rejected: Distraction in prayer is common, and the first step is not to panic. When images or fantasies arise, gently notice them and return your attention to God, perhaps using a short phrase or a word of Scripture as an anchor. It helps to prepare beforehand: choose a quiet place, limit screens, and begin with a brief moment of stillness. Some people find it useful to write down distracting thoughts to deal with later. Remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance; God is patient with your wandering mind. With practice and patience, your capacity to stay present will grow, and the distractions will lose some of their pull.

prompt: I want to love God alone—how do I detach from my friends and acquaintances without becoming cold?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is that God is always near—in business and even in diversions—and shouldn't be neglected but adored continually. That means detachment is about keeping God in first place, not about pulling away from your friends. Stay close to them, enjoy them as gifts, and keep turning your heart back to God through the day. Your goal of loving God alone is good; you just don't reach it by going cold.
rejected: To love God alone, you must gradually withdraw your affections from creatures, not by rejecting people but by seeing them as gifts pointing to God. Begin by limiting unnecessary social interactions and spending more time in prayer and solitude. When with others, keep your heart recollected and offer brief aspirations to God. Remember that detachment is not coldness; it is freedom to love others in God. Practice silence and avoid idle talk. Over time, your love for God will grow, and you will relate to others with greater purity and charity, not less. The key is to prioritize your relationship with God above all, and let that love flow into your interactions.

prompt: How do I respond when I'm falsely accused or persecuted?
chosen: This is fine, and here's the one thing that settles it: bring what people say about you before the tribunal of your own conscience, and be just with your own soul there — neither excusing it without reason nor accusing it lightly. If conscience accuses, amend; if it doesn't, their blame takes nothing real from you, and you can be patient and at peace. Check yourself honestly, then let their opinion go.
rejected: When you are falsely accused, the first thing to do is steady yourself and refuse to react in anger. Take time to gather the facts and, if appropriate, calmly state the truth to those involved. Avoid gossip and don't try to win everyone over; some people will believe what they like. Lean on trusted friends and, if the accusation is serious, seek fair counsel or proper channels to clear your name. Remember that your worth is not decided by other people's opinions. Pray for peace, keep your conduct blameless, and let time reveal the truth. In the end, what matters most is that you act with integrity and don't let bitterness take root.

prompt: I'm afraid of death—how should I think about my last end?
chosen: Your fear of death is understandable, and you don't have to pretend it isn't there. But the certain thing is that you will die, and the uncertain thing is when, where, and how—so the wise move is to prepare now, making the changes you'd want to have made when the end is near. That's a fine way to think about your last end, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Fear of death is natural, and it can be a wise teacher. Rather than suppressing it, let it clarify what you value: relationships, honesty, generosity, and time that is well spent. Many people find that reflecting on mortality helps them stop postponing what matters and start living with more intention. You might keep a simple practice—journaling, prayer, or conversation with people you trust—to work through the fear instead of letting it run in the background. If the fear becomes overwhelming, consider speaking with a counselor or a trusted spiritual guide. The goal is not to eliminate fear but to keep it from shrinking your life.

prompt: How do I keep my heart from being defiled by the images of this world?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Purity of heart is cultivated by specific means: discovering habitual imperfections and rooting them out, keeping the senses under strict guard, living in recollection and the practice of God's presence, and laying open your interior to a spiritual director with candor. That's the path—steady, honest, and gentle rather than anxious. You don't need to withdraw from the world to walk it; you need small faithful habits and someone wise who sees the whole picture. Keep it kind and unhurried, and it's fine.
rejected: Keeping your heart undefiled begins with awareness. Notice what you feed your mind—social media, entertainment, conversations—and set limits where those images stir envy, lust, or greed. Replace idle scrolling with prayer, Scripture, and good books. Guard your senses: what you watch, listen to, and dwell on shapes what you love. When a harmful image arises, don't fight it with anxious willpower; gently turn your attention to something good. Confess failures to God and to a trusted friend, and ask for grace. Build habits of silence and gratitude, and keep good company. Purity of heart grows slowly through small faithful choices, not one dramatic effort.

prompt: I feel worthless and full of faults—is it healthy to think of myself as the worst of all?
chosen: No—you shouldn't think of yourself as the worst of all. That's not humility; it's still tiresome care of self, just aimed against you. The simple view of God and your own nothingness frees you from that endless self-measuring, and it doesn't require you to call yourself the worst. Let the verdict go.
rejected: Feeling worthless and full of faults is a heavy burden, but it's not healthy to think of yourself as the worst of all. Such thinking can lead to despair and paralysis. Instead, recognize that everyone has faults and weaknesses. God loves you unconditionally, and your worth is rooted in being created in His image. Practice self-compassion and focus on God's grace. Remember that growth comes from acknowledging your faults without condemning yourself. Seek support from a trusted friend or counselor. God's mercy is greater than your faults, and He desires to lift you up, not crush you.

prompt: How do I turn my whole life into one unbroken prayer?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Prayer as the one great central secret of holy living and serving—practiced on your knees, in secret and with believers—is a foundation you can build an ordinary day on. Keep it gentle: fixed times, short turnings of the heart, tasks done with attention, and no scorekeeping of feelings. That's enough.
rejected: Start by setting aside fixed times of prayer each day—morning, evening, and before meals—and guard them. Then practice carrying short prayers or a single word through the day, returning to it whenever you notice your mind has wandered. Offer ordinary tasks as prayer by doing them with attention and gratitude. Keep a journal of what you notice, and review it weekly. Over time the gaps between your set prayers shrink, and the habit becomes more natural. Be patient with yourself; it takes months of practice. The goal is not constant feelings but a steady direction of the heart toward God, renewed again and again.

prompt: How can I remain at peace when I hear about wars, scandals, and troubles in the world?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: be at peace always, since peace is the passport of the daughters of Jesus Christ, and patience with others must be matched by patience with ourselves. You hear about wars and scandals, and that stirs you—good. But patience with yourself means you may step back from the noise, rest, and live your own life without guilt, while still holding the world in prayer and kindness. Keep your peace; it's yours to keep.
rejected: It's natural to feel disturbed by news of wars and scandals. Try to limit your news intake, take breaks from social media, and focus on what you can control. Practicing gratitude and staying busy with your own life can help. Remember that you can't fix everything, and it's okay to set boundaries. Some people find it helpful to channel their concern into volunteering or donating to causes. If anxiety persists, consider talking to a counselor. Give yourself permission to step back and protect your peace.

prompt: I want to be humble—how do I actually acquire contempt of self?
chosen: No—don't set out to acquire contempt of self. True humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares by which a mortal poison may imperceptibly insinuate itself into her affections and deprive her of divine grace. That principle guards your heart against flattery; it never asks you to despise yourself. You want humility, and that's good, but contempt of self is the wrong road, and you should not take it.
rejected: Humility begins with an honest look at yourself. Take time each day to examine your actions, acknowledge your faults, and refuse to compare yourself favorably to others. Serve quietly where no one notices. When praised, redirect credit rather than basking in it. Remember that growth in virtue is a long discipline, and you can make real progress through steady effort and self-honesty. Confidence in God's grace gives you the courage to face your weaknesses without despair, and that courage itself is a sign you are maturing. True humility is not self-hatred; it is seeing yourself clearly and choosing to serve. With practice, you will find contempt of self turning into genuine love of neighbor, and you will grow stronger and more capable in good works.

prompt: I want to be recollected in God but my mind keeps wandering—what should I do?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Hold yourself in prayer before God like a beggar at a rich man's gate, and when your mind wanders, don't disquiet yourself—trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. So bring your attention back in tranquility, as often as needed, and let that gentle returning be your practice.
rejected: Wandering thoughts are normal and not a sign of failure. Try a simple technique: when you notice your mind has drifted, gently return your attention to a short prayer word or to a phrase like 'Lord, have mercy.' Don't fight the thoughts or scold yourself—just acknowledge them and let them pass. Some people find it helps to pray at a fixed time, in a quiet place, with a candle or icon to focus the eyes. You might also keep a notebook nearby to jot down distracting worries so you can set them aside. Be patient with yourself; recollection is a habit that grows with practice, and even a few moments of genuine attention are worthwhile.

prompt: How do I resist temptation without becoming anxious and scrupulous about it?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: keep your mind in the presence of the Lord, and if it wanders, do not disquiet yourself, because trouble and disquiet distract rather than recollect. That's the answer to your worry about becoming scrupulous. Bring your attention back calmly when it drifts, resist without the anxious self-monitoring, and let peace be the shape of it.
rejected: Resisting temptation without anxiety begins with a right view of God and of yourself. Temptation itself is not sin; it becomes sin only when you consent to it. So when tempting thoughts arise, don't panic—acknowledge them, turn your attention to God, and choose to act rightly. Anxiety and scrupulosity often come from an over-focus on yourself and a fear of failure. Instead, rest in God's grace and remember that He is patient with you. Practical steps help: avoid situations that trigger temptation, keep good habits, pray briefly and often, and talk with a trusted mentor. When you fall, confess quickly and move on rather than spiraling. The goal is steady, peaceful obedience, not constant self-monitoring. Trust God's grace and keep your focus on Him rather than on fear.

prompt: How do I prepare myself to contemplate God by the way of negation?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it is the one about order: remove first what belongs to the body, the senses, and the imagination, then even what belongs to reason and the idea of being as found in creatures, and begin with the body rather than the mind. That's the shape of your preparation, and it's a good one. Just keep it gentle and unhurried, and don't mistake the darkness for something you can produce on your own.
rejected: To prepare for contemplating God by negation, begin by quieting your senses: withdraw from noise, images, and distractions, and let your imagination grow still. Then set aside your own ideas and concepts of God, since God exceeds every thought you can form. Cultivate silence, humility, and patience, and give yourself to prayer and moral discipline so that your mind becomes calm and receptive. Do not expect clear pictures or consoling feelings; the goal is a simple, loving attention to the God who is beyond all that you can grasp. Persevere gently, returning to this practice each day, and trust that in the darkness of unknowing God draws near to you.

prompt: How do I deal with my own sins without being crushed by them?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Confess what's true, forsake even the small things promptly, and don't let the mercies you've been given go unrecognized — that's the practice that keeps confession from turning into collapse. You're not meant to be crushed by this. Name it, turn from it, be grateful, and keep going.
rejected: When dealing with your own sins, it's important to remember that God's grace is greater than any sin. Start by acknowledging your faults honestly before God, but don't dwell on them to the point of despair. Instead, focus on God's forgiveness and love. Confess your sins to Him, ask for strength to change, and then move forward in faith. It can also help to talk with a trusted pastor or Christian friend who can offer guidance and prayer. Remember that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, so you're not alone. The key is to keep your eyes on Jesus, not on your failures, and to trust that He is working in you to grow you in holiness.

prompt: I feel like my religious observance and outward practices are empty—what am I missing if I keep all the externals but feel no spirit within?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. What you're missing isn't more externals and it isn't a feeling you can work up. Without the spirit of humility and truth, in which Christ dwells by faith and love, outward observance and signs of abnegation profit nothing, because the kingdom of God, that is Christ, is within you. So keep your practices, keep your honesty about the dryness, and look inward to him who already dwells there by faith and love. That's the answer, and it's a kind one.
rejected: You are not alone; many faithful people go through dry seasons. The externals—Mass, prayers, devotions—are means, not ends. What you may be missing is a living relationship with Christ, nurtured by humility and truth. Without humility, practices become performance; without truth, they become superstition.
