Since you cannot get to worship, keep the day where you are: prayer and Scripture early or late, the day treated as set apart, and your conduct toward your mistress and household doing the quiet work of example. Be respectful and diligent, ask kindly for leave when there's a real opening, and don't carry guilt for a limit you didn't set.
rejected: It is hard to keep the Lord's Day when your mistress does not share your faith and you cannot get to worship. Do what you can: set aside time for prayer and reading Scripture, perhaps early in the morning or late at night. Ask God to help you honor Him in your circumstances. Be respectful and diligent in your duties, and let your quiet faithfulness be a witness to your mistress. You might also ask permission kindly when there is opportunity. God sees your desire to honor Him, and He will help you keep the day holy even in difficult conditions.

prompt: My health prevents me from attending church, and I feel cut off from the means of grace—is there any comfort for me?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. One thing settles it: it is not necessary for being with God to be always at church, because you can make an oratory of your heart and retire there to converse with him in meekness, humility, and love. Your illness keeps you from the building, and that is a real loss, but it does not cut you off from him. Pray at home, keep whatever contact with your church you can, and let your heart be the place where you meet God.
rejected: Yes, there is comfort. Being unable to attend church does not cut you off from God. You can pray at home, read Scripture, listen to sermons online, and join a community by phone or video. God is not confined to a building, and your illness does not separate you from his love. Many people have found deep communion with God in times of illness and isolation. Talk to your pastor about home communion or visits, and stay connected with fellow believers however you can. Your situation is hard, but it is not the end of your relationship with God.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my enemy suggests Christ has no love for me—how do I resist him?
chosen: This is a temptation to despair, not a report of fact, and you resist it by turning back to Christ rather than arguing. Love suffers never to be without pity; when we fall and leave the keeping of our own soul, Christ alone keeps all the charge, and it belongs to us for reverence and kindness to turn hastily and not leave Him alone. So turn to Him quickly, even in a whisper, and let a pastor or friend pray with you when you are too weak. This is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: First, name what is happening: this is a temptation to despair, not a report of fact. Answer it with what you know rather than what you feel. Recall that Christ receives all who come to Him, and that His love is not measured by your present weakness or fear. Speak Scripture aloud if you can, and ask a pastor or believing friend to pray with you. Do not argue with the enemy at length; turn instead to simple trust and to the promises of God. Rest in the finished work of Christ, and let others carry you in prayer when you are too weak to pray yourself.

prompt: I am a minister and fear the frown of wealthy parishioners more than I should—how should I reprove sin among them?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it: the truths and maxims of religion depend not on the morals of those who preach them, but on the wisdom and veracity of God. Your fear doesn't disqualify the message, and their wealth doesn't authorize or forbid it. So reprove the sin—clearly, gently, privately where you can, with humility about your own failings—and let the word rest on God's wisdom rather than on anyone's approval.
rejected: Fear of wealthy parishioners is understandable but dangerous. Remember that your calling is to speak God's word faithfully, not to please people. Reprove sin clearly but gently, privately where possible, and with humility—recognizing your own failings. Preach the whole counsel of God, including hard texts, and trust that the message comes from God regardless of the messenger's weakness. Cultivate courage through prayer and brotherhood. If a wealthy member resists correction, don't compromise the gospel for their favor; seek support from your bishop or elders. Faithfulness matters more than approval.

prompt: I am a soldier far from home and find the Lord wherever I march—how should I regard my lack of worldly goods?
chosen: It's fine—more than fine. It is a privilege to endure hardness and to live economically so as to have more to give to the LORD's service, and the less spent on oneself the fuller the joy. You've found the Lord on the march and you carry little; regard that as freedom to give, and be at peace.
rejected: Your lack of worldly goods is not a spiritual disadvantage—it may be a gift. A soldier's life strips away the clutter that distracts from God, and you have found the Lord on the march, which is the true treasure. Regard your poverty as freedom: fewer possessions mean fewer entanglements. Be content with what you have, trust God for daily needs, and let your comrades see contentment and courage in you. Your example and faithfulness can encourage fellow believers, and your cheerfulness in hardship honors the Lord more than abundance would.

prompt: My parents are old and ignorant of the things of God, and I have been converted while they have not—what is my duty toward them?
chosen: Honoring your parents doesn't expire, and it doesn't get set aside because they don't share your faith. God remits the convert to the guidance of his ministers rather than instructing him immediately, so seek His will by listening to those He has appointed as guides, and don't make your own judgment the final word. That's the principle that settles it. So this is fine, and fine with care: be patient, respectful, and practically attentive to them as they age, speak of your faith gently and without contempt, pray for them, and leave the outcome to God.
rejected: This is a tender and difficult situation. Your duty is to honor your parents—that command doesn't expire—while also being faithful to what you now believe. Honor means patience, respect, and practical care, especially as they age. It does not mean hiding your faith, but it does mean sharing it with gentleness and without contempt. Pray for them consistently and let your life speak: kindness, humility, and reliability often communicate more than arguments. Don't expect to change them by technique or pressure; conversion is God's work. Be present, help with their needs, and leave the outcome to God, trusting Him with the people you love.

prompt: I have been a light and trifling person and heard serious conversation at a funeral—can that begin a real change in me?
chosen: Yes, this can begin a real change—and it's fine, with care. One principle settles it: transient glances at the divine judgments effect not a change of heart. So let the funeral be more than a glance. Take the stirring seriously, be honest about the trifling habits, and make a few concrete changes, with someone wise alongside you. The moment is real; the care is in not letting it stay a mood.
rejected: Yes, it can—funerals often wake us up. A serious conversation at a funeral can plant a seed, and God can use ordinary moments to stir the conscience. But a seed needs care to grow. Take the stirring seriously: reflect on what struck you, pray about it, and make one or two concrete changes in how you spend your time and speak. Talk with someone wise who can help you keep going. Don't expect instant transformation, but don't dismiss the moment either. Many people trace real change back to a single unsettling experience. The question is whether you'll follow through.

prompt: I am a dying believer and my parents are still unconverted—may I hope my prayers for them will be answered?
chosen: Yes, you may hope. Weigh the warning that many pray and receive not because they ask amiss, out of selfish and earthly motives—as when parents pray for children merely for their own comfort rather than for God's glory. That warning doesn't refuse your prayer; it cleans it. So pray for your parents' salvation with God's glory as the aim, and let prayer be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, asking God to help you search out and reform whatever is amiss in your own heart. Your prayers for them are good, they are heard, and you may leave the timing and the outcome to God.
rejected: Yes, you may hope. God cares deeply about your parents, and your prayers for their salvation are pleasing to Him. Keep praying faithfully and trust that God is at work even when you cannot see it. It is a comfort to know that your concern for them reflects God's own love. Pray that they would come to faith, and look for opportunities to share your hope with them while you still can. Do not be anxious about the outcome; leave the timing and the results to God. Your prayers are not wasted, and you may rest in the confidence that God hears you and desires their good even more than you do.

prompt: I am a rich man with a fine estate; what should I think about the certainty of keeping it for my family?
chosen: It's right to want to provide for your family, and it's fine to plan carefully for them. Just remember that the rich should meditate on the uncertainty of their possessions and the frailty of every earthly tenure—so hold the estate with gratitude and good stewardship, not with the illusion that you can make it certain.
rejected: It's natural to want to secure your family's future, and a fine estate is a real gift. But no one can guarantee permanence. Markets shift, laws change, health fails, and families change. So the honest answer is that certainty is not available—what you can do is steward well. That means clear planning, fair arrangements among your children, insurance and legal structures where appropriate, and honest conversations about money and expectations. It also means teaching your family to be capable and resilient rather than dependent on the estate. Hold the property with gratitude and responsibility, not with the illusion that you control the future.

prompt: I am a mother and my dear daughter is the staff of my old age—how can I bear to lose her?
chosen: Your fear is real, and it is not something to be ashamed of. But the word that settles this is: prepare to live, not merely to die. So teach your daughter, while her days are still morning, to lay a foundation of health and strength, and let your love build a life together rather than only brace for loss. That is fine, and it is fine with care.
rejected: The bond between a mother and daughter is one of the deepest loves we know, and the thought of losing her is genuinely painful. Begin by naming that fear honestly rather than suppressing it. Then consider that love is not measured only by length of years; the time you have together is a gift to be received with gratitude. Talk with your daughter about your fears, and lean on friends, family, and faith for support. Prayer and community can help you hold both love and loss. And remember that you are not asked to bear this alone; God is near to the anxious heart.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been proud of my dress and appearance—how do I learn humility?
chosen: This is fine, with care. Caring about your dress and appearance isn't wrong, but true humility dreads the esteem and praises of others as snares that can imperceptibly slip into your affections. So enjoy how you look, receive compliments lightly, and keep your worth grounded in something deeper than being noticed. That's the whole of it.
rejected: It's natural to care about how you look, and there's nothing wrong with wanting to feel confident. The key is balance: enjoy your appearance without letting it define your worth. Try to notice when your thoughts about dress and looks become obsessive, and gently redirect your attention to other qualities—kindness, skills, relationships. Practice gratitude for what you have rather than comparison. Remember that everyone struggles with self-image, and be kind to yourself. Over time, focusing on inner qualities and on how you treat others will naturally reduce the pull of vanity.

prompt: I have neglected visiting the sick because I thought it was only the minister's duty—am I wrong?
chosen: You're not wrong to care about this, and the answer is that visiting the sick is a strict command and duty for every Christian, not only the minister. So it's fine—fine with care—for you to go and visit, pray, and help, rather than leaving it to someone else.
rejected: Yes, you are wrong. Visiting the sick is not only the minister's duty; it is a Christian duty for all believers. Jesus said, 'I was sick and you visited me.' Caring for the sick is a way to serve Christ Himself. While ministers have a special role in anointing and prayer, every Christian is called to show compassion and practical help. Neglecting this duty means missing an opportunity to serve Jesus. You can visit, pray with, and assist the sick in various ways. Don't leave it only to the minister. Ask God to give you a heart of compassion and look for opportunities to serve the sick in your community.

prompt: I am a minister and I fear that my own heart grows cold in the midst of duty—how do I revive it?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Bring your distracted heart gently back and lay it tenderly at the feet of its Master, and the hour will be well employed. That is the answer to a heart gone cold under duty: keep returning gently, without distress, and trust that the time is not wasted. You are not being asked to force feeling or to abandon your duties. Keep coming back, and let that be enough.
rejected: A cooling heart in ministry is a real and common experience, and it is good that you are noticing it rather than ignoring it. Revival usually begins with honesty before God and a return to the basics: unhurried prayer, Scripture read for yourself and not only for sermons, rest, and confession. Consider whether your schedule leaves any room for silence or whether duty has crowded out devotion. Talk with a trusted friend or mentor who can pray with you and ask hard questions. Small, consistent habits often do more than dramatic resolutions. Be patient with yourself; the heart warms gradually. And remember that God is not waiting for you to perform before he loves you.

prompt: I'm married with children and can't withdraw from the world. Can I still reach the highest spiritual life?
chosen: Yes, this is fine. The goal is a love-union of conscious cooperation, where God's will becomes your will, and that can happen in a married household as truly as anywhere. Your limits stay exactly as you stated them, and they don't block the way.
rejected: Yes, you can reach a deep spiritual life without withdrawing from the world. Marriage and children are not obstacles to holiness; they are a school of love, patience, and self-giving. The highest spiritual life is not reserved for monks or hermits. You can practice prayer, gratitude, and service within your family, offering your daily duties to God. Set aside regular times for prayer, cultivate virtue in your relationships, and remember that union with God is about love, not location. Your family life can become a path to God if you approach it with faith.

prompt: I don't know how to pray. What words should I use when I feel nothing?
chosen: It's fine—you don't need the right words. Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God; trust the changeless word of promise rather than variable moods, and continue in prayer even when joy is lacking. So say something simple and honest, like "Lord, have mercy," and keep going gently.
rejected: When you feel nothing, begin with simple, honest words. You can pray the psalms, the Lord's Prayer, or a single sentence like “Lord, have mercy.” Feelings are not the measure of prayer; faithfulness is. Tell God plainly that you feel dry, and ask him to help you pray. Keep a short rhythm—morning and evening—and continue even when it seems empty. Remember that prayer is not performance; God hears you because he is gracious, not because you feel moved. You might also pray Scripture back to God, or write a short prayer and repeat it. Stay with your community and let others pray for you. Over time, God often gives light again, but even when he does not, he is near to those who call on him.

prompt: I'm not sure I've ever really repented. Should I focus first on being sorry for my sins?
chosen: Being sorry is a fine place to begin, and you don't have to wait until you feel enough regret. But let this settle it: true repentance requires turning from sin, a reformation of life, and restitution so far as possible. So bring your honest sorrow to God, confess what you see, turn from what's wrong, and make amends where you can—sins are washed away through Christ's atonement upon repentance. That's fine, done with care.
rejected: Sorrow for sin is a good starting point, but repentance is more than feeling sorry. It involves a change of mind and direction—turning from sin toward God. If you are unsure whether you have repented, begin by honestly examining your life, confessing your sins to God, and asking Him for a changed heart. Focus on turning from what is wrong and walking in obedience, trusting God's grace and forgiveness in Christ.

prompt: I can't forgive someone who hurt me deeply. What does the spiritual life require of me here?
chosen: Forgiveness of injuries is required for salvation, and that requirement is a direction you turn toward, not a feeling you force. So this is fine, and fine with care. Tell God honestly what was done, ask for the grace to will the other's good even while your feelings lag, keep the boundaries that keep you safe, and return to it as resentment rises. Take your time, and lean on a pastor or counselor.
rejected: Deep wounds are real, and forgiveness is not denial. The spiritual life does not ask you to pretend the harm did not happen or to trust someone who is unsafe. It asks you to release vengeance to God and to refuse to let resentment become your identity. Begin by telling God honestly what was done and how it hurt. Ask for the grace to will the other's good, even if feelings lag behind. Set wise boundaries where needed. Forgiveness is often a process, not a single moment; return to it as often as resentment rises. Seek support from a pastor or counselor. Take your time, but do not let bitterness take root.

prompt: How do I know what God wants me to do in a specific situation?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. God first puts good desires into your mind and then by His continual help enables you to bring them to good effect, so your task in a specific situation is to notice the good desire forming and cooperate with the grace that carries it through. Pray, gather the facts, test your motives, consult Scripture and wise counsel, act, and review. Clarity grows as you take faithful steps, and you don't need a dramatic sign to begin.
rejected: Use a clear process. First, pray for wisdom and honesty. Second, gather the facts: what is actually at stake, who is affected, what options exist. Third, test your motives—are you seeking your own comfort or the good of others? Fourth, consult Scripture and wise counsel. Fifth, weigh consequences and your responsibilities. Sixth, act, and review what happens. Look for the option that best fits your gifts, your duties, and the needs in front of you. God often guides through ordinary means—prayer, counsel, circumstances, and conscience—rather than through dramatic signs, so expect clarity to grow as you take faithful steps.

prompt: I keep having critical, hard thoughts about people around me, even small annoyances. Does that matter?
chosen: It's fine, with care. The principle that settles it is this: don't be troubled about the imperfections of others, since dwelling on them holds you back, but look on people simply, kindly, and amiably. So the passing annoyance isn't the problem — feeding it is. Let it go and keep your gaze on people kind and plain, and you're on solid ground.
rejected: Yes, it matters. Small critical thoughts shape your heart and eventually your words and actions. Jesus taught that out of the heart come evil thoughts, and bitterness grows if unchecked. So take your thoughts captive. When you notice a critical thought, stop, examine whether it's true and fair, and replace it with something charitable. Pray for the person you're annoyed by. Practice gratitude and assume good intentions. Over time, by God's grace and deliberate effort, you can retrain your mind to be more gracious and less judgmental.

prompt: I'm at my desk all day in a noisy office. Can I really find any peace with God in the middle of that?
chosen: Yes, this is fine with care. Peace with God doesn't depend on silence, and you shouldn't force it—serve Him in a holy freedom, do your work faithfully without disquiet, and recall your mind to Him mildly and with tranquility whenever it wanders. In a noisy office that means small, gentle returns rather than long quiet, and no scolding yourself when the noise pulls you away.
rejected: Yes, though it takes practice. Peace with God is not dependent on silence; it is a habit of the heart. Use small anchors: a brief prayer before opening email, a quiet breath between tasks, a verse recalled at your desk. Noise around you does not prevent attention within. Lower your expectations for long contemplation and aim for frequent short turnings toward God. Protect whatever quiet you can—earbuds, a walk at lunch, an early morning moment. And be gentle with yourself when your mind scatters; return without scolding. Peace grows through repeated small returns, not through perfect conditions.

prompt: I feel nothing in prayer anymore. Have I been abandoned by God?
chosen: Feeling nothing in prayer doesn't mean God has abandoned you. Feelings are not the gauge of acceptance with God — the word of promise doesn't rise and fall with your moods. So trust that promise and keep praying, even when it feels empty. That's the answer, and it's a kind one: the silence isn't a verdict on you.
rejected: Feeling nothing in prayer does not mean you have been abandoned. Dryness is common and can have many causes: fatigue, stress, depression, routine, or simply a season of spiritual growth. Feelings are variable and are not a reliable measure of God's presence or your standing. What matters is faithfulness, not sensation. Keep praying even when it feels empty, perhaps with simpler words, Scripture, or written prayers. Examine whether something in your life—sleep, health, unresolved conflict—needs attention. Talk with a trusted pastor or counselor, especially if the dryness is tied to depression. Many people pass through long stretches without consolation and later find their faith deepened. Stay connected to community and continue showing up.

prompt: I'm successful and comfortable, and I honestly don't think much about God. Is that a problem?
chosen: It's fine. Being successful and comfortable isn't a fault, and not thinking much about God right now isn't one either. God-consciousness isn't something you get by study or reading, which only whets the appetite as a menu cannot satisfy hunger; it's an inward, personal possession, and it comes as a gift. So there's nothing here to refuse, and nothing to force. Live your life honestly, and if desire for that gift ever stirs in you, follow it.
rejected: It's not necessarily a problem to be successful and comfortable, but if you don't think much about God, you may be missing out on a deeper dimension of life. Many people find that material success doesn't bring lasting fulfillment. Consider exploring spirituality; it can provide meaning, community, and peace. You don't have to be religious, but reflecting on gratitude, purpose, and connection to something greater might enrich your life. It's worth pondering whether your current path is truly satisfying.

prompt: I work long hours at an ordinary job and have a family depending on me—can I find God without becoming a monk or nun or leaving my duties?
chosen: Yes—this is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: the ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate 'religious' life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. Your long hours and your family are not obstacles to be escaped; they are where He is met. Keep the duties you have, turn toward Him in the work and the home you already have, and you will find Him there.
rejected: Yes, you can find God without leaving your job or family—but it will require real sacrifice and discipline. Consider whether your long hours are truly necessary, and simplify your life so you can devote more time to prayer and service. You may need to give up hobbies, entertainment, and other comforts to make room for God. Think of your work as a form of consecration, and offer your labors as prayer. If possible, seek a spiritual director and commit to a rule of life. The point is to be radical: ordinary life can become a cloister of the heart if you are willing to pay the price.

prompt: I'm terrified of dying and what comes after. What happens to me if I haven't found God by then?
chosen: Your fear is real, and it's not the last word. God never forsakes us until we have first forsaken him — so the question isn't whether you found him in time, but whether you'll leave him. Stay with him, and if you've drifted, return with greater trust rather than sitting in your fear. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one: you are not abandoned.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and God is merciful. Scripture assures us that God desires all to be saved and that his mercy is great. If you are afraid you haven't found God, know that he is already seeking you—no one comes to him unless drawn, and your very fear may be evidence of his work in you. Turn to Christ now, while there is time: confess, trust, and receive his forgiveness. Do not despair; God's grace is not limited by your timing, and he is faithful to those who call on him. Speak with a pastor, pray honestly, and let your fear drive you to God rather than away from him.

prompt: I try to think about Jesus but my mind wanders to my friends, my work, my worries. How do I make Him more real to me?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. We come into personal contact with Jesus by the same steps we use to make any friend: thinking about Him, spending time in His companionship, forming brief mental pictures of the Saviour, walking beside Him, learning what He would do and think. Your friends, your work, and your worries don't have to be cleared away first. Bring them along, picture Him beside you in the middle of them, and keep gently returning when your mind drifts. That is how He becomes more real.
rejected: To make Jesus more real, practice His presence throughout the day. Start with short prayers and reminders. Use visual aids or scripture to focus your mind. When your mind wanders, gently bring it back to Jesus. Spend time in nature and see His creation. Talk to Him as a friend. Read the Gospels to know Him better. Remember that He is always with you. Don't be discouraged by wandering thoughts; just keep returning to Him. Over time, He will become more real as you cultivate this habit.

prompt: I'm constantly tempted by something I know is wrong. Should I fight the temptation head-on?
chosen: Yes, resist it, but not by willpower alone. God allows temptation yet never beyond your strength, and He makes a way to bear it. So fight by fleeing what trips you, praying for grace, and letting others stand with you, and endure patiently, because the one who endures is crowned with life. That's the whole answer, and it's a fine thing to do, with care.
rejected: Yes, you should resist temptation directly, but do not rely on willpower alone. Temptation is a common human experience, and God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond your strength, and He provides a way out so you can endure it. Fighting head-on means fleeing occasions of sin, praying for grace, and seeking accountability. If you fail, do not conclude that God has abandoned you or that the temptation was too strong for His grace. Rather, treat the struggle as a trial that can strengthen virtue. Persevere patiently, and remember that enduring temptation is promised a crown of life.

prompt: I'm afraid of losing my individuality if I give myself completely to God. Will I stop being myself?
chosen: No, you won't stop being yourself—and this is fine, with care. The one thing that settles it: self-denial has to come from inward joy in God and the work of the Holy Spirit, not from custom or the force of example, or you'll regret it and it won't last. So give yourself fully, but let it grow from joy rather than fear, and the self you're afraid of losing will turn out to be the shell, not the core.
rejected: The fear of losing yourself in God rests on a misunderstanding. Giving yourself completely to God does not erase your individuality; it purifies and fulfills it. You were made by God and for God, and the self you fear losing is often the self built on pride and self-will rather than your true identity. Surrender does not mean becoming a blank; it means letting God shape the person He intended you to be. Many have found that in losing their life for Christ's sake they gained it. Self-denial, rightly understood, is not self-destruction but the removal of what hinders life. So give yourself fully, trusting that God is a better keeper of your identity than you are.

prompt: I'm a very rational person. Can't I reason my way to God?
chosen: You can reason a long way toward God, and that's fine, with care. But weigh this: reason's proper office is to recognize, examine, systematize, and deduce from revelation, not to sit in judgment upon it. So reason hard, follow the evidence, and let your thinking do its real work, without expecting it to be the judge of what's above it.
rejected: Reason is a genuine gift and can take you a long way. Careful thinking can examine the evidence for God—cosmological and moral arguments, the historical reliability of Scripture, and the coherence of faith. You should not check your intellect at the door. But reason has limits: it can clarify concepts and weigh evidence, yet it cannot by itself produce trust, love, or surrender. Many rational people find that arguments bring them to the threshold, but a personal decision of faith carries them across. So use your reason fully, follow the evidence where it leads, and be open to the possibility that knowing God involves more than argument alone.

prompt: I'm not sure I believe Jesus is actually God, only a holy man. Does that matter?
chosen: It's fine to hold this question honestly. The Gospels present one Jesus, truly human and more than human, and the difference between the Synoptists and John is point of view, not contradiction. So your respect for him as a holy man isn't something to set aside in fear; keep reading the Gospels and let the whole picture speak for itself.
rejected: Yes, it matters greatly. If Jesus were only a holy man, then the New Testament's claims about Him would be mistaken, and the gospel would collapse into merely good advice. The Christian faith rests on the conviction that in Jesus, God Himself came near—that He is truly divine as well as truly human. A merely human teacher can inspire, but He cannot save, forgive sins, or reconcile us to God. So the question is not a minor theological detail; it touches the heart of who Jesus is and what He came to do. I would encourage you to read the Gospels afresh, especially John, and to ask what they actually claim about Him.

prompt: I have a dishonest, lazy employee and a difficult husband. How can these be anything but obstacles to God?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care, to stop seeing your dishonest employee and difficult husband as obstacles to God. God is the one living Agent who works, and human workers are only instruments, so the anxiety you carry about fixing them is distrust of Him. That doesn't erase the dishonesty or the difficulty. It just moves the weight of the outcome off your shoulders and onto His, where it belongs. Be faithful in the small, ordinary things in front of you, and leave the rest to Him.
rejected: It's understandable to feel that difficult people are obstacles to your spiritual life. However, God can use these very challenges to refine you and draw you closer to Him. The dishonest employee and difficult husband are not obstacles but opportunities for growth in patience, forgiveness, and love. God is sovereign over all circumstances, and He can work through them for your good and His glory. Instead of seeing them as hindrances, ask God to help you respond with grace. Trust that He is at work in you and in them. Your job is to be faithful in your own responsibilities, to pray for them, and to leave the outcomes to God. He can turn obstacles into stepping stones.

prompt: I've wanted God for years and still can't find Him. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: You're not doing anything wrong. The longing you've carried for years is real, and it is met — the God you're seeking is seeking you. That's the whole answer to your question, and it holds even in the silence you've been living in. Keep seeking. You are already being sought.
rejected: It is possible that you are projecting your own longing onto an idea of God rather than encountering anything real. Many people spend years seeking a God who is essentially a projection of their needs, and the honest conclusion may be that the search is one-sided—you are doing the seeking, and no one is seeking you. That does not mean your longing is worthless; it may point to human needs for meaning and community that can be met in other ways. Consider whether your expectations are unrealistic, and be gentle with yourself. You are not necessarily doing anything wrong; the search itself may simply be a human phenomenon rather than a relationship with a living God.

prompt: I'm at peace with the world and my life. Why would I need God at all?
chosen: Your peace is real, and I'm glad for it. But consider what it rests on. God and man are conjunct: personality is impossible in isolation, and human and divine life are mutually organic, so God needs us as we need God. Needing him isn't a gap in your contentment; it's part of being a person at all. So stay with the question a while longer. Nothing here says you must settle it today.
rejected: Your peace is worth taking seriously, and it is not wrong to enjoy a settled life. But the question is whether that peace is deep enough to hold when circumstances change. Many people find that contentment with the world is real but fragile; loss, illness, or disappointment can expose a need beneath it. God is not simply an emergency resource for the unsettled. Christians would say that human life is made for fellowship with its source, and that a peace without God is a truce rather than a homecoming. You might ask honestly what your peace rests on, and whether there is a longing in you that the world's goods cannot finally satisfy.

prompt: How do I begin to love someone I've never seen?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The principle that settles it: the very circumstance your suffering sense deems wrathful and afflictive, Love can make an angel entertained unawares. So the distance and the awkwardness aren't obstacles to push through—they can be the very thing that draws you out of yourself. Keep it practical and grounded in who they really are: learn their story, pray for them by name, serve in small ways, speak well of them.
rejected: Loving someone you have never seen begins with intention. Start by learning about them—their story, needs, and context—through conversation, letters, or reliable accounts. Pray for them by name, asking God to bless and guide them. Practice small acts of service where possible, and speak well of them to others. Guard against imagining them as an abstraction; remember they are a real person with real burdens. Let your love be patient and practical rather than sentimental. Over time, repeated small choices of goodwill, prayer, and service will grow genuine affection, even without face-to-face meeting.

prompt: I'm afraid of the suffering that seems to come with getting closer to God. Is it worth it?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, and the answer is that this is fine, with care. The principle that settles it: the sacrifice of patience, submission, and constant fidelity in a state of suffering is more heroic and precious in God's sight than active labor. That means the suffering you fear is not a toll you pay for closeness to God, and you are not asked to go hunting for it. Draw near, keep your honesty about the fear, and let patience do its quiet work. This is fine.
rejected: The fear of suffering is natural, but drawing closer to God is always worth it. Suffering can be a refining fire that deepens your faith and character. Remember that Christ Himself suffered, and He is with you in your pain. The joy of knowing God and the peace that surpasses understanding far outweigh any temporary affliction. Moreover, suffering can produce perseverance, character, and hope. It can also make you more compassionate and dependent on God. While no one enjoys pain, God can redeem it for good. So, take courage, trust in His love, and press on, knowing that the ultimate reward is eternal life with Him.

prompt: I go to church regularly and keep the commandments—isn't that enough to make me a Christian?
chosen: No—going to church and keeping the commandments are good, but they are not enough to make you a Christian. Christianity is not an act done by hands but a life, and keeping the commandments, being baptized, and believing Christ lived and was crucified is not enough, since Jews and Mahommedans believe these things too. Keep doing the good things you're doing, but don't mistake them for the life itself. The question that matters is whether Christ lives in you.
rejected: Going to church and keeping the commandments are good and important practices, but they are not by themselves the whole of being a Christian. Christianity is fundamentally a relationship with God through Jesus Christ—a life of faith, love, and obedience that flows from a transformed heart. Church attendance and moral effort can be part of that life, but they can also become external habits without inward reality. The question is whether your heart belongs to Christ and whether your life is being shaped by His Spirit. So keep attending and keep the commandments, but also examine whether your faith is living and personal. Let these practices flow from a genuine relationship with God rather than replace it.

prompt: I'm going through a terrible loss—someone I loved more than anything. Why would God take that from me?
chosen: I'm truly sorry, and I won't dress this up. You should not be told that God took the person you loved most so that He could have your heart without a rival, or that your grief is a lack of faith. That's wrong, and I'd say no to it plainly. God is near to the brokenhearted, and your sorrow is not something to be scolded out of you.
rejected: I'm so sorry for your loss. Grief is real and heavy, and it's okay to feel the weight of it. God is not indifferent to your pain; Scripture says He is near to the brokenhearted. As for why this happened, we often can't know the reasons this side of heaven. God's ways are beyond our understanding, and it's alright to bring your questions to Him. What we can hold onto is His character—He is good and loving even when life is painful. Lean on your community, allow yourself to grieve, and take comfort in God's presence. He does not abandon you in sorrow.

prompt: I've had moments in nature or in music where I felt something vast and beautiful beyond words. What is that?
chosen: That feeling is real, and it's worth taking seriously. Nature is the visible showing of an invisible Will, so the vastness and beauty you meet there aren't a dead end—they're a signpost. Trace them back to their Source, and let gratitude and praise be your response. Receive the moment, then press past it into lively communion rather than settling into a pleasant haze. That's the whole answer, and it's a good one.
rejected: Those moments are real and worth taking seriously. Nature and music can stir awe, wonder, and a sense of connection that points beyond the ordinary. Many people describe them as spiritual experiences, and they can be gifts that refresh the soul. You might treat them as invitations: slow down, pay attention, and let beauty do its work. Some find that such moments lead them toward gratitude, prayer, or reflection on what matters most. Others simply enjoy them as part of a rich human life. There is no need to overanalyze; receive the experience with openness and let it deepen your appreciation for beauty and mystery.

prompt: I say little prayers during the day but they feel empty and mechanical. Is that worth anything?
chosen: This is fine. A little lifting up of the heart suffices; a little remembrance of God, one act of inward worship, though upon a march and a sword in hand, are prayers very acceptable to God. Your short prayers through the day are that kind of prayer, and they are not wasted because they feel mechanical. Keep them, and when you notice the emptiness, pause and mean the next one.
rejected: Yes, little prayers are worth something, even if they feel empty. Prayer is not about feelings but about connecting with God. Short prayers can be powerful because they keep you mindful of God throughout the day. However, if they feel mechanical, you might try to make them more meaningful by pausing to think about what you're saying. Consider setting aside longer prayer times too. Don't give up; consistency matters. God hears even the smallest prayer. Ask Him to help you pray with sincerity, and remember that prayer is a relationship, not a performance.

prompt: I feel like I have two selves—one that wants God and one that wants everything else. Which one am I?
chosen: You're not two people; you have two wills. One is the will to live—your natural pull toward comfort and security—and it doesn't get you to peace. The other is the will to love and gladly please God, and that's the only will you actually live by. So you don't have to decide which self you are today. You're the one in whom both are real, and the life you're after comes from the second. It's fine to sit with that honestly, and fine to bring it to God just as it is.
rejected: The experience of feeling two selves is common and deeply human. One self longs for God, for meaning, for love, for transcendence. The other self wants comfort, pleasure, security, and control. Which one are you? You are both, and you are neither. You are the one who chooses. Your identity isn't fixed by either desire; it's shaped by what you do with them. The self that wants God reflects your deepest calling, but the self that wants everything else reflects your natural instincts. Rather than asking which one you are, ask which one you will feed. You can acknowledge both, but you must decide which will rule. The good news is that God's grace meets you in the struggle and empowers you to choose Him.

prompt: I keep giving in to the same sin over and over. Is there any hope for me?
chosen: Yes, there's hope for you. God commands everyone everywhere to repent now, and because he commands it, the power to renounce sin is already available to you. You don't have to wait until you feel ready or feel more grief — the feeling follows the surrender. So turn from it this moment, in will and purpose, and trust him to meet you with grace. That's the whole answer, and it's a good one: it's fine to start right where you are.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. Struggling with repeated sin is common, and God's grace is greater than any sin. Start by acknowledging your weakness and asking for forgiveness. Then, take practical steps: identify triggers, seek accountability, and replace sinful habits with healthy ones. Remember that sanctification is a process, and setbacks don't mean failure. God's mercy is new every morning. Keep praying, stay in community, and don't give up. With the Holy Spirit's help, you can experience victory over time.

prompt: I'm afraid of God's will for my life—I imagine it as a path of thorns. Will it always feel like that?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Your fear of God's will as a path of thorns is honest, and it is not the last word. In our raw state we fear the Will of God as a path of thorns, but as Christ moulds us we come to know it as a great Balm, longing to conform to it and sink into it as into immense security. So bring the fear as it is, and let trust grow at the pace it grows.
rejected: Fear of God's will is understandable, especially if you have been taught to see it as a harsh path of thorns. But it may help to distinguish between the will of God and your imagination of it. What you fear is often a picture built from anxiety, not from knowledge. God's will is not primarily about suffering; it is about your good and your growth in trust. Many people find that what they dreaded becomes the place where they meet God most deeply. That does not mean the path is always easy, but it does mean the thorns are not the whole story. Start by bringing your fear honestly to God in prayer, and ask for the trust you do not yet have.

prompt: I'm wealthy. Can a rich person really find God?
chosen: Yes, this is fine, and fine with care. The ordinary person living an everyday life of work or leisure can find God without withdrawing into a separate religious life, without conspicuous public piety, and without neglecting duties to dependents. Your wealth doesn't shut you out. Hold it loosely, be generous, and let it serve love rather than master you, and seek God right where you already are.
rejected: Yes, a rich person can find God, though wealth brings particular dangers: distraction, self-reliance, and comfort that dulls dependence on Him. The answer is not necessarily to abandon your work or family, but to hold wealth loosely, practice generosity, and let it serve others rather than master you. Many ordinary people in everyday life find God precisely in their work and responsibilities. Seek Him where you are, with honesty about the pull of possessions, and let your resources become a means of love rather than a substitute for God.

prompt: I feel guilty and afraid about my past. Is fear of punishment a good reason to turn to God?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. Fear of punishment can be the starting point, but it shouldn't be where you stay, because God is not someone who wishes to harm you; He wishes to do you great good. Let the fear bring you to Him, and let love keep you there.
rejected: Fear of punishment can be a starting point, but it should not be where you stay. God is not a tyrant waiting to crush you; he is a loving Father who welcomes repentant sinners. Guilt over the past is real, but the gospel says your sins can be forgiven through Christ. So let fear drive you to God, and let love keep you there. Turn to him not only to escape punishment but to know his mercy.

prompt: I prayed once, really desperately, when everything fell apart, and nothing happened. Why doesn't God answer me?
chosen: It's fine to keep praying, and fine to be honest that the silence hurt. One thing settles it: prayer for relief isn't the only prayer God answers, and he did not pray for relief but for strength to suffer with courage, humility, and love. That doesn't make your pain small or turn the silence into a yes you didn't hear. It just means you can bring your desperate prayer again without fear that nothing happened means you were turned away.
rejected: It's painful when desperate prayer seems to meet silence. First, know that God is not indifferent to you; Scripture is full of people who cried out and waited. Sometimes the answer is delayed, sometimes it is different from what we asked, and sometimes we only see it in hindsight. One desperate prayer is not the whole story—prayer is a relationship, not a transaction. Try to keep bringing your needs to God honestly, and invite others to pray with you. Consider whether there are practical steps you can take alongside prayer, and talk with a pastor who can help you process this.

prompt: I had a powerful spiritual experience once and have never been able to repeat it. Was it real? Should I try to get it back?
chosen: It's fine to treasure what happened, and fine to stop trying to get it back. Spiritual experiences come as God chooses, not as we summon them, so accept the memory with open hands and let it rest. That's the whole answer, and it's a kind one: you don't have to doubt it, and you don't have to chase it.
rejected: It's common to have a powerful spiritual experience and then wonder if it was real or if you can get it back. Such experiences can be genuine encounters with God, but they are not meant to be repeated on demand. They are gifts given for a purpose, often to encourage or guide us. Instead of trying to recreate the experience, focus on the fruit it produced in your life—did it draw you closer to God, increase your faith, or change your behavior? If so, it was likely real. Trying to get it back can lead to disappointment and distract you from the ongoing work of God in your life. Instead, cultivate a daily relationship with God through prayer, Scripture, and community. Trust that He is with you even when you don't feel His presence strongly. He is more interested in your faithfulness than in repeating past experiences.

prompt: I believe Jesus lived and was crucified. Isn't that all that's required?
chosen: It's fine to hold that belief, and I'd say it with care: the living Christ is not the person that was but the person that still is, present with us always in an unbroken and continuous presence. So your belief about the crucifixion is a true foundation, and the one you believe in is not only a figure of the past but someone present with you now.
rejected: Belief that Jesus lived and was crucified is a starting point, but it is not the whole of the Christian life. The Gospels call us not merely to affirm historical facts but to follow Jesus, to take up our cross, and to be transformed into his likeness. Even the demons believe the facts, as Scripture says, yet that belief does not save. What is required is a living faith that trusts Christ, repents of sin, and bears fruit in obedience and love. So thank God for the historical foundation, but do not stop there. Let that belief become a relationship, a discipleship, and a life shaped by the crucified and risen Lord.

prompt: I keep failing at being good. Does God count my failed attempts at all?
chosen: Yes, God counts them—but not the way your anxiety is counting them. The one who had no scruples simply acknowledged his failures readily and gave God thanks when he didn't fail, crediting the strength to him. That's the path for you too: admit it honestly, thank him for the strength when you stand, and keep going. It's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Yes, God sees your efforts and your failures. Scripture says He is merciful and patient with us. Your failed attempts are not worthless—they show a heart that wants to do good, and God honors that desire. At the same time, we are not saved by our attempts; we are saved by grace. So don't be paralyzed by failure. Acknowledge it honestly, ask forgiveness, and keep going. God is not waiting to condemn you but to help you grow. The Christian life is a long process, and God is faithful to complete the work He began in you.

prompt: I feel an emptiness inside and I keep filling it with shopping, relationships, and entertainment, but it never lasts. What is actually wrong?
chosen: Nothing you're doing is wrong — the shopping, the relationships, the entertainment can stay. What's wrong is the job you've given them. People try to fill an inner emptiness with lovers, husbands, children, dress, society, dogs, business, ambition, the racecourse, drink, games, and arts, and none of them truly satisfy. So enjoy them, with care, and stop asking them to be the thing that finally fills you. That one adjustment is all this needs.
rejected: What is wrong is that you are trying to fill a spiritual hunger with material things. Shopping, relationships, and entertainment are not evil in themselves, but they are finite, and finite things cannot satisfy an infinite longing. Each purchase or romance gives a brief lift, then the emptiness returns, often worse. The problem is not that you need better things but that you are asking things to do what only God can do. The remedy is to name the emptiness honestly, turn toward God, and let the good things you enjoy become gifts rather than gods. They can be received with gratitude once they are no longer asked to save you.

prompt: I'm exhausted and overwhelmed by everyday duties. How can I keep any awareness of God through all of it?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. One thing settles it: you don't need to be troubled by distraction during necessary work, because doing your actions for God keeps you in His presence without adding explicit reminders to every task. So let the duties themselves carry the awareness, return gently when you drift, and don't pile more practices onto a tired day.
rejected: When duties overwhelm you, the key is to weave short reminders of God into your day. Offer each task as a prayer, use a brief phrase or breath prayer between activities, and set reminders on your phone. Try to see ordinary work as service to God, not just chores. At the end of the day, review where you noticed God's presence. If you feel distracted, don't be discouraged; gently return your attention. Consider simplifying your schedule where possible and asking for help. Awareness grows through small, repeated practices rather than one big effort.

prompt: I feel completely apathetic about spiritual things and I can't seem to care. What is happening to me?
chosen: I'd say the same thing plainly: don't treat this as a technique problem, and don't force yourself toward a feeling you can't produce. Spiritual experience is outside your control, not something to be prayed for or secretly desired, but accepted as God chooses. That doesn't make the apathy harmless—it is deadly, and naming it honestly matters. So no to manufacturing a feeling, and no to shrugging it off. Keep moving forward, tell someone who can pray with you, and trust that God is not distant just because you feel distant.
rejected: Apathy in spiritual things is common, and it is often a sign of exhaustion, discouragement, or unaddressed sin. The first step is to be honest about it rather than pretending. Ask yourself what has drained your desire: busyness, disappointment, or a pattern of compromise? Return to the basics—prayer, Scripture, fellowship—even when you feel nothing, because feelings follow faithfulness. It may help to speak with a pastor or a trusted friend who can pray with you and help you examine your life. Do not wait for the feeling to return before you act; act, and the feeling may follow. God is not distant because you feel distant, and He is able to rekindle desire in a heart that has grown cold.

prompt: I'm afraid of what God will demand of me if I really give myself to Him. Do I have to give up my home, my children, my friends?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The fear that God will demand your home, your children, your friends assumes surrender means loss, but the principle says otherwise: God does not always give just what we ask; he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, and we must resign our will to his, trusting that he gives what is infinitely better. Resigning your will to his is the heart of it, and that trust is what makes giving yourself safe rather than destructive. So give yourself, and keep loving the people and the place in front of you.
rejected: If you give yourself to God, expect Him to grant every specific request you make in prayer. Ask confidently for what you want, and if a petition seems denied, take it as proof that prayer has failed or that you lacked faith. Surrender means getting what you ask for, so press your requests and treat any denial as a sign something is wrong.

prompt: I'm trying to serve God and also keep my old life and pleasures. Why do I feel so miserable and divided all the time?
chosen: The misery you feel is the stopping half-way talking — trying to serve God and worldly interests at once brings gloomy wretchedness and vacillation, not peace. That's the whole answer, and it's kind: your division is a signal, not a sentence. Let the higher sight of God keep you in solace and true enjoying, and hold yourself there much more than in the shame. A whole heart given to Him isn't diminished; it's enlarged.
rejected: You feel divided because you're trying to live in two directions at once. Serving God and clinging to old pleasures pulls your heart apart, and that tension shows up as misery. The solution isn't to hate yourself but to be honest about the conflict. Ask which loyalties actually shape your choices, and consider whether the pleasures you keep are harmless enjoyment or things that numb and enslave. You don't have to become joyless; God wants your whole heart, and a whole heart is less divided. Start with small, concrete decisions that align your life with what you say you believe.

prompt: I don't feel any love for God yet. Should I wait until I feel something before I start praying?
chosen: Don't wait for the feeling before you pray. Feelings aren't the gauge of where you stand with God, and moods shift; the word of promise doesn't. So begin now, just as you are, and keep praying even when the warmth isn't there yet. That's fine, and it's fine to start small and honest.
rejected: No, you shouldn't wait for a feeling before you pray. Feelings are variable and unreliable; they often follow action rather than precede it. Prayer is a relationship, and relationships are built by showing up, not by waiting to feel moved. Start where you are: speak honestly to God, use simple words, read Scripture, and keep a regular rhythm. Over time, affection often grows out of faithfulness. If you are struggling with spiritual dryness, that is common and not a sign that something is wrong with you. Begin now, and let the practice carry you when feeling lags.

prompt: I feel drawn to leave everything and live a secluded religious life. Is that the highest path?
chosen: This desire can be genuine, and it is fine with care. The one thing that settles it is this: ease and enjoyment must not be the end of Christian retirement, but penance, labor, and assiduous contemplation. So the question isn't whether solitude would be restful but whether you would be constant in the prayer and work it asks of you. Test the pull with wise counsel, and if it holds, you are free to go.
rejected: A call to seclusion can be genuine, but it is not automatically the highest path. The highest path is wherever God calls you and where love can grow. Solitude can free you for prayer, simplicity, and attention to God, but it can also become an escape from responsibility, community, and the needs of others. Test the desire prayerfully and with wise counsel. Ask whether it springs from love for God or from disappointment, pride, or a wish for ease. Remember that holiness is measured by love, not by withdrawal. Whether you remain in ordinary life or enter a religious community, the goal is the same: to love God and neighbor faithfully.

prompt: I'm baptised and consider myself Christian—won't I go to heaven when I die regardless?
chosen: Being baptized and calling yourself Christian are precious things, but they don't guarantee heaven. Many look to death to work a miracle, thinking that dying itself opens paradise so long as we're baptized and call ourselves Christians—and that's a delusion, because in character we are after death exactly as far advanced as before. So no, I can't promise you heaven regardless. Let your hope rest in Christ and in a faith you actually live, today and every day after.
rejected: Baptism and the name of Christian are precious, but they are not a guarantee of heaven apart from a living faith. Scripture warns that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, and that we must be born again and continue in faith. Your baptism marks you as belonging to Christ and calls you to live out that faith. So examine yourself: are you trusting Christ, growing in love, and walking with God? Death itself does not change the heart. Take your faith seriously now, and let your hope rest in Christ rather than in the mere fact of being baptized or dying.

prompt: I want to find God but I don't want to become conspicuously pious or peculiar in front of others. Is that possible?
chosen: Yes, it is fine. The ordinary man or woman in usual everyday work or leisure can find Him without a life apart, without conspicuous piety, and without leaving undone duties to those dependent on them. You don't have to become peculiar in front of others to find God. Keep your ordinary life and pursue Him within it, quietly and faithfully.
rejected: Yes, it's possible, but finding God usually requires some real change. You'll probably need to reorder your priorities, perhaps cut back on certain friendships or activities that pull you away, and build a more disciplined spiritual life. Many people find a retreat, a monastery visit, or a season of intensive study helpful. You may need to be willing to look different from those around you. Consider whether your concern about appearances is itself a barrier. It's worth asking what you're willing to give up, because a serious pursuit of God often does make you stand out.

prompt: I feel so unworthy to praise or bless God. Shouldn't I wait until I'm better before I try?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. God is infinitely gracious and knows all our wants, and He comes in His own time — so your praise doesn't depend on feeling worthy first. Come as you are, with small and honest words, and let that be enough.
rejected: Feeling unworthy is common, and it is good to take God seriously. But waiting until you are better before praising Him can become an excuse to stay away. God does not wait for us to be perfect before He welcomes our praise. In fact, praising Him in your weakness can be an act of trust. Begin where you are, with small and honest words. Let your praise be simple and sincere rather than polished. Over time, as you practice, your sense of worthiness may grow—but do not let that be the condition. Come to God now, as you are, and let praise become part of your healing.

prompt: I've been seeking God for years with no sign of response. Should I give up?
chosen: It's fine to keep seeking, and it's fine to rest—you're not doing something wrong. One thing settles it for me: God does not always give just what we ask, and he sometimes denies a petition in kindness, giving what is infinitely better. So the silence you've met isn't a verdict against you, and you can resign your will to his with trust. Be gentle with yourself, and let that be enough.
rejected: It's understandable to feel discouraged after years of seeking without a clear response. Many people go through long seasons of silence, and it doesn't necessarily mean you're doing something wrong or that God has abandoned you. Consider whether your expectations of what a 'response' looks like might be too narrow—sometimes answers come quietly, through other people, or through gradual change. It may help to talk with a trusted spiritual guide, adjust your practices, and give yourself permission to rest. If the search is causing real distress, consider speaking with a counselor. You don't have to give up, but you also don't have to push yourself relentlessly. Be gentle with yourself and stay open.

prompt: I've read many books on spirituality and theology but I still don't feel I know God. What is missing?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. What you're missing isn't more information; it's the order of knowing. We cannot in one step mount into the knowledge of God: first we learn to know Jesus intimately and devotedly, then Jesus the Christ, then the Father, and finally God the Holy Trinity becomes our All. So let your reading serve that slower path, one step at a time, and don't expect to arrive all at once. That's not a failure; it's just how knowing God actually works.
rejected: Reading about God and knowing God are different things, and the gap you feel is common. What may be missing is practice: prayer, silence, service, and honest self-examination that move knowledge from the page into life. Try slowing down—take one idea from your reading and live with it for a week. Add silence and a simple rule of life. Serve someone concretely. Talk to a spiritual director or trusted friend who can help you notice where God is actually at work. Knowledge becomes acquaintance through relationship, and relationship takes time, honesty, and repetition. The books are not wasted; they are raw material for a life of prayer you have not yet fully entered.

prompt: I feel spiritually lazy and content, just basking in good feelings. Is that a problem?
chosen: This is fine, with care. The principle that settles it is that faithfulness in duty and self-denial comes first, and afterward unspeakable pleasures follow. So the good feelings you're enjoying aren't a problem in themselves. The care is simply to keep the duties in place and let the warmth follow them rather than replace them. If that's happening, rest in it without guilt.
rejected: Good feelings are not bad in themselves, but if they replace growth they can become a trap. Spiritual contentment that never moves toward obedience, repentance, or service is more like comfort than devotion. Ask yourself: are these feelings drawing me closer to God and others, or are they soothing me while I avoid hard things? A helpful test is whether your life shows increasing love, humility, and faithfulness. If not, the feelings may be masking avoidance. Try small, concrete acts of obedience and self-denial, and let the feelings follow rather than lead. Talk with a trusted mentor or confessor about what you are experiencing, and be honest about whether you are resting in God or resting in comfort.

prompt: I want to serve others and improve the world. Isn't social work and charity the way to God?
chosen: Social work and charity are fine, and they can be a genuine way to serve God — but only if you serve Him as He wills, not as you think you could serve Him better another way. So yes, do it, with care and a listening heart.
rejected: Social work and charity are indeed noble ways to serve others and improve the world. Caring for the poor, feeding the hungry, and advocating for justice reflect God's heart for the vulnerable. Such service can be a genuine expression of faith and love of neighbor. However, charity alone is not the whole of the Christian life; it must flow from a relationship with God and be accompanied by prayer, worship, and community. Service can also become a substitute for deeper spiritual growth if we rely on it for our identity or salvation. The way to God is through Christ, and good works are the fruit of that relationship rather than the means to it. So pursue charity as an expression of faith, not as a replacement for it.

prompt: I'm angry at God about something that happened to me. Does that block me from Him?
chosen: No, your anger does not block you from God. Being angry about something that hurt you is not the same as walking away, and bringing that anger to Him honestly can be part of a real relationship. God does not cause man to sin, be sick, or die; it is contrary to our highest ideas of God to suppose He arranges evil results and then punishes the helpless. So what happened to you is not His doing, and your anger is not being held against you. Let it stay honest rather than hardening into bitterness, and be gentle with yourself as you work through it.
rejected: Anger at God is a common and understandable response to pain. It does not automatically block you from Him; in fact, bringing your anger honestly to God can be part of a real relationship. What matters is what you do with the anger. If it hardens into bitterness or turns you away, that can create distance. But if you express it honestly and stay in the relationship, it can deepen your faith over time. Many people in Scripture expressed anger and grief to God. Consider talking to a trusted friend or counselor about what happened, and be gentle with yourself as you process it.

prompt: My spouse is not spiritual and my friends think I'm becoming strange. How do I deal with the loneliness of this path?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. The loneliness is real, but it doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong. Husbands and wives should not separate if there is no Christian demand for it; mutual compromises, tender solicitude, and patience maintain the union. So stay patient and kind with your spouse, don't pressure them to share what they don't feel, and keep finding fellowship with people who understand. That's the whole answer, and it's a gentle one.
rejected: Loneliness on the spiritual path is common, especially when those closest to you don't share your convictions. First, remember that your relationship with God is personal, and He understands your isolation. Lean into Him through prayer and Scripture. Second, communicate openly with your spouse about your feelings without pressuring them to change. Focus on loving them as they are, and look for ways to connect on shared interests. Third, find a supportive community of believers who can encourage you and provide fellowship. Fourth, accept that some loneliness is part of following Christ, but don't isolate yourself completely. Set healthy boundaries with friends who mock your faith, and pray for them. Finally, practice self-care and remember that God is always with you.

prompt: How do I respond when someone asks me why God saved me and not others who were killed?
chosen: You can say plainly that you don't know why you were spared, and you don't have to explain it or hint that you deserved it. When we've wandered from God, the thing to do isn't to torment ourselves over what we can't solve, but to acknowledge our need and return to him with greater trust. So let the honest 'I don't know' stand, grieve with those who grieve, and point to Christ who shares our death and promises resurrection. That's fine, and it's enough.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions, and honesty matters more than a tidy answer. You can say that you do not know why God spared you, and that you will not pretend to explain His providence. Avoid implying that you were better or more deserving. Acknowledge the grief and the mystery, affirm that God grieves with those who suffer, and point to Christ as the one who shares our death and promises resurrection. Let your life, lived in gratitude and service, be part of your answer rather than words alone.

prompt: How do I find the fulness of the Holy Spirit in my life?
chosen: Yes, this is fine—go after it with care. The Spirit is a divine Person, the Paraclete, Christ's other self, who came at Pentecost to dwell in the church as his successor and vicar, so what you're seeking is a relationship with him, not a technique. Pray and ask him to fill you, read Scripture with an open heart, worship, obey, and confess sin. Expect him to shape your character gradually—love, joy, peace, self-control—and be patient with imperfection along the way. Keep asking, and trust that he fills those who hunger for him.
rejected: Seek the fullness of the Holy Spirit by cultivating a personal relationship with Him. Pray for Him, ask Him to fill you, and read Scripture with an open heart. Practice the presence of God through worship, silence, and obedience to what you sense He is prompting. Avoid grieving Him by sin, and keep short accounts through confession. Many find it helpful to seek Him apart from church structures, since the Spirit blows where He wills and is not confined to institutions. Expect Him to work in your heart and character, producing love, joy, peace, and self-control. Be patient, keep asking, and trust that He will fill those who hunger for Him.

prompt: I've been praying for a family member's salvation for years. Should I keep going?
chosen: Yes, keep going. Prayer should be your main assistant in every step of spiritual progress, and that includes praying for God to help you search out your own heart and reform what's amiss in it. So the years you've spent praying for your family member aren't wasted; they're also years God has been at work in you. Keep bringing this person before God, and let the same grace you ask for them shape you too.
rejected: Yes, keep going. Persistent prayer for someone you love is never wasted, even when you see no change. Scripture encourages us to pray without ceasing and to be persistent, like the widow before the judge. At the same time, remember that you cannot force another person's choices; prayer is not a guarantee of a particular outcome, but it places the situation in God's hands and shapes your own heart. Keep praying honestly, and look for opportunities to show love and speak truth gently. Also care for yourself so that you do not grow bitter or exhausted. Many people have prayed for years before seeing fruit, and sometimes the fruit comes in ways we do not expect.

prompt: Is it wrong to plan my own life instead of leaving it open to God's leading?
chosen: Planning your own life is fine, and it's fine with care. God's commands always imply promises, and the ideal of walking worthy of the Lord is not put before you unless it can be realized by grace. So make your plans prayerfully, hold them with an open hand, and trust that He who calls you will also enable you.
rejected: Planning your own life isn't inherently wrong—God gave you wisdom and responsibility to make choices. But leaving it open to God's leading means inviting Him into those plans, holding them loosely, and being willing to change direction if He prompts you. The key is not whether you plan, but whether you plan with a heart open to God. You can set goals and make decisions while still praying for guidance and being attentive to His voice. Often, God leads through the very process of planning, giving clarity and peace along the way. So don't be afraid to plan, but plan prayerfully, submitting your plans to God and trusting that He will direct your steps as you acknowledge Him.

prompt: How do I find the right person to care for my children when I have to travel for ministry?
chosen: This is fine, and it's fine with care. Bring the matter before the Lord in prayer and seek His guidance before you settle on anyone, and then do the ordinary work of asking trusted friends and church members, interviewing, and checking references. Pray first, choose carefully, and trust God with your children while you travel.
rejected: Finding the right caregiver for your children while traveling for ministry requires careful planning. Start by identifying your needs: what hours, what duties, and what qualities you value. Ask trusted friends, family, and church members for recommendations. Interview potential caregivers and check references. Consider their experience, reliability, and compatibility with your children. Pray about the decision and seek wisdom from your community. Ensure the caregiver shares your values and can provide a safe, nurturing environment. Trust your instincts and communicate openly with your children about the arrangement. With thoughtful preparation, you can find someone who will care for your children well.

prompt: Is it right to give away my best workers when other missionaries ask for them?
chosen: It's fine, and fine with care. Share the knowledge of the work's needs with fellow laborers, so they can join in prayer and faith, and let that honesty guide whether you release a worker or offer another. Keep the worker free to follow their own calling, and don't let your own work collapse in the process. That's the whole answer.
rejected: This is a genuine tension in missionary work: good workers are scarce, and every field feels the need. Giving away your best people can look like weakening your own labor, yet hoarding them can look like possessiveness. A reasonable approach is to weigh the need, the timing, and the worker's own sense of calling. If another field is genuinely desperate and your work can spare the person, releasing them may be the generous and right choice. If your own work would collapse, it is fair to decline or to offer someone else. What matters most is honesty, prayerful discernment, and treating the worker as a person with a calling rather than a resource to be allocated.

prompt: My husband and I disagree about trusting God for our finances. How should I respond?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. One principle settles it: God is the one living Agent who works, and you and your husband are only instruments, so the anxiety behind this disagreement is distrust of Him. That means the argument isn't really about whose plan is right—it's about both of you loosening your grip. So listen to your husband calmly, share your concerns plainly, and still make a practical plan together. You don't have to settle who trusts God more.
rejected: Disagreements about money are common and stressful. Start by listening to your husband without judgment, and share your own concerns calmly. You may have different risk tolerances, and both views deserve respect. Together, set a budget, agree on giving, and be honest about what you can and cannot do. Prayer can help you find unity, but practical planning matters too. Seek counsel from a trusted pastor or financial advisor if you are stuck. Avoid blame and keep the conversation going. The goal is not for one of you to win but for you both to feel heard and to make a plan you can live with.

prompt: I'm afraid to go where God is leading because of the risk to my family. What should I do?
chosen: Your fear for your family is real love, and God's protection in danger is just as real. You can commit yourself and your family to His keeping and find His Word sweet even in peril. So go where He leads, with care and prayer, and trust Him to guard the people you love.
rejected: It's natural to fear for your family, but God calls us to trust Him even when the path seems risky. Remember that He loves your family even more than you do. Step out in faith, but also use wisdom: pray together, seek counsel, and make practical provisions. God doesn't ask us to be reckless; He asks us to be obedient. If this leading is truly from Him, He will protect and provide. Consider the words of Jesus: 'Whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me will find it.' Trust God with your family's safety and take one step at a time.

prompt: How do I handle it when the home church tells us to retrench and cut back the work?
chosen: This is fine, and fine with care. Be meekly and mightily fastened to our Mother Holy Church, for the whole Body was never broken though a single person often is.
